1. Ship the velocity-band sheet as a queue item, or hold it until one of the three current items clears?

# Case Study: Grade 3 MCL Sprain With Meniscal Involvement (Case 4)

**What it is** — Grade 3 MCL sprain with a posterior meniscal tear, direct contact mechanism, AFL - the only contact-mechanism, and only joint (rather than muscle-tendon), case of the four. RTP day 49: eight rehab-running sessions, one partial-training session, four full-training sessions. The athlete was **braced for the first three to four weeks**, and the first run (day 17) was performed in the brace, after indoor running-prep sessions (low-intensity ankle-dominant jumps, dribbles over ankles, A-skips) (~36:52-37:18). Weeks 3-4: three non-consecutive running sessions per week. Week 5: running frequency deliberately reduced to two larger-load sessions to bridge into a bigger planned session at the end of week 6 (a match-load-comparable rehab session preparing for a week 7 return). Week 7: small session early, moderate midweek (matching the team's normal in-season schedule), RTP at week's end.

**Max velocity progression.** Classic linear-then-undulating pattern (as in Cases 1-2): sessions 1-7/8 built linearly; sessions 9-13 onward undulated high-intensity exposures against recovery. **Only one exposure above 90% MV was achieved before return** - Harries says he would have preferred a second, on day 47, but for an unspecified reason the athlete did not hit it that day; he calls the single exposure "conservative" (~38:52-39:07). Example sessions: session 3 - dribbles/mechanics, then two sets of eight 100 m repeats (set 1 at 14-16 km/h, set 2 at 16-18 km/h). Session 5 (still early rehab) - three sets of 400 m repeats progressing speed each set, then two to three 60 m strides at 70-75% - "the first exposure to higher intensity running." Session 7 (levels 4-5) - 60 m strides progressing 70% to 85%, then two 60 m fly runs at 85-88%. Session 10 (return-to-sport phase) - warm-up strides at 70-80%, two 60 m flies at 88-93%, plus one set of the standard 40 m repeat-sprint format under fatigue.

**Straight-line-only constraint and its inconsistency in the source.** Because this was a knee-joint injury requiring brace time, change-of-direction (COD) work was deliberately delayed. The transcript states this constraint two different ways at different points: "sessions one to six was straight line running only" (~41:15-41:22) and, describing MDSA specifically, "sessions one to four, we had no change direction whatsoever" with low-intensity COD introduced starting session 5 (~42:30-43:08). These two statements are not fully reconciled in the source; the most consistent reading is that the broader "straight line only" framing describes the higher-intensity max-velocity running work specifically, while a separate, low-intensity COD introduction (50-60% effort forward/backward ladders and easy lateral shuffles/cuts) began at session 5, distinct from and earlier than any higher-intensity cutting.

**HSR/VHSR/sprint volumes.** Sessions 1-7 showed a linear increase in HSR/VHSR/sprint markers. **Session 4 produced an unplanned HSR overshoot** as the athlete gained confidence running in the brace, mixing 100 m repeats with three-minute intervals - another example of a low HSR threshold inflating totals (see [[heuristic--low-speed-threshold-inflates-hsr-totals]]). Peak VHSR exposure reached 90% of game value; Harries notes a higher dose might have been ideal but the return was "well tolerated nonetheless."

**MDSA.** Session 6: braking/deceleration progressions begin at 50-60% effort (fast-easy-fast accelerations, low-intensity go-and-stop drills, low-intensity controlled cutting over a 30-degree angle: side step, crossover, split step). Session 8: expanded COD intensity and space - braking over 5/10/15 m accelerations into a 3-5 m braking zone at 85-90% effort, partner chase-and-tag (athlete in both offensive and defensive roles), 2v1 attacking squares (small/medium). Session 10 (full-training reintegration): high-velocity reactive cuts (a "wire cut" drill), gate-space work requiring a reaction to a cue followed by a second stimulus (a turnover simulation or a defensive chase/press) - heavy emphasis on reactivity and deceleration tolerance under load.

**Sport-specific skill.** Sessions 1-2: no skill involvement. Session 3: technical skills reintroduced (stationary). Session 5: movement added, minimal COD requirement. Session 6: positional drills with more fatigue. Session 7 onward: small competitive group play (modified handball, 2v3/4v4), emphasizing cognitive demand and decision-making. Week 8: large competitive group play, then return to play.

**Why it works** — This is the framework's clearest demonstration of sequencing pillars independently by constraint: straight-line MV running advanced substantially while COD work was deliberately held back for joint-healing reasons, then COD, reactivity and deceleration tolerance were compressed into a shorter late window once the brace constraint lifted.

**When to apply** — Use as the template for a braced-joint RTP where one locomotor pillar (COD) must lag the others for structural-healing reasons; it shows that lagging one pillar does not require lagging all of them.

**When NOT to apply** — n=1, retrospective, self-reported, with an internal inconsistency in how the COD delay itself is described (noted above) - treat the exact session-number cutoff for "no COD" as approximate, not precise.

**Related** — [[framework--invasion-sport-locomotor-pillars]]; [[heuristic--low-speed-threshold-inflates-hsr-totals]]

# Case Study: Proximal Hamstring Strain, Grade 2 (Case 1)

**What it is** — Grade 2 strain at the musculotendinous junction of biceps femoris and semitendinosus, acute non-contact running mechanism, AFL. Return to play (RTP) day 28: six rehab-running sessions, three partial-training sessions, two full-training sessions (~01:53-02:18, ~04:18-05:04). Days 0-5 off legs (isometrics, low-intensity eccentrics, general strength, running-prep drills); first run day 6; running sessions days 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 17; modified training day 19; full training day 25; RTP day 28.

**Max velocity progression.** Sessions 1-2: basic running-mechanics drills, jog-walk intervals at 8-12 km/h, then 100 m repeats at a time-based pace averaging ~16-20 km/h. Sessions 3-4: 60 m repeats progressing 13 s down to 10.5 s (18-22.5 km/h target). Session 5: strides with an acceleration/maintenance/deceleration structure targeting 70-85% MV. Session 8: continued strides plus higher-intensity flies at 85-92% MV. From session 6 onward, periodization shifted from linear to undulating. **The athlete did not reach above 90% MV before returning to play** - Harries attributes this to external pressure (approaching finals), calling it "an example of... a tension here between the ideal programming and some of the contextual demands" (~06:48-07:09).

**HSR/VHSR/sprint volumes.** Speed thresholds for this dataset: high-speed running (HSR) >17 km/h, very-high-speed running (VHSR) >23 km/h, sprint >27 km/h (~85% max for these athletes) (~09:57-10:17). VHSR peaked at 86% of game value by day 21 ("slightly lower than desired, but still okay"). Sprint-zone exposure was under-dosed: Harries states he wanted closer to 50-60% of game demands and did not get the drill design and execution right to hit it (~10:53-11:04; this passage is somewhat garbled in the transcript and should not be conflated with Case 2's separate 40%-of-game-volume under-dose at its own session 7).

**Multidirectional speed/agility (MDSA).** Session 3: introductory curvilinear/S-bend runs, forward/backward ladders, non-reactive diamond drills (low intensity, fully planned). Session 5: fast-easy-fast accelerations, go-and-stop drills, a closed-reactive compass drill (45-135 degrees at ~75-80% effort), a defensive reaction (mirror) drill. Session 8: higher-velocity crossover cuts and Z-runs at 85-90% effort, extended compass drills (added evasive movement after the cut), 2v1 attacking squares (small to large), modified handball games with obstacles (3v2, three x two-minute efforts with two-minute recovery). From session 10, MDSA was delivered mainly through sport-specific/competitive drills.

**Sport-specific skill.** Sessions 3-5: low-intensity technical actions (stationary kicking/handball), then controlled movement. From session 6: positional-specific drills under fatigue (volume/technical output under load). Sessions 8-10: competitive play in modified small-sided formats (3v2 handball), increasing decision-making demand. Full training at session 10 included large-group competitive play under near-match conditions.

**Why it works** — This is Harries' example of a low-grade injury run against a compressed timeline; every design choice (linear-then-undulating, HSR via short intervals from session 5, sport-skill drills carrying more of the late HSR load) reflects deliberately trading off ideal dosage against a hard return-date constraint.

**When to apply** — Use as the reference case for "the framework applied under real season-timing pressure, with an honestly reported miss." It illustrates that the 90%-MV exit rule and the sprint-volume target are both aspirational floors that can be missed and still result in a tolerated return, not hard gates.

**When NOT to apply** — This is n=1, retrospective and self-reported by the practitioner who ran it; there is no outcome data here beyond "returned to play," no re-injury follow-up window reported, and no independent verification of the %MV or %game-value figures. Do not treat "he returned fine despite missing the sprint target" as evidence that the target doesn't matter.

**Example** — See [[heuristic--two-exposures-above-90-percent-mv-exit-rule]] and [[heuristic--low-speed-threshold-inflates-hsr-totals]] for the general rules this case both illustrates and, in the exit-rule case, misses.

**Related** — [[strength-and-conditioning/fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/principle--watch-them-run-in-sprint-return-to-play]] (suggested reciprocal link: "a same-sport worked RTP timeline with the running-progression numbers this principle argues for filming and comparing, see on-field-rtp--harries"); [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]]

# Case Study: Recurrent Lateral Soleus Strain, Grade 2 (Case 3)

**What it is** — Grade 2 recurrent lateral soleus strain, acute non-contact running incident, AFL. RTP day 44: five rehab-running sessions, one partial-training session, three full-training sessions. **Return to play was deliberately delayed a further week** by the medical/performance team specifically to add training exposure (~26:59-27:28). Twelve days off legs (longer than Cases 1-2); running resumed day 13 after two low-intensity running-prep sessions (days 9, 11). From that point, **running occurred only twice per week** with at least 48 hours (sometimes 72-96 hours) between sessions - a deliberate low-frequency strategy because this athlete had responded well to reduced running frequency in the past, and reduced frequency/weekly load has worked for the club's other recurrent calf injuries (~27:59-28:33).

**Max velocity progression.** Familiar stages (mechanics, 60 m repeats, strides, flies), but periodization was distinct: the first four sessions built linearly, then **from session 4 onward the athlete consistently exceeded 90% MV in every remaining session** - a flat, non-undulating pattern, which Harries attributes simply to the low running frequency giving each session enough inherent recovery spacing. The athlete accumulated **six separate exposures above 90% MV before return - the most of any of the four cases** (~29:03-29:37). Session 1 deliberately used low volume and long recoveries to minimize localized calf fatigue: 60 m repeats limited to four reps per set every 45 seconds, then a couple of 100 m repeats at four reps per set every 60 seconds. Session 4 transitioned to higher intensity: progressive 60 m repeats, 60 m strides, and a single 60 m fly at 88-93% MV. The return-to-sport-phase session (~session 7) used two 60 m strides in the warm-up, three 60 m fly runs building to peak effort, and **one set** (not two, unlike Case 2) of three to four 40 m repeat sprints above 85% MV on a 30-second turnaround.

**HSR/VHSR/sprint volumes.** Sessions 1-3 deliberately held HSR very low (30-40% of match load) and did not progress it, specifically to protect the calf from cumulative loading. Interval durations followed a **short-to-long model** (60 m repeats first, progressing to longer 100 m repeats and 40-60 s intervals) - the opposite sequencing from the hamstring cases' long-to-short approach (see [[heuristic--short-to-long-vs-long-to-short-intervals-by-injury]]). Between sessions 7-9, HSR exposure was deliberately *reduced* to prioritize mechanical (accel/decel/COD) and sport-specific loads instead, once the extended timeline had already banked enough HSR volume. VHSR/sprint built linearly sessions 3-8, reaching 75% of game values on days 30 and 38 (Harries would have preferred 85-100% for more robust preparation).

**MDSA and sport-skill.** Because of the reduced running frequency, "each session entailed a suitable progression" on its own (session = progression step), rather than being spread across many sessions: sessions 2-3 change-of-direction introduction, session 4 low-velocity cutting/accel/decel, session 5 moderate velocity change with closed reactivity (the athlete placed only in the offensive role, matching his real game role), session 6 higher entry velocities and evasion in smaller spaces, sessions 7-9 high-velocity evasive MDSA fully integrated into live team training (no isolated MDSA work needed by session 7). Sport skill followed the standard stationary -> movement -> positional/fatigue -> competitive-play progression, with three high-quality full-training sessions carrying complex tactical demands before return.

**Why it works** — This case demonstrates the framework's structure (levels, intensity/complexity progression) holding while the actual periodization (frequency, undulation, interval length sequencing) was substantially rebuilt around one specific, recurring-injury constraint: minimizing cumulative local fatigue to the calf.

**When to apply** — Use as the template for adapting session frequency and interval sequencing for a *recurrent* soft-tissue injury, not just a first-time strain - see [[heuristic--reduce-frequency-for-recurrent-calf-injury]].

**When NOT to apply** — n=1, retrospective, self-reported. This is also the case with the most conservative constraint (recurrence) and the most extended timeline; its specific frequency/interval choices should not be generalized to a first-time strain of the same tissue.

**Related** — [[heuristic--reduce-frequency-for-recurrent-calf-injury]]; [[heuristic--short-to-long-vs-long-to-short-intervals-by-injury]]; [[heuristic--linear-then-undulating-mv-progression]] (this case is the exception to that default)

# Case Study: Semimembranosus Strain With Adductor Magnus Involvement (Case 2)

**What it is** — Grade 2 strain, classified as "`[classification name unclear]` 2B, proximal hamstring strain with a longitudinal tendon split" (the classification system name is unclear in the audio near ~02:24 and is left unresolved here), acute non-contact running mechanism, AFL. RTP day 30: six rehab-running sessions, two modified-training sessions, three full-training sessions. **The athlete returned to play one week earlier than the medical/performance team's own recommendation** - Harries flags this explicitly as "the real world nature of decision making" (~02:36-02:46).

**Max velocity progression.** Days 0-4 off legs; two non-consecutive running exposures week 1 (days 5, 7); three non-consecutive sessions week 2, increasing intensity/volume. Sessions 1-5: linear increase (mechanics drills, time-based 100 m repeats, then faster 60 m repeats, then strides, then flies). Sessions 6-8: undulating pattern. **Two exposures above 90% MV were achieved before return**: day 22 at 96.7% and day 27 at 92.1% - Harries calls this "a strong application of progressive loading." Session 5 is stated to be functionally identical to Case 1's session 5 (60 m reps building 18-22.5 km/h, then six strides: two at 70-75%, two at 75-80%, two at ~82.5% MV, effort-based and GPS-confirmed), which he says typifies a mid-rehab max-velocity checkpoint around day 10-14 post-injury, with ~85% MV treated as a sound ceiling until force-production and reactive-strength criteria are confirmed. Session 8 (coinciding with return to full training): progressive 60 m strides, three 20 m flies at 85-95% MV, and **repeat sprint intervals**: two sets of three to four reps over 40 m, all above 85% MV, on a 30-second rolling start (rep 1 at 0 s, rep 2 at 30 s, rep 3 at 60 s) - see [[framework--repeat-sprint-interval-format-under-fatigue]].

**HSR/VHSR/sprint volumes.** Same thresholds as Case 1 (17/23/27 km/h). Session 2 produced an unexpected HSR overshoot via 100 m repeats; Harries notes this matters less here because 17 km/h is only ~55-60% of max for these athletes (see [[heuristic--low-speed-threshold-inflates-hsr-totals]]). From session 3, HSR delivered via short-interval formats (10 s on/10 s off, 20 s on/20 s off); from session 8, small-sided games contributed HSR organically. VHSR/sprint built linearly sessions 4-8, but **session 7/day 19 under-dosed at only 40% of game volume** (Harries wanted 70-80%); session 8 then peaked at 120% of game value.

**MDSA.** Sessions 2-3: basic curvilinear runs, linear/lateral shuffling. Session 4: low-velocity cutting, basic accel/decel drills. Sessions 5-6: velocity change graded up, closed reactivity (visual/verbal cues) added. Session 7: higher entry/change velocities, larger spaces, still closed-reactive. Session 8: evasive drills at lower velocities in smaller spaces (deliberately lower isolated-MDSA volume that session, offset by a fortunate scheduling window - the reserves team's bye gave more athletes for higher-quality skill-drill exposure instead). Session 9 onward: high-velocity evasive MDSA in realistic/competitive contexts.

**Sport-specific skill.** Sessions 2-3: low-load stationary handball/short kicking. Sessions 3-4: controlled movement added to technical execution. Sessions 5-6: positional-specific drills with movement fatigue. Sessions 7-8: small-group competitive play (3v3, 5v5 handball). Week 4: large-group competitive play in the main training session before return.

**Why it works** — This case shows the framework producing a well-dosed sprint exposure (two exposures >90% MV, repeat-sprint intervals for fatigue-state sprinting) even while the actual return date was moved up by organizational decision-making outside the physical-readiness plan.

**When to apply** — Use as the reference case for "physical readiness criteria met or exceeded, but the actual return decision still overridden by other factors" - a reminder that meeting the framework's numbers does not by itself control the return-to-play date.

**When NOT to apply** — n=1, retrospective, self-reported; the one-week-early return is presented as a fact of what happened, not validated as safe by any outcome data beyond it being reported without a stated recurrence.

**Example** — See [[framework--repeat-sprint-interval-format-under-fatigue]] for the reusable session-design pattern this case's session 8 exemplifies.

**Related** — [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]]; [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]

# Case Study: Grade 3 MCL Sprain With Meniscal Involvement (Case 4)

**What it is** — Grade 3 MCL sprain with a posterior meniscal tear, direct contact mechanism, AFL - the only contact-mechanism, and only joint (rather than muscle-tendon), case of the four. RTP day 49: eight rehab-running sessions, one partial-training session, four full-training sessions. The athlete was **braced for the first three to four weeks**, and the first run (day 17) was performed in the brace, after indoor running-prep sessions (low-intensity ankle-dominant jumps, dribbles over ankles, A-skips) (~36:52-37:18). Weeks 3-4: three non-consecutive running sessions per week. Week 5: running frequency deliberately reduced to two larger-load sessions to bridge into a bigger planned session at the end of week 6 (a match-load-comparable rehab session preparing for a week 7 return). Week 7: small session early, moderate midweek (matching the team's normal in-season schedule), RTP at week's end.

**Max velocity progression.** Classic linear-then-undulating pattern (as in Cases 1-2): sessions 1-7/8 built linearly; sessions 9-13 onward undulated high-intensity exposures against recovery. **Only one exposure above 90% MV was achieved before return** - Harries says he would have preferred a second, on day 47, but for an unspecified reason the athlete did not hit it that day; he calls the single exposure "conservative" (~38:52-39:07). Example sessions: session 3 - dribbles/mechanics, then two sets of eight 100 m repeats (set 1 at 14-16 km/h, set 2 at 16-18 km/h). Session 5 (still early rehab) - three sets of 400 m repeats progressing speed each set, then two to three 60 m strides at 70-75% - "the first exposure to higher intensity running." Session 7 (levels 4-5) - 60 m strides progressing 70% to 85%, then two 60 m fly runs at 85-88%. Session 10 (return-to-sport phase) - warm-up strides at 70-80%, two 60 m flies at 88-93%, plus one set of the standard 40 m repeat-sprint format under fatigue.

**Straight-line-only constraint and its inconsistency in the source.** Because this was a knee-joint injury requiring brace time, change-of-direction (COD) work was deliberately delayed. The transcript states this constraint two different ways at different points: "sessions one to six was straight line running only" (~41:15-41:22) and, describing MDSA specifically, "sessions one to four, we had no change direction whatsoever" with low-intensity COD introduced starting session 5 (~42:30-43:08). These two statements are not fully reconciled in the source; the most consistent reading is that the broader "straight line only" framing describes the higher-intensity max-velocity running work specifically, while a separate, low-intensity COD introduction (50-60% effort forward/backward ladders and easy lateral shuffles/cuts) began at session 5, distinct from and earlier than any higher-intensity cutting.

**HSR/VHSR/sprint volumes.** Sessions 1-7 showed a linear increase in HSR/VHSR/sprint markers. **Session 4 produced an unplanned HSR overshoot** as the athlete gained confidence running in the brace, mixing 100 m repeats with three-minute intervals - another example of a low HSR threshold inflating totals (see [[heuristic--low-speed-threshold-inflates-hsr-totals]]). Peak VHSR exposure reached 90% of game value; Harries notes a higher dose might have been ideal but the return was "well tolerated nonetheless."

**MDSA.** Session 6: braking/deceleration progressions begin at 50-60% effort (fast-easy-fast accelerations, low-intensity go-and-stop drills, low-intensity controlled cutting over a 30-degree angle: side step, crossover, split step). Session 8: expanded COD intensity and space - braking over 5/10/15 m accelerations into a 3-5 m braking zone at 85-90% effort, partner chase-and-tag (athlete in both offensive and defensive roles), 2v1 attacking squares (small/medium). Session 10 (full-training reintegration): high-velocity reactive cuts (a "wire cut" drill), gate-space work requiring a reaction to a cue followed by a second stimulus (a turnover simulation or a defensive chase/press) - heavy emphasis on reactivity and deceleration tolerance under load.

**Sport-specific skill.** Sessions 1-2: no skill involvement. Session 3: technical skills reintroduced (stationary). Session 5: movement added, minimal COD requirement. Session 6: positional drills with more fatigue. Session 7 onward: small competitive group play (modified handball, 2v3/4v4), emphasizing cognitive demand and decision-making. Week 8: large competitive group play, then return to play.

**Why it works** — This is the framework's clearest demonstration of sequencing pillars independently by constraint: straight-line MV running advanced substantially while COD work was deliberately held back for joint-healing reasons, then COD, reactivity and deceleration tolerance were compressed into a shorter late window once the brace constraint lifted.

**When to apply** — Use as the template for a braced-joint RTP where one locomotor pillar (COD) must lag the others for structural-healing reasons; it shows that lagging one pillar does not require lagging all of them.

**When NOT to apply** — n=1, retrospective, self-reported, with an internal inconsistency in how the COD delay itself is described (noted above) - treat the exact session-number cutoff for "no COD" as approximate, not precise.

# Case Study: Proximal Hamstring Strain, Grade 2 (Case 1)

**What it is** — Grade 2 strain at the musculotendinous junction of biceps femoris and semitendinosus, acute non-contact running mechanism, AFL. Return to play (RTP) day 28: six rehab-running sessions, three partial-training sessions, two full-training sessions (~01:53-02:18, ~04:18-05:04). Days 0-5 off legs (isometrics, low-intensity eccentrics, general strength, running-prep drills); first run day 6; running sessions days 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 17; modified training day 19; full training day 25; RTP day 28.

**Max velocity progression.** Sessions 1-2: basic running-mechanics drills, jog-walk intervals at 8-12 km/h, then 100 m repeats at a time-based pace averaging ~16-20 km/h. Sessions 3-4: 60 m repeats progressing 13 s down to 10.5 s (18-22.5 km/h target). Session 5: strides with an acceleration/maintenance/deceleration structure targeting 70-85% MV. Session 8: continued strides plus higher-intensity flies at 85-92% MV. From session 6 onward, periodization shifted from linear to undulating. **The athlete did not reach above 90% MV before returning to play** - Harries attributes this to external pressure (approaching finals), calling it "an example of... a tension here between the ideal programming and some of the contextual demands" (~06:48-07:09).

**HSR/VHSR/sprint volumes.** Speed thresholds for this dataset: high-speed running (HSR) >17 km/h, very-high-speed running (VHSR) >23 km/h, sprint >27 km/h (~85% max for these athletes) (~09:57-10:17). VHSR peaked at 86% of game value by day 21 ("slightly lower than desired, but still okay"). Sprint-zone exposure was under-dosed: Harries states he wanted closer to 50-60% of game demands and did not get the drill design and execution right to hit it (~10:53-11:04; this passage is somewhat garbled in the transcript and should not be conflated with Case 2's separate 40%-of-game-volume under-dose at its own session 7).

**Multidirectional speed/agility (MDSA).** Session 3: introductory curvilinear/S-bend runs, forward/backward ladders, non-reactive diamond drills (low intensity, fully planned). Session 5: fast-easy-fast accelerations, go-and-stop drills, a closed-reactive compass drill (45-135 degrees at ~75-80% effort), a defensive reaction (mirror) drill. Session 8: higher-velocity crossover cuts and Z-runs at 85-90% effort, extended compass drills (added evasive movement after the cut), 2v1 attacking squares (small to large), modified handball games with obstacles (3v2, three x two-minute efforts with two-minute recovery). From session 10, MDSA was delivered mainly through sport-specific/competitive drills.

**Sport-specific skill.** Sessions 3-5: low-intensity technical actions (stationary kicking/handball), then controlled movement. From session 6: positional-specific drills under fatigue (volume/technical output under load). Sessions 8-10: competitive play in modified small-sided formats (3v2 handball), increasing decision-making demand. Full training at session 10 included large-group competitive play under near-match conditions.

**Why it works** — This is Harries' example of a low-grade injury run against a compressed timeline; every design choice (linear-then-undulating, HSR via short intervals from session 5, sport-skill drills carrying more of the late HSR load) reflects deliberately trading off ideal dosage against a hard return-date constraint.

**When to apply** — Use as the reference case for "the framework applied under real season-timing pressure, with an honestly reported miss." It illustrates that the 90%-MV exit rule and the sprint-volume target are both aspirational floors that can be missed and still result in a tolerated return, not hard gates.

**When NOT to apply** — This is n=1, retrospective and self-reported by the practitioner who ran it; there is no outcome data here beyond "returned to play," no re-injury follow-up window reported, and no independent verification of the %MV or %game-value figures. Do not treat "he returned fine despite missing the sprint target" as evidence that the target doesn't matter.

**Example** — See [[heuristic--two-exposures-above-90-percent-mv-exit-rule]] and [[heuristic--low-speed-threshold-inflates-hsr-totals]] for the general rules this case both illustrates and, in the exit-rule case, misses.

**Related** — [[strength-and-conditioning/fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/principle--watch-them-run-in-sprint-return-to-play]] (suggested reciprocal link: "a same-sport worked RTP timeline with the running-progression numbers this principle argues for filming and comparing, see on-field-rtp--harries"); [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]]

# Case Study: Recurrent Lateral Soleus Strain, Grade 2 (Case 3)

**What it is** — Grade 2 recurrent lateral soleus strain, acute non-contact running incident, AFL. RTP day 44: five rehab-running sessions, one partial-training session, three full-training sessions. **Return to play was deliberately delayed a further week** by the medical/performance team specifically to add training exposure (~26:59-27:28). Twelve days off legs (longer than Cases 1-2); running resumed day 13 after two low-intensity running-prep sessions (days 9, 11). From that point, **running occurred only twice per week** with at least 48 hours (sometimes 72-96 hours) between sessions - a deliberate low-frequency strategy because this athlete had responded well to reduced running frequency in the past, and reduced frequency/weekly load has worked for the club's other recurrent calf injuries (~27:59-28:33).

**Max velocity progression.** Familiar stages (mechanics, 60 m repeats, strides, flies), but periodization was distinct: the first four sessions built linearly, then **from session 4 onward the athlete consistently exceeded 90% MV in every remaining session** - a flat, non-undulating pattern, which Harries attributes simply to the low running frequency giving each session enough inherent recovery spacing. The athlete accumulated **six separate exposures above 90% MV before return - the most of any of the four cases** (~29:03-29:37). Session 1 deliberately used low volume and long recoveries to minimize localized calf fatigue: 60 m repeats limited to four reps per set every 45 seconds, then a couple of 100 m repeats at four reps per set every 60 seconds. Session 4 transitioned to higher intensity: progressive 60 m repeats, 60 m strides, and a single 60 m fly at 88-93% MV. The return-to-sport-phase session (~session 7) used two 60 m strides in the warm-up, three 60 m fly runs building to peak effort, and **one set** (not two, unlike Case 2) of three to four 40 m repeat sprints above 85% MV on a 30-second turnaround.

**HSR/VHSR/sprint volumes.** Sessions 1-3 deliberately held HSR very low (30-40% of match load) and did not progress it, specifically to protect the calf from cumulative loading. Interval durations followed a **short-to-long model** (60 m repeats first, progressing to longer 100 m repeats and 40-60 s intervals) - the opposite sequencing from the hamstring cases' long-to-short approach (see [[heuristic--short-to-long-vs-long-to-short-intervals-by-injury]]). Between sessions 7-9, HSR exposure was deliberately *reduced* to prioritize mechanical (accel/decel/COD) and sport-specific loads instead, once the extended timeline had already banked enough HSR volume. VHSR/sprint built linearly sessions 3-8, reaching 75% of game values on days 30 and 38 (Harries would have preferred 85-100% for more robust preparation).

**MDSA and sport-skill.** Because of the reduced running frequency, "each session entailed a suitable progression" on its own (session = progression step), rather than being spread across many sessions: sessions 2-3 change-of-direction introduction, session 4 low-velocity cutting/accel/decel, session 5 moderate velocity change with closed reactivity (the athlete placed only in the offensive role, matching his real game role), session 6 higher entry velocities and evasion in smaller spaces, sessions 7-9 high-velocity evasive MDSA fully integrated into live team training (no isolated MDSA work needed by session 7). Sport skill followed the standard stationary -> movement -> positional/fatigue -> competitive-play progression, with three high-quality full-training sessions carrying complex tactical demands before return.

**Why it works** — This case demonstrates the framework's structure (levels, intensity/complexity progression) holding while the actual periodization (frequency, undulation, interval length sequencing) was substantially rebuilt around one specific, recurring-injury constraint: minimizing cumulative local fatigue to the calf.

**When to apply** — Use as the template for adapting session frequency and interval sequencing for a *recurrent* soft-tissue injury, not just a first-time strain - see [[heuristic--reduce-frequency-for-recurrent-calf-injury]].

**When NOT to apply** — n=1, retrospective, self-reported. This is also the case with the most conservative constraint (recurrence) and the most extended timeline; its specific frequency/interval choices should not be generalized to a first-time strain of the same tissue.

**Related** — [[heuristic--reduce-frequency-for-recurrent-calf-injury]]; [[heuristic--short-to-long-vs-long-to-short-intervals-by-injury]]; [[heuristic--linear-then-undulating-mv-progression]] (this case is the exception to that default)

# Case Study: Semimembranosus Strain With Adductor Magnus Involvement (Case 2)

**What it is** — Grade 2 strain, classified as "`[classification name unclear]` 2B, proximal hamstring strain with a longitudinal tendon split" (the classification system name is unclear in the audio near ~02:24 and is left unresolved here), acute non-contact running mechanism, AFL. RTP day 30: six rehab-running sessions, two modified-training sessions, three full-training sessions. **The athlete returned to play one week earlier than the medical/performance team's own recommendation** - Harries flags this explicitly as "the real world nature of decision making" (~02:36-02:46).

**Max velocity progression.** Days 0-4 off legs; two non-consecutive running exposures week 1 (days 5, 7); three non-consecutive sessions week 2, increasing intensity/volume. Sessions 1-5: linear increase (mechanics drills, time-based 100 m repeats, then faster 60 m repeats, then strides, then flies). Sessions 6-8: undulating pattern. **Two exposures above 90% MV were achieved before return**: day 22 at 96.7% and day 27 at 92.1% - Harries calls this "a strong application of progressive loading." Session 5 is stated to be functionally identical to Case 1's session 5 (60 m reps building 18-22.5 km/h, then six strides: two at 70-75%, two at 75-80%, two at ~82.5% MV, effort-based and GPS-confirmed), which he says typifies a mid-rehab max-velocity checkpoint around day 10-14 post-injury, with ~85% MV treated as a sound ceiling until force-production and reactive-strength criteria are confirmed. Session 8 (coinciding with return to full training): progressive 60 m strides, three 20 m flies at 85-95% MV, and **repeat sprint intervals**: two sets of three to four reps over 40 m, all above 85% MV, on a 30-second rolling start (rep 1 at 0 s, rep 2 at 30 s, rep 3 at 60 s) - see [[framework--repeat-sprint-interval-format-under-fatigue]].

**HSR/VHSR/sprint volumes.** Same thresholds as Case 1 (17/23/27 km/h). Session 2 produced an unexpected HSR overshoot via 100 m repeats; Harries notes this matters less here because 17 km/h is only ~55-60% of max for these athletes (see [[heuristic--low-speed-threshold-inflates-hsr-totals]]). From session 3, HSR delivered via short-interval formats (10 s on/10 s off, 20 s on/20 s off); from session 8, small-sided games contributed HSR organically. VHSR/sprint built linearly sessions 4-8, but **session 7/day 19 under-dosed at only 40% of game volume** (Harries wanted 70-80%); session 8 then peaked at 120% of game value.

**MDSA.** Sessions 2-3: basic curvilinear runs, linear/lateral shuffling. Session 4: low-velocity cutting, basic accel/decel drills. Sessions 5-6: velocity change graded up, closed reactivity (visual/verbal cues) added. Session 7: higher entry/change velocities, larger spaces, still closed-reactive. Session 8: evasive drills at lower velocities in smaller spaces (deliberately lower isolated-MDSA volume that session, offset by a fortunate scheduling window - the reserves team's bye gave more athletes for higher-quality skill-drill exposure instead). Session 9 onward: high-velocity evasive MDSA in realistic/competitive contexts.

**Sport-specific skill.** Sessions 2-3: low-load stationary handball/short kicking. Sessions 3-4: controlled movement added to technical execution. Sessions 5-6: positional-specific drills with movement fatigue. Sessions 7-8: small-group competitive play (3v3, 5v5 handball). Week 4: large-group competitive play in the main training session before return.

**Why it works** — This case shows the framework producing a well-dosed sprint exposure (two exposures >90% MV, repeat-sprint intervals for fatigue-state sprinting) even while the actual return date was moved up by organizational decision-making outside the physical-readiness plan.

**When to apply** — Use as the reference case for "physical readiness criteria met or exceeded, but the actual return decision still overridden by other factors" - a reminder that meeting the framework's numbers does not by itself control the return-to-play date.

**When NOT to apply** — n=1, retrospective, self-reported; the one-week-early return is presented as a fact of what happened, not validated as safe by any outcome data beyond it being reported without a stated recurrence.

**Example** — See [[framework--repeat-sprint-interval-format-under-fatigue]] for the reusable session-design pattern this case's session 8 exemplifies.

# Speed Gains Shift From Ankle-Dominant to Hip-Dominant

**What it is** — Harries claims that the mechanism by which an athlete increases running speed changes as speed rises. From slow jogging to moderate running speeds (~6-7 m/s), speed is gained mainly by increasing stride length, which he calls "typically an ankle-dominant strategy." Once an athlete reaches moderate speeds where a striding pattern emerges, further speed increases come mainly from increasing stride frequency, which he calls "typically a more hip-dominant strategy" (~02:35-03:19). He states this has direct rehab implications: tailor drill selection toward ankle-loading tasks for calf/Achilles/ankle injuries at lower speeds, and toward hip-loading tasks for hip-region injuries as speed approaches striding/sprinting.

**Why it works** — No mechanism or citation is given beyond the assertion itself; it reads as an established coaching heuristic in sprint biomechanics circles (stride length increases dominate early acceleration, stride frequency and ground-contact mechanics dominate near top speed) but Harries presents it as fact without evidence.

**When to apply** — Use it as a reason to sequence drill emphasis by injury site: for an ankle/Achilles/calf injury, prioritize competency in the lower-speed, longer-ground-contact, ankle-loaded phases (jogging, running) before pushing toward striding; for a hip-region injury (adductor, proximal hamstring), be more cautious as speed approaches the striding-to-sprinting transition where hip-dominant, higher-frequency mechanics take over.

**When NOT to apply** — This is stated as fact, not tested against Baylor's own case data or cited to a specific biomechanics source in the course, and the ankle/hip split is almost certainly an oversimplification: sprint mechanics research shows both joints contribute throughout, with relative contribution shifting gradually rather than switching at a discrete speed. Do not use this as a precise cutoff for clearing an athlete to a given speed based on which joint "took over"; use it only as a soft prioritization heuristic, and verify any specific injury-tailoring decision against the athlete's own force-plate and Nordic/Iso Seated Calf data rather than this claim alone.

**Example** — A returning athlete with an Achilles repair would spend more deliberate time in ankle-loaded dribble/A-skip preparatory drills (see [[framework--running-prep-drill-menu]]) before advancing toward the striding-pattern band (~75-85% MV) where hip-dominant mechanics become more prominent, per this claim.

# 17 km/h ≈ 55-60% MV, 27 km/h ≈ 85% MV, For This AFL Cohort

**What it is** — Harries states the organization's fixed GPS speed-zone cutoffs converted, for these athletes, to roughly: high-speed running threshold (17 km/h) ≈ 55-60% of max velocity; sprint threshold (27 km/h) ≈ 85% of max velocity "for most of our athletes at that club" (~09:57-10:17, ~22:54-23:11). Very-high-speed running (23 km/h) sits between the two, roughly 70% MV by the same logic, though he does not state that conversion explicitly.

**Why it works** — This is a cohort-average conversion, presented as an observed fact about this specific group of AFL athletes' typical max velocities relative to the club's fixed absolute speed zones, not a derived or universal formula.

**When to apply** — Use as a worked example of *how* to convert an absolute GPS speed threshold into a %MV figure for a given population, and as the reason a fixed km/h threshold behaves differently across athletes with different MVs (see [[heuristic--low-speed-threshold-inflates-hsr-totals]]).

**When NOT to apply** — This conversion is specific to Harries' AFL cohort's own average max velocities; it should not be applied to Baylor football athletes, whose MV distribution (and therefore the %MV a given km/h threshold represents) will differ by sport and very likely by position. Baylor's own speed-zone thresholds are not yet position-specific (`method-baseline.md`), so the correct move is to compute the equivalent conversion from Baylor's own Catapult MV data per player or position group, not to reuse these percentages.

**Example** — A Baylor GPS threshold set generically at, say, 16 km/h for "high-speed running" would represent a very different %MV for a 30 km/h-MV wide receiver than for a 24 km/h-MV offensive lineman; this claim is the reminder to check that conversion per player/position rather than assume it.

# Broken-Stride Timing: Time Only the Middle Phase

**What it is** — Once an athlete progresses beyond ~70-75% of MV, Harries moves from full-distance timed repeats to a "broken stride": a run divided into an acceleration phase, a speed-maintenance phase and a deceleration phase, e.g. 60 m split into 20 m / 20 m / 20 m (adjustable, e.g. 15/10/15 to demand a more aggressive acceleration into the same target speed) (~17:01-18:20). Critically, he times only the middle (speed-maintenance) phase, not the whole distance, because that isolates the actual target speed from the acceleration and deceleration mechanics around it. Worked example: hitting 2.88-3.0 seconds across the middle phase equates to ~24-25 km/h, which is ~70-75% of that athlete's MV (~18:29-18:51); the next progression steps require 2.77-2.88 seconds through the same phase, pushing speed up roughly 1 km/h more. He prefers a stopwatch for immediate feedback, using GPS/video as a secondary confirmation of peak velocity, not the primary control method (~18:51-19:17).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: timing the whole distance conflates three different physical demands (accelerating, holding speed, decelerating) into one number, so it can't precisely control what speed was actually reached in the middle. Isolating and timing only the maintenance phase gives a direct, controllable readout of the target velocity, and lets the acceleration/deceleration phase lengths be manipulated independently to change the aggressiveness of the accel or decel without changing the target maintenance speed.

**When to apply** — Use for on-field rehab levels roughly 2 through 5, once an athlete is working above ~70-75% MV, as the standard method for prescribing and verifying max-velocity exposures. At later levels, continue shortening the acceleration-phase distance (while keeping the target maintenance speed) to increase acceleration magnitude, and build in fatiguing conditions before high-%MV maintenance-phase reps.

**When NOT to apply** — Harries explicitly becomes "far less rigid" with these time targets in later rehab stages, adding a percentage-bandwidth range instead of a single time, because forcing a fixed time can push an athlete faster than they are comfortable with or unnecessarily hold them back; he pairs each rep with a conversation (how did that feel, are you comfortable) rather than treating the stopwatch number as absolute (~20:17-20:48). # Intensity and Complexity as Two Independent Axes

**What it is** — Harries frames on-field rehab progression along two separate continuums that must both be advanced but do not have to move together. **Intensity** runs from a competency focus (reintroducing movements, building toward submaximal) to a capacity focus (submaximal through maximal, under added metabolic/mechanical demand). **Complexity** runs along what he explicitly credits as Matt Taberner's control-to-chaos continuum: control means high structure, predictable behavior/actions/movement (low risk); chaos means unpredictable, random or reactive behavior (high risk) (~04:48-08:00). Early on-field rehab levels are low-complexity and highly controlled; later levels deliberately build unpredictability. The **explicit misconception he corrects**: moving to a later on-field rehab level does not mean every drill in that level becomes more chaotic. Some locomotor actions are still climbing the intensity continuum (submaximal to maximal) and need a controlled environment even at a late stage, while other, already-developed actions can be pushed into more complex environments sooner (~08:44-09:47). By the end of on-field rehab, the target is both high intensity and high complexity simultaneously.

**Why it works** — Treating intensity and complexity as one variable causes two failure modes: pushing speed and unpredictability up together (risking a reload injury before the athlete can handle either alone), or holding both down together (leaving the athlete underprepared for the chaos of competition even though physically capable). Separating them lets a practitioner grade each independently and combine them deliberately only when both are ready.

**When to apply** — Use this distinction explicitly with Athletic Medicine and coaching staff: "he's ready for near-max speed but not yet ready for it in an unpredictable drill" is a defensible, gradeable statement under this framework, whereas "he's at level 4" alone is not. Baylor's own control-chaos foundation is Taberner's own published work already in the library (see Related) - Harries adds nothing new to the theory here; his contribution is packaging it with the specific %MV numbers (see [[framework--on-field-rehab-levels-with-mv-bands]]).

**When NOT to apply** — The complexity axis as Harries operationalizes it rests on an older, information-processing model of motor learning (blocked-to-serial-to-random practice, described in Part 5; see [[framework--practice-structure-block-serial-random-by-level]]), not on ecological dynamics/representative learning design. His example of "closed reactivity" is a coach throwing a hand signal - a generic, arbitrary stimulus, not the game-relevant information a player actually reads (a defender's hips, a gap opening). He names "constraints-based learning design" once, in this same module, and never operationalizes it. In this model, complexity is switched on once intensity is judged safe; in an ecological model, representative information should be present and scaled from the start, not withheld until Level 4. This is a genuine theoretical gap, flagged here as **contested** against the library's ecological-dynamics sources, not a reason to discard the intensity/complexity distinction itself, which still holds.

**Example** — A hamstring athlete at 82% max velocity with force benchmarks not yet cleared should still run in a controlled, closed environment even if his skill work has already moved to a positional, semi-random drill; conversely, an athlete cleared on force benchmarks but still hesitant in decision-making needs complexity pushed even at a plateaued running intensity.

**Related** — [[research-papers/taberner-2022-contextual-considerations-using-the-control-chaos-continuum-for-return-to-sport-in-elite-f]] (Taberner's own control-chaos continuum, the framework Harries is built on: suggested reciprocal link, "applied and re-dosed by a Sportsmith practitioner course, see on-field-rtp--harries"); [[research-papers/taberner-2019-physical-preparation-and-return-to-sport-of-the-football-player-with-a-tibia-fibula-fractu]]; [[skill-acquisition/enhancing-skill--myszka/framework--nonlinear-pedagogy-and-constraint-classes]] and [[skill-acquisition/enhancing-skill--myszka/principle--representative-design]] (the ecological-dynamics alternative to Harries' complexity operationalization); [[framework--practice-structure-block-serial-random-by-level]]

# Speed Gains Shift From Ankle-Dominant to Hip-Dominant

**What it is** — Harries claims that the mechanism by which an athlete increases running speed changes as speed rises. From slow jogging to moderate running speeds (~6-7 m/s), speed is gained mainly by increasing stride length, which he calls "typically an ankle-dominant strategy." Once an athlete reaches moderate speeds where a striding pattern emerges, further speed increases come mainly from increasing stride frequency, which he calls "typically a more hip-dominant strategy" (~02:35-03:19). He states this has direct rehab implications: tailor drill selection toward ankle-loading tasks for calf/Achilles/ankle injuries at lower speeds, and toward hip-loading tasks for hip-region injuries as speed approaches striding/sprinting.

**Why it works** — No mechanism or citation is given beyond the assertion itself; it reads as an established coaching heuristic in sprint biomechanics circles (stride length increases dominate early acceleration, stride frequency and ground-contact mechanics dominate near top speed) but Harries presents it as fact without evidence.

**When to apply** — Use it as a reason to sequence drill emphasis by injury site: for an ankle/Achilles/calf injury, prioritize competency in the lower-speed, longer-ground-contact, ankle-loaded phases (jogging, running) before pushing toward striding; for a hip-region injury (adductor, proximal hamstring), be more cautious as speed approaches the striding-to-sprinting transition where hip-dominant, higher-frequency mechanics take over.

**When NOT to apply** — This is stated as fact, not tested against Baylor's own case data or cited to a specific biomechanics source in the course, and the ankle/hip split is almost certainly an oversimplification: sprint mechanics research shows both joints contribute throughout, with relative contribution shifting gradually rather than switching at a discrete speed. Do not use this as a precise cutoff for clearing an athlete to a given speed based on which joint "took over"; use it only as a soft prioritization heuristic, and verify any specific injury-tailoring decision against the athlete's own force-plate and Nordic/Iso Seated Calf data rather than this claim alone.

**Example** — A returning athlete with an Achilles repair would spend more deliberate time in ankle-loaded dribble/A-skip preparatory drills (see [[framework--running-prep-drill-menu]]) before advancing toward the striding-pattern band (~75-85% MV) where hip-dominant mechanics become more prominent, per this claim.

# Broken-Stride Timing: Time Only the Middle Phase

**What it is** — Once an athlete progresses beyond ~70-75% of MV, Harries moves from full-distance timed repeats to a "broken stride": a run divided into an acceleration phase, a speed-maintenance phase and a deceleration phase, e.g. 60 m split into 20 m / 20 m / 20 m (adjustable, e.g. 15/10/15 to demand a more aggressive acceleration into the same target speed) (~17:01-18:20). Critically, he times only the middle (speed-maintenance) phase, not the whole distance, because that isolates the actual target speed from the acceleration and deceleration mechanics around it. Worked example: hitting 2.88-3.0 seconds across the middle phase equates to ~24-25 km/h, which is ~70-75% of that athlete's MV (~18:29-18:51); the next progression steps require 2.77-2.88 seconds through the same phase, pushing speed up roughly 1 km/h more. He prefers a stopwatch for immediate feedback, using GPS/video as a secondary confirmation of peak velocity, not the primary control method (~18:51-19:17).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: timing the whole distance conflates three different physical demands (accelerating, holding speed, decelerating) into one number, so it can't precisely control what speed was actually reached in the middle. Isolating and timing only the maintenance phase gives a direct, controllable readout of the target velocity, and lets the acceleration/deceleration phase lengths be manipulated independently to change the aggressiveness of the accel or decel without changing the target maintenance speed.

**When to apply** — Use for on-field rehab levels roughly 2 through 5, once an athlete is working above ~70-75% MV, as the standard method for prescribing and verifying max-velocity exposures. At later levels, continue shortening the acceleration-phase distance (while keeping the target maintenance speed) to increase acceleration magnitude, and build in fatiguing conditions before high-%MV maintenance-phase reps.

**When NOT to apply** — Harries explicitly becomes "far less rigid" with these time targets in later rehab stages, adding a percentage-bandwidth range instead of a single time, because forcing a fixed time can push an athlete faster than they are comfortable with or unnecessarily hold them back; he pairs each rep with a conversation (how did that feel, are you comfortable) rather than treating the stopwatch number as absolute (~20:17-20:48). Do not apply this as a rigid pass/fail number in late-stage rehab without that check-in.

**When to apply** — Use this as the design method for building a Baylor-specific drill library (per level, per pillar): rather than copying Harries' AFL drill menu directly, run each candidate drill (including a proposed contact/collision drill for football) through this same plotting exercise using Baylor's own constraint vocabulary.

**When NOT to apply** — This tool depends on practitioner judgment for where a drill sits on each axis; it produces a defensible visual, not an objectively validated coordinate. Do not treat the resulting chart placement as more precise than the judgment calls that produced it.

**Example** — [[framework--mdsa-drill-menu-by-level]] is the output of running this exercise for Harries' own case-study drills.

# Intensity and Complexity as Two Independent Axes

**What it is** — Harries frames on-field rehab progression along two separate continuums that must both be advanced but do not have to move together. **Intensity** runs from a competency focus (reintroducing movements, building toward submaximal) to a capacity focus (submaximal through maximal, under added metabolic/mechanical demand). **Complexity** runs along what he explicitly credits as Matt Taberner's control-to-chaos continuum: control means high structure, predictable behavior/actions/movement (low risk); chaos means unpredictable, random or reactive behavior (high risk) (~04:48-08:00). Early on-field rehab levels are low-complexity and highly controlled; later levels deliberately build unpredictability. The **explicit misconception he corrects**: moving to a later on-field rehab level does not mean every drill in that level becomes more chaotic. Some locomotor actions are still climbing the intensity continuum (submaximal to maximal) and need a controlled environment even at a late stage, while other, already-developed actions can be pushed into more complex environments sooner (~08:44-09:47). By the end of on-field rehab, the target is both high intensity and high complexity simultaneously.

**Why it works** — Treating intensity and complexity as one variable causes two failure modes: pushing speed and unpredictability up together (risking a reload injury before the athlete can handle either alone), or holding both down together (leaving the athlete underprepared for the chaos of competition even though physically capable). Separating them lets a practitioner grade each independently and combine them deliberately only when both are ready.

**When to apply** — Use this distinction explicitly with Athletic Medicine and coaching staff: "he's ready for near-max speed but not yet ready for it in an unpredictable drill" is a defensible, gradeable statement under this framework, whereas "he's at level 4" alone is not. Baylor's own control-chaos foundation is Taberner's own published work already in the library (see Related) - Harries adds nothing new to the theory here; his contribution is packaging it with the specific %MV numbers (see [[framework--on-field-rehab-levels-with-mv-bands]]).

**When NOT to apply** — The complexity axis as Harries operationalizes it rests on an older, information-processing model of motor learning (blocked-to-serial-to-random practice, described in Part 5; see [[framework--practice-structure-block-serial-random-by-level]]), not on ecological dynamics/representative learning design. His example of "closed reactivity" is a coach throwing a hand signal - a generic, arbitrary stimulus, not the game-relevant information a player actually reads (a defender's hips, a gap opening). He names "constraints-based learning design" once, in this same module, and never operationalizes it. In this model, complexity is switched on once intensity is judged safe; in an ecological model, representative information should be present and scaled from the start, not withheld until Level 4. This is a genuine theoretical gap, flagged here as **contested** against the library's ecological-dynamics sources, not a reason to discard the intensity/complexity distinction itself, which still holds.

**Example** — A hamstring athlete at 82% max velocity with force benchmarks not yet cleared should still run in a controlled, closed environment even if his skill work has already moved to a positional, semi-random drill; conversely, an athlete cleared on force benchmarks but still hesitant in decision-making needs complexity pushed even at a plateaued running intensity.

**Related** — [[research-papers/taberner-2022-contextual-considerations-using-the-control-chaos-continuum-for-return-to-sport-in-elite-f]] (Taberner's own control-chaos continuum, the framework Harries is built on: suggested reciprocal link, "applied and re-dosed by a Sportsmith practitioner course, see on-field-rtp--harries"); [[research-papers/taberner-2019-physical-preparation-and-return-to-sport-of-the-football-player-with-a-tibia-fibula-fractu]]; [[skill-acquisition/enhancing-skill--myszka/framework--nonlinear-pedagogy-and-constraint-classes]] and [[skill-acquisition/enhancing-skill--myszka/principle--representative-design]] (the ecological-dynamics alternative to Harries' complexity operationalization); [[framework--practice-structure-block-serial-random-by-level]]

# Invasion-Sport Locomotor Pillars

**What it is** — Harries' starting point for building any on-field rehab process: map a sport's technical, tactical and physical domains, then simplify by using what invasion-based team sports (football, soccer, rugby, AFL) have in common. Every invasion sport reduces to two tactical patterns, offense (creating space: pressing forward, overlapping, running into space; technically: moving/passing/catching the ball) and defense (closing space: covering, retreating, closing down; technically: tackling, intercepting, contesting possession) (~03:33-06:46). Underneath both are the same physical actions: sprinting, accelerating, decelerating and changing direction. He names these four as the **primary locomotor pillars of on-field rehab**, usable as a starting template "to any rehab running framework you create" regardless of sport (~07:41-08:22).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: the exact loading numbers differ by sport, but the actual locomotor actions "don't change too much" across invasion sports, so building a rehab framework around them is a transferable shortcut instead of having to model every sport's full technical/tactical catalogue from scratch (~07:19-07:41).

**When to apply** — Use as the skeleton for any Baylor RTP conversation with Athletic Medicine: whatever the sport or position, the questions are the same four - can this athlete sprint, accelerate, decelerate and change direction at the required intensity, in an environment as complex as competition. It gives Applied Performance and Athletic Medicine a shared, sport-agnostic starting vocabulary before adding position-specific detail (GPS zones, skill demands).

**When NOT to apply** — Harries' own case-study sport is AFL, an unusually continuous, low-collision invasion game. Two gaps matter for Baylor football specifically: (1) **contact is missing as a pillar.** Tackling appears once, as a single word, never developed into its own progression. For football, collision and contact (block, shed, tackle, hand-fight, stance start) functions as a fourth pillar with its own dosage question, and this course gives it none. (2) The four pillars are a taxonomy of locomotor actions, not a testing or clearance protocol; they tell you what to progress, not how much force production or healing time is required before progressing it (see [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]] for that layer). Do not treat "the four pillars are covered" as equivalent to "the athlete is ready."

**Example** — A returning offensive lineman needs sprint/accel/decel/COD rebuilt like any other position, but the highest-risk gap in his return is a pillar this course never names: reintroducing collision tolerance. That has to be built separately, in coordination with position coaching, not inferred from his running progression.

**Related** — [[framework--on-field-rehab-levels-with-mv-bands]] (how the levels operationalize these pillars); Baylor's own documented gap that GPS/load thresholds are not yet sport- or position-specific (`method-baseline.md`, Load monitoring and GPS).

# Multidirectional Speed & Agility Drill Menu by On-Field Rehab Level

**What it is** — Harries' worked drill menu for the hamstring case study, by level (~11:56-21:11; confirmed Part-4.pdf p.3):
- **Levels 1-2** (low intensity, low complexity, block practice): fast-easy-fast accelerations (accelerate ~5 m, ease off, re-accelerate); go-and-stop accelerations (accelerate a set distance, brake to a stop in a deceleration zone); curvy-linear ("half bend") accelerations; 30-degree cutting gates with a pre-planned side step, crossover step, or split step; a 3x3 m diamond/square drill with athlete-chosen lateral/forward/backward shuffling.
- **Level 3** (rising velocity/space, controlled/closed reactivity introduced): fast-easy-fast acceleration with a closed-reactive defender (defender moves laterally to open space); a defensive reaction (mirror) drill in a small square; a "compass drill" with pre-determined or reactive 45/90/135-degree direction changes at ~75-80% effort, cued by a hand signal.
- **Level 4** (near-maximal velocity ~80-85%, bigger spaces, more open reactivity): partner chase-and-tag; a large-space gate drill with a turnover cue requiring a hard deceleration and chase; a reactive compass drill in a bigger space followed by a second reactive task (react to a rolled ball).
- **Level 5** (highly chaotic, near-maximal/maximal): sport-specific, competitive, multi-athlete scenarios; where extra players/coaches aren't available, use constrained drills designed to replicate unpredictability as closely as possible.

**Why it works** — Each level's drills are the concrete output of running the levers in [[framework--eight-intensity-levers-mdsa]] through the plotting exercise in [[framework--intensity-complexity-drill-plotting-tool]]: space shrinks or grows, reactivity moves from none to closed to open, and entry velocity/COD angle both rise, in a sequence matched to the level's target physical readiness.

**When to apply** — Use this menu as a starting drill bank for building a Baylor-specific version; the drill *shapes* (accelerate-then-react, gated cutting, chase-and-tag, compass drill) transfer across sports even where the specific angles or spaces would be adjusted for football positions.

**When NOT to apply** — This is one practitioner's AFL menu, built for an athlete with no contact restriction; none of these drills involve or prepare for a blocking, tackling or hand-fighting demand, so a football-specific menu needs an added contact-drill category this course does not supply (see [[framework--invasion-sport-locomotor-pillars]]). The "reactivity" drills here are also limited to hand signals and mirrored defenders, not genuine game-representative cues (see [[heuristic--closed-vs-open-reactivity-drill-design]]).

**Example** — In [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]], sessions 3, 5 and 8 map closely onto this Level 1-3 / Level 3-4 / Level 4-5 menu progression.

**Related** — [[framework--eight-intensity-levers-mdsa]]; [[heuristic--closed-vs-open-reactivity-drill-design]]

# The Five On-Field Rehab Levels, With Max-Velocity Bands

**What it is** — Harries splits on-field rehab into five levels, aligned to early/mid/late rehab, followed by return-to-training and return-to-play (Part 2, ~02:54-04:16). Each level targets a max-velocity (MV) band for linear running (Part 3, ~08:39-09:14; confirmed Part-3.pdf p.2):

| Level | Target % of max velocity |
|---|---|
| 1 | ~50-70% |
| 2 | ~70-75% |
| 3 | ~75-85% |
| 4 | ~85-95% |
| 5 | >95% up to 100% |

For his illustrative low-grade hamstring case, this maps to one session per level (sessions 1-5), then two return-to-training sessions (sessions 6-7) with the team, then return to play as session 8 (~03:30-04:16). He is explicit this is a minor-injury example: "with a more severe injury or different type of injury... you may do a number of sessions in each level before moving on."

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: splitting rehab into named levels gives structure to the gradual stressing of sport-specific locomotor actions, aligned to where the athlete sits in the overall rehab (gym-based early, on-field mid, transition-to-training late).

**When to apply** — Use the five-level structure as the shared vocabulary between Applied Performance and Athletic Medicine: "Level 3" means a defined, measurable thing (75-85% of *that athlete's own* MV, from the Catapult pipeline), not a vague stage description. The number of sessions per level is explicitly not fixed by the framework and should scale with injury severity and history (see [[principle--framework-is-a-guide-not-a-protocol]]).

**When NOT to apply** — The MV bands are Harries' own teaching example and expert-opinion breakpoints, not derived from trial data; he presents no evidence citation for why the boundaries sit at exactly 70/75/85/95%. They are AFL-cohort numbers (based on GPS-derived %MV for the sport). Football's per-position sprint demands are different from AFL's continuous locomotor profile, so the level *structure* (five stages, submax-to-max) transfers, but the specific %MV/km-h breakpoints should be checked against Baylor's own GPS data per position before being treated as a Baylor standard, and Baylor's data dictionary does not yet have position-specific thresholds built (`method-baseline.md`, Load monitoring and GPS section notes this as unfinished work).

**Example** — See [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]] for a real (non-illustrative) case where this level structure was applied but the athlete never reached the desired >90% exposure due to external season-timing pressure - the levels held, the ideal endpoint did not.

**Related** — [[framework--invasion-sport-locomotor-pillars]]; [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]] (the criteria for crossing Level 2 into Level 3); [[heuristic--two-exposures-above-90-percent-mv-exit-rule]] (the Level 5 exit criterion)

# Block, Then Serial, Then Random Practice Across the Levels

**What it is** — Harries maps sport-specific skill drills onto a practice-structure continuum borrowed from motor-learning theory: **block practice** (the same drill repeated, low variability), **serial practice** (a known sequence of actions, predictable order), and **random practice** (unpredictable, variable order/decisions). He assigns these across levels (~04:03-07:26, confirmed Part-5.pdf p.2): Level 1 - solely block, tightly controlled; Level 2 - still block, intensity of the drills rises; Level 3 - roughly 50/50 block and serial, chaining action sequences; Level 4 - block dropped entirely, mostly serial with some random; Level 5 - substantial random practice, with some serial retained deliberately for actions not yet ready for full unpredictability. On return to training, levels 1-2 of training itself are "pretty much all" random.

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: block-to-serial-to-random is a graded route from fully predictable to fully unpredictable practice, which lets an athlete build a skill under low cognitive/decision load first and only add decision-making demand once the movement itself is competent.

**When to apply** — Use the general shape (predictable early, unpredictable late) as the practice-structure axis alongside drill type and movement level (see [[framework--sport-skill-drill-type-continuum-by-level]]) when designing sport-specific skill sessions.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested.** Block/serial/random and its associated "contextual interference effect" come from the Schmidt information-processing tradition of motor learning, not from ecological dynamics/representative learning design, which the library's skill-acquisition sources treat as the better-supported model for sport skill transfer. The practical difference matters: under an information-processing view, predictability itself is the variable being controlled, and the task's informational content is secondary; under an ecological view, the key variable is whether the *information* driving the action is representative of the game (a real defender, a real developing gap) regardless of how "predictable" the drill's structure is. A block-practice drill against a live, representative defender can be more transferable than a "random" drill built on arbitrary, non-representative cues. Do not assume moving along this block-serial-random axis is equivalent to moving toward game transfer; check whether the *information* in the drill, not just its unpredictability, is representative.

**Example** — Harries' own hamstring case study at Level 1 uses stationary, block-practiced kicking with the uninjured limb only (see [[principle--tailor-skill-restrictions-to-injured-structure]]); by Level 5 it moves to a 2v1 attacking-squares game, which is "random" in his sense but still uses arbitrary defender constraints rather than a fully representative game defense.

**Related** — [[skill-acquisition/enhancing-skill--myszka/framework--newell-interacting-constraints]] and [[skill-acquisition/enhancing-skill--myszka/framework--nonlinear-pedagogy-and-constraint-classes]] (suggested reciprocal link: "a practitioner RTP course whose practice-structure continuum this framework's representative-design view supersedes, see on-field-rtp--harries"); [[heuristic--closed-vs-open-reactivity-drill-design]]; [[framework--intensity-complexity-two-independent-axes]]

# Repeat-Sprint Interval Format for Late-Stage Fatigue Exposure

**What it is** — In the back half of late-rehab sessions, Harries introduces repeat-sprint intervals to expose the athlete to high velocity under fatigue and simulate conditioning demand alongside sprint load. The format, used across three of the four case studies: **1-2 sets of three to four repetitions over 40 m, all above 85% MV, on a 30-second rolling start** (rep 1 at 0 s, rep 2 at 30 s, rep 3 at 60 s, etc.). Case 2 used **two sets**; Cases 3 and 4 used **one set** (~21:23-21:59, ~30:49-30:58, ~40:14-40:23).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: placing these in the back half of the session, after other running/skill work has already introduced some fatigue, "blends" high-speed exposure with a controlled recovery interval, giving both a sprint-load-accumulation stimulus and a conditioning stimulus at once, and rehearses producing near-maximal velocity in a fatigued state closer to what a game actually demands late in a match.

**When to apply** — Use in the return-to-sport-phase session(s), once an athlete has already cleared the 75-85% MV gate and is accumulating >90% MV exposures elsewhere in the session (see [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]] and [[heuristic--two-exposures-above-90-percent-mv-exit-rule]]). Scale the number of sets (one vs two) to the athlete's overall session load and injury type - the lower-frequency recurrent-calf case ([[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]) used only one set.

**When NOT to apply** — This is placed deliberately late in rehab, after force-production benchmarks are already cleared; it should not be used as an early-rehab or pre-gate exposure, since it combines near-maximal velocity with accumulated fatigue, precisely the combination the earlier gate criteria are designed to screen for readiness against.

**Example** — See [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]] session 8 for the two-set version and [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]] session 10 for the one-set version used alongside a knee-joint injury.

# Running Gait Speed Categories

**What it is** — Harries defines a shared vocabulary for running speed categories, each with a km/h range and a %MV range (~00:31-01:57; the km/h bin edges are stated more crisply in Part-3.pdf p.2 than in the spoken audio):

| Category | Speed | % of max velocity |
|---|---|---|
| Walking | <6 km/h | <25% |
| Jogging | ~7-14 km/h | ~25-50% |
| Running | ~14-20 km/h | ~50-75% |
| Striding | ~21-27 km/h | ~75-85% |
| Sprinting | >27 km/h | >85% |

As speed increases, vertical ground reaction force, the rate of force application, muscle activity, and hip/knee/ankle power all increase (~00:00-00:47, ~02:15-02:35).

**Why it works** — This is a descriptive taxonomy of gait mechanics at increasing speed, not a claim requiring justification beyond the mechanical logic: faster locomotion demands larger forces applied in shorter ground-contact times.

**When to apply** — Use this vocabulary to translate a GPS speed-zone reading into a plain-language gait category when talking with Athletic Medicine or coaching staff, and to sanity-check whether a prescribed drill speed is actually eliciting the gait pattern intended (e.g., confirming a "striding" prescription isn't accidentally just a fast jog for a given athlete's own MV).

**When NOT to apply** — These are population-typical bin edges from Harries' AFL context, not a fixed physiological law; an individual athlete's actual transition points between jogging/running/striding/sprinting will vary with limb length, MV, and technique, so the km/h numbers should be treated as illustrative, with %MV as the more transferable anchor.

**Example** — A player with a 34.2 km/h max velocity (Harries' hamstring case-study demographic, Part 1 ~02:20-02:33) would be striding at roughly 25.5-29 km/h and sprinting above 29 km/h, meaningfully different absolute speeds than a player with a lower MV even though both are in the same %MV band.

**Related** — [[claim--ankle-then-hip-dominant-speed-mechanism]] (the mechanism behind these transitions); [[framework--on-field-rehab-levels-with-mv-bands]]

# Running Preparation Drill Menu (Pre-Running to Level 1)

**What it is** — Before an athlete returns to actual running, Harries prescribes a menu of low-intensity drills to re-familiarize the athlete with upright-running postures and prepare tissue for repetitive loading (~03:41-08:03; confirmed Part-3.pdf p.2):
- **Dribble walks/runs** over ankle, shin and knee height - front-side mechanics focus, flat foot contact, "nothing goes out the back."
- **Dribble transitions** between ankle/shin/knee heights over 5 m segments, transitioning into a typical running gait.
- **Skipping variations**, e.g. A-skips, to add stiffness and reactivity on ground contact.
- **Low-intensity jumping**: pogos and unilateral pogos, for repetitive loading-cycle and system-stiffness preparation.
- **Scissor shuffles and scissor bounds**: aggressive hip flexion/extension, striking under center of mass, building horizontal displacement.

Basic clinical criteria (appropriate range of motion, minimal pain/swelling, sufficient local endurance/strength) plus a demonstrated ability to produce force quickly in a dynamic task and tolerate repetitive impact are the prerequisites before commencing actual running; often this is judged functionally (can they do these drills without issue) rather than via a formal test (~07:43-08:28).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: these drills rebuild the specific postures, coordination and ground-contact stiffness of upright running at low tissue stress before loading the same patterns at running speed, and build the athlete's confidence in the injured area.

**When to apply** — Use as the standard Level-1/pre-running menu for any lower-limb soft-tissue RTP at Baylor. Because these are low intensity, they can also stay in the warm-up throughout later on-field rehab levels, not just at the start (~07:32-07:43).

**When NOT to apply** — This is a generic menu, not tailored by injury site beyond the general logic in [[claim--ankle-then-hip-dominant-speed-mechanism]] (e.g., dribble drills over knee height load the hip flexors more than ankle-height dribbles). Do not treat "completed the drill menu" as a substitute for the actual clinical criteria (ROM, pain, strength) it is meant to sit alongside; the drills demonstrate functional tolerance, they do not replace a clinical assessment.

**Example** — Harries' hamstring case study begins on-field rehab with this drill menu before any timed running, confirming the athlete can tolerate repetitive ground contact and produce force dynamically before session 1's 60 m repeats begin (see [[heuristic--fixed-distance-timed-repeats-for-pacing]]).
