# Sport-Specific Skill Drill Type, by Level

**What it is** — Harries' drill-type continuum for sport-specific technical/tactical skill work, layered on top of the intensity/complexity model (~03:14-03:52, confirmed Part-5.pdf p.2-3): Level 1 - technical skill actions performed stationary; Level 2 - technical skill actions with some low-velocity movement, still pre-planned; Level 3 - positional-specific drills, still predictable/sequenced, with limited sprinting or high-intensity multidirectional opportunity; Level 4 - positional-specific drills with an added fatigue layer, testing capacity to hold technical output under load; Level 5 - random/unpredictable, evasive and competitive drills, ideally in a modified training or small-sided-game environment, using additional players/coaches to add pressure. His hamstring case study's specific progression: Level 1, stationary technical skills only, uninjured limb only; Level 2, kicking introduced on the injured limb but still stationary/pre-planned; Level 3, positional sequences with some unpredictability, still limited sprinting; Level 4, random/unpredictable drills with added player/coach pressure; Level 5, evasive 2v1 attacking-squares (small -> medium -> large grids) and small-sided handball games with variable defensive pressure and interval length.

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: technical/tactical execution and locomotor intensity have to be rebuilt together because neither is performed in isolation in a game; sequencing drill type, movement level and practice structure together lets both climb in a controlled, matched way rather than one racing ahead of the other.

**When to apply** — Use this level-by-level drill-type shape as the sport-skill-specific analogue to the MDSA drill menu (see [[framework--mdsa-drill-menu-by-level]]), adapted to the sport's actual technical/tactical catalogue (for football: throwing/catching/blocking/route-running rather than kicking/handballing).

# Invasion-Sport Locomotor Pillars

**What it is** — Harries' starting point for building any on-field rehab process: map a sport's technical, tactical and physical domains, then simplify by using what invasion-based team sports (football, soccer, rugby, AFL) have in common. Every invasion sport reduces to two tactical patterns, offense (creating space: pressing forward, overlapping, running into space; technically: moving/passing/catching the ball) and defense (closing space: covering, retreating, closing down; technically: tackling, intercepting, contesting possession) (~03:33-06:46). Underneath both are the same physical actions: sprinting, accelerating, decelerating and changing direction. He names these four as the **primary locomotor pillars of on-field rehab**, usable as a starting template "to any rehab running framework you create" regardless of sport (~07:41-08:22).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: the exact loading numbers differ by sport, but the actual locomotor actions "don't change too much" across invasion sports, so building a rehab framework around them is a transferable shortcut instead of having to model every sport's full technical/tactical catalogue from scratch (~07:19-07:41).

**When to apply** — Use as the skeleton for any Baylor RTP conversation with Athletic Medicine: whatever the sport or position, the questions are the same four - can this athlete sprint, accelerate, decelerate and change direction at the required intensity, in an environment as complex as competition. It gives Applied Performance and Athletic Medicine a shared, sport-agnostic starting vocabulary before adding position-specific detail (GPS zones, skill demands).

**When NOT to apply** — Harries' own case-study sport is AFL, an unusually continuous, low-collision invasion game. Two gaps matter for Baylor football specifically: (1) **contact is missing as a pillar.** Tackling appears once, as a single word, never developed into its own progression. For football, collision and contact (block, shed, tackle, hand-fight, stance start) functions as a fourth pillar with its own dosage question, and this course gives it none. (2) The four pillars are a taxonomy of locomotor actions, not a testing or clearance protocol; they tell you what to progress, not how much force production or healing time is required before progressing it (see [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]] for that layer). Do not treat "the four pillars are covered" as equivalent to "the athlete is ready."

**Example** — A returning offensive lineman needs sprint/accel/decel/COD rebuilt like any other position, but the highest-risk gap in his return is a pillar this course never names: reintroducing collision tolerance. That has to be built separately, in coordination with position coaching, not inferred from his running progression.

**Related** — [[framework--on-field-rehab-levels-with-mv-bands]] (how the levels operationalize these pillars); Baylor's own documented gap that GPS/load thresholds are not yet sport- or position-specific (`method-baseline.md`, Load monitoring and GPS).

# Multidirectional Speed & Agility Drill Menu by On-Field Rehab Level

**What it is** — Harries' worked drill menu for the hamstring case study, by level (~11:56-21:11; confirmed Part-4.pdf p.3):
- **Levels 1-2** (low intensity, low complexity, block practice): fast-easy-fast accelerations (accelerate ~5 m, ease off, re-accelerate); go-and-stop accelerations (accelerate a set distance, brake to a stop in a deceleration zone); curvy-linear ("half bend") accelerations; 30-degree cutting gates with a pre-planned side step, crossover step, or split step; a 3x3 m diamond/square drill with athlete-chosen lateral/forward/backward shuffling.
- **Level 3** (rising velocity/space, controlled/closed reactivity introduced): fast-easy-fast acceleration with a closed-reactive defender (defender moves laterally to open space); a defensive reaction (mirror) drill in a small square; a "compass drill" with pre-determined or reactive 45/90/135-degree direction changes at ~75-80% effort, cued by a hand signal.
- **Level 4** (near-maximal velocity ~80-85%, bigger spaces, more open reactivity): partner chase-and-tag; a large-space gate drill with a turnover cue requiring a hard deceleration and chase; a reactive compass drill in a bigger space followed by a second reactive task (react to a rolled ball).
- **Level 5** (highly chaotic, near-maximal/maximal): sport-specific, competitive, multi-athlete scenarios; where extra players/coaches aren't available, use constrained drills designed to replicate unpredictability as closely as possible.

**Why it works** — Each level's drills are the concrete output of running the levers in [[framework--eight-intensity-levers-mdsa]] through the plotting exercise in [[framework--intensity-complexity-drill-plotting-tool]]: space shrinks or grows, reactivity moves from none to closed to open, and entry velocity/COD angle both rise, in a sequence matched to the level's target physical readiness.

**When to apply** — Use this menu as a starting drill bank for building a Baylor-specific version; the drill *shapes* (accelerate-then-react, gated cutting, chase-and-tag, compass drill) transfer across sports even where the specific angles or spaces would be adjusted for football positions.

**When NOT to apply** — This is one practitioner's AFL menu, built for an athlete with no contact restriction; none of these drills involve or prepare for a blocking, tackling or hand-fighting demand, so a football-specific menu needs an added contact-drill category this course does not supply (see [[framework--invasion-sport-locomotor-pillars]]). The "reactivity" drills here are also limited to hand signals and mirrored defenders, not genuine game-representative cues (see [[heuristic--closed-vs-open-reactivity-drill-design]]).

**Example** — In [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]], sessions 3, 5 and 8 map closely onto this Level 1-3 / Level 3-4 / Level 4-5 menu progression.

# The Five On-Field Rehab Levels, With Max-Velocity Bands

**What it is** — Harries splits on-field rehab into five levels, aligned to early/mid/late rehab, followed by return-to-training and return-to-play (Part 2, ~02:54-04:16). Each level targets a max-velocity (MV) band for linear running (Part 3, ~08:39-09:14; confirmed Part-3.pdf p.2):

| Level | Target % of max velocity |
|---|---|
| 1 | ~50-70% |
| 2 | ~70-75% |
| 3 | ~75-85% |
| 4 | ~85-95% |
| 5 | >95% up to 100% |

For his illustrative low-grade hamstring case, this maps to one session per level (sessions 1-5), then two return-to-training sessions (sessions 6-7) with the team, then return to play as session 8 (~03:30-04:16). He is explicit this is a minor-injury example: "with a more severe injury or different type of injury... you may do a number of sessions in each level before moving on."

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: splitting rehab into named levels gives structure to the gradual stressing of sport-specific locomotor actions, aligned to where the athlete sits in the overall rehab (gym-based early, on-field mid, transition-to-training late).

**When to apply** — Use the five-level structure as the shared vocabulary between Applied Performance and Athletic Medicine: "Level 3" means a defined, measurable thing (75-85% of *that athlete's own* MV, from the Catapult pipeline), not a vague stage description. The number of sessions per level is explicitly not fixed by the framework and should scale with injury severity and history (see [[principle--framework-is-a-guide-not-a-protocol]]).

**When NOT to apply** — The MV bands are Harries' own teaching example and expert-opinion breakpoints, not derived from trial data; he presents no evidence citation for why the boundaries sit at exactly 70/75/85/95%. They are AFL-cohort numbers (based on GPS-derived %MV for the sport). Football's per-position sprint demands are different from AFL's continuous locomotor profile, so the level *structure* (five stages, submax-to-max) transfers, but the specific %MV/km-h breakpoints should be checked against Baylor's own GPS data per position before being treated as a Baylor standard, and Baylor's data dictionary does not yet have position-specific thresholds built (`method-baseline.md`, Load monitoring and GPS section notes this as unfinished work).

**Example** — See [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]] for a real (non-illustrative) case where this level structure was applied but the athlete never reached the desired >90% exposure due to external season-timing pressure - the levels held, the ideal endpoint did not.

**Related** — [[framework--invasion-sport-locomotor-pillars]]; [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]] (the criteria for crossing Level 2 into Level 3); [[heuristic--two-exposures-above-90-percent-mv-exit-rule]] (the Level 5 exit criterion)

# Block, Then Serial, Then Random Practice Across the Levels

**What it is** — Harries maps sport-specific skill drills onto a practice-structure continuum borrowed from motor-learning theory: **block practice** (the same drill repeated, low variability), **serial practice** (a known sequence of actions, predictable order), and **random practice** (unpredictable, variable order/decisions). He assigns these across levels (~04:03-07:26, confirmed Part-5.pdf p.2): Level 1 - solely block, tightly controlled; Level 2 - still block, intensity of the drills rises; Level 3 - roughly 50/50 block and serial, chaining action sequences; Level 4 - block dropped entirely, mostly serial with some random; Level 5 - substantial random practice, with some serial retained deliberately for actions not yet ready for full unpredictability. On return to training, levels 1-2 of training itself are "pretty much all" random.

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: block-to-serial-to-random is a graded route from fully predictable to fully unpredictable practice, which lets an athlete build a skill under low cognitive/decision load first and only add decision-making demand once the movement itself is competent.

**When to apply** — Use the general shape (predictable early, unpredictable late) as the practice-structure axis alongside drill type and movement level (see [[framework--sport-skill-drill-type-continuum-by-level]]) when designing sport-specific skill sessions.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested.** Block/serial/random and its associated "contextual interference effect" come from the Schmidt information-processing tradition of motor learning, not from ecological dynamics/representative learning design, which the library's skill-acquisition sources treat as the better-supported model for sport skill transfer. The practical difference matters: under an information-processing view, predictability itself is the variable being controlled, and the task's informational content is secondary; under an ecological view, the key variable is whether the *information* driving the action is representative of the game (a real defender, a real developing gap) regardless of how "predictable" the drill's structure is. A block-practice drill against a live, representative defender can be more transferable than a "random" drill built on arbitrary, non-representative cues. Do not assume moving along this block-serial-random axis is equivalent to moving toward game transfer; check whether the *information* in the drill, not just its unpredictability, is representative.

**Example** — Harries' own hamstring case study at Level 1 uses stationary, block-practiced kicking with the uninjured limb only (see [[principle--tailor-skill-restrictions-to-injured-structure]]); by Level 5 it moves to a 2v1 attacking-squares game, which is "random" in his sense but still uses arbitrary defender constraints rather than a fully representative game defense.

**Related** — [[skill-acquisition/enhancing-skill--myszka/framework--newell-interacting-constraints]] and [[skill-acquisition/enhancing-skill--myszka/framework--nonlinear-pedagogy-and-constraint-classes]] (suggested reciprocal link: "a practitioner RTP course whose practice-structure continuum this framework's representative-design view supersedes, see on-field-rtp--harries"); [[heuristic--closed-vs-open-reactivity-drill-design]]; [[framework--intensity-complexity-two-independent-axes]]

# Repeat-Sprint Interval Format for Late-Stage Fatigue Exposure

**What it is** — In the back half of late-rehab sessions, Harries introduces repeat-sprint intervals to expose the athlete to high velocity under fatigue and simulate conditioning demand alongside sprint load. The format, used across three of the four case studies: **1-2 sets of three to four repetitions over 40 m, all above 85% MV, on a 30-second rolling start** (rep 1 at 0 s, rep 2 at 30 s, rep 3 at 60 s, etc.). Case 2 used **two sets**; Cases 3 and 4 used **one set** (~21:23-21:59, ~30:49-30:58, ~40:14-40:23).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: placing these in the back half of the session, after other running/skill work has already introduced some fatigue, "blends" high-speed exposure with a controlled recovery interval, giving both a sprint-load-accumulation stimulus and a conditioning stimulus at once, and rehearses producing near-maximal velocity in a fatigued state closer to what a game actually demands late in a match.

**When to apply** — Use in the return-to-sport-phase session(s), once an athlete has already cleared the 75-85% MV gate and is accumulating >90% MV exposures elsewhere in the session (see [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]] and [[heuristic--two-exposures-above-90-percent-mv-exit-rule]]). Scale the number of sets (one vs two) to the athlete's overall session load and injury type - the lower-frequency recurrent-calf case ([[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]) used only one set.

**When NOT to apply** — This is placed deliberately late in rehab, after force-production benchmarks are already cleared; it should not be used as an early-rehab or pre-gate exposure, since it combines near-maximal velocity with accumulated fatigue, precisely the combination the earlier gate criteria are designed to screen for readiness against.

**Example** — See [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]] session 8 for the two-set version and [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]] session 10 for the one-set version used alongside a knee-joint injury.

# Running Gait Speed Categories

**What it is** — Harries defines a shared vocabulary for running speed categories, each with a km/h range and a %MV range (~00:31-01:57; the km/h bin edges are stated more crisply in Part-3.pdf p.2 than in the spoken audio):

| Category | Speed | % of max velocity |
|---|---|---|
| Walking | <6 km/h | <25% |
| Jogging | ~7-14 km/h | ~25-50% |
| Running | ~14-20 km/h | ~50-75% |
| Striding | ~21-27 km/h | ~75-85% |
| Sprinting | >27 km/h | >85% |

As speed increases, vertical ground reaction force, the rate of force application, muscle activity, and hip/knee/ankle power all increase (~00:00-00:47, ~02:15-02:35).

**Why it works** — This is a descriptive taxonomy of gait mechanics at increasing speed, not a claim requiring justification beyond the mechanical logic: faster locomotion demands larger forces applied in shorter ground-contact times.

**When to apply** — Use this vocabulary to translate a GPS speed-zone reading into a plain-language gait category when talking with Athletic Medicine or coaching staff, and to sanity-check whether a prescribed drill speed is actually eliciting the gait pattern intended (e.g., confirming a "striding" prescription isn't accidentally just a fast jog for a given athlete's own MV).

**When NOT to apply** — These are population-typical bin edges from Harries' AFL context, not a fixed physiological law; an individual athlete's actual transition points between jogging/running/striding/sprinting will vary with limb length, MV, and technique, so the km/h numbers should be treated as illustrative, with %MV as the more transferable anchor.

**Example** — A player with a 34.2 km/h max velocity (Harries' hamstring case-study demographic, Part 1 ~02:20-02:33) would be striding at roughly 25.5-29 km/h and sprinting above 29 km/h, meaningfully different absolute speeds than a player with a lower MV even though both are in the same %MV band.

**Related** — [[claim--ankle-then-hip-dominant-speed-mechanism]] (the mechanism behind these transitions); [[framework--on-field-rehab-levels-with-mv-bands]]

# Running Preparation Drill Menu (Pre-Running to Level 1)

**What it is** — Before an athlete returns to actual running, Harries prescribes a menu of low-intensity drills to re-familiarize the athlete with upright-running postures and prepare tissue for repetitive loading (~03:41-08:03; confirmed Part-3.pdf p.2):
- **Dribble walks/runs** over ankle, shin and knee height - front-side mechanics focus, flat foot contact, "nothing goes out the back."
- **Dribble transitions** between ankle/shin/knee heights over 5 m segments, transitioning into a typical running gait.
- **Skipping variations**, e.g. A-skips, to add stiffness and reactivity on ground contact.
- **Low-intensity jumping**: pogos and unilateral pogos, for repetitive loading-cycle and system-stiffness preparation.
- **Scissor shuffles and scissor bounds**: aggressive hip flexion/extension, striking under center of mass, building horizontal displacement.

Basic clinical criteria (appropriate range of motion, minimal pain/swelling, sufficient local endurance/strength) plus a demonstrated ability to produce force quickly in a dynamic task and tolerate repetitive impact are the prerequisites before commencing actual running; often this is judged functionally (can they do these drills without issue) rather than via a formal test (~07:43-08:28).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: these drills rebuild the specific postures, coordination and ground-contact stiffness of upright running at low tissue stress before loading the same patterns at running speed, and build the athlete's confidence in the injured area.

**When to apply** — Use as the standard Level-1/pre-running menu for any lower-limb soft-tissue RTP at Baylor. Because these are low intensity, they can also stay in the warm-up throughout later on-field rehab levels, not just at the start (~07:32-07:43).

**When NOT to apply** — This is a generic menu, not tailored by injury site beyond the general logic in [[claim--ankle-then-hip-dominant-speed-mechanism]] (e.g., dribble drills over knee height load the hip flexors more than ankle-height dribbles). Do not treat "completed the drill menu" as a substitute for the actual clinical criteria (ROM, pain, strength) it is meant to sit alongside; the drills demonstrate functional tolerance, they do not replace a clinical assessment.

**Example** — Harries' hamstring case study begins on-field rehab with this drill menu before any timed running, confirming the athlete can tolerate repetitive ground contact and produce force dynamically before session 1's 60 m repeats begin (see [[heuristic--fixed-distance-timed-repeats-for-pacing]]).

---
type: library-entry
kind: heuristic

# The 75-85% Max-Velocity Gate

**What it is** — Before progressing an athlete past roughly 75-85% of MV (Harries states the gate at "75-85%" in most places and once as "75-80%," ~13:04-16:35; the broken-stride worked example itself targets 70-75%, a step below the gate, not the gate threshold), Harries checks four things (~13:31-15:45, confirmed Part-3.pdf p.3):
1. **Time for biological healing** appropriate to the injury.
2. **Symptom response**: previous running sessions completed with minimal pain or awareness of the injured area.
3. **Force production benchmarks** in the injured area, e.g. eccentric hamstring strength via Nordic at roughly 80-85% of pre-injury baseline; seated calf isometric peak force at roughly 1.7-1.8x bodyweight (spoken range) or "≥1.8x bodyweight" (Part-3.pdf p.3 states it as a single floor rather than a range - the two sources are not perfectly consistent, use 1.7-1.8x as the working range and confirm against the athlete's own baseline).
4. **Reactive strength/stretch-shortening-cycle function**, e.g. via a hopping task, to check the athlete can produce high force in a short timeframe before near-maximal speed.

He is explicit that a seated-calf-related injury term near ~15:51 is unclear in the audio (marked `[injury term unclear]` in the source transcript) and has been left unresolved rather than guessed.

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: "there are of course varied opinions in the field on this criteria, especially in regard to the assessment of force production capacities... it seems sensible to me and has almost zero downside" (~15:21-15:36). He states outright that these are expert-opinion, common-practice benchmarks, not results from trials - label them that way whenever they are used, and do not present the 80-85%, 1.7-1.8x, or hop-test criteria as validated thresholds.

**When to apply** — This is the single most transferable number in the course: a decision gate that Applied Performance can compute and hand to Athletic Medicine as a shared go/no-go check before a returning athlete is exposed to higher-velocity running. At Baylor, the direct instrument matches already exist: NordBord hamstring eccentric testing (retained specifically for small, clinically-targeted RTP groups per Applied Performance's own documented practice, not roster-wide), the Iso Seated Calf protocol on the ForceDecks "Mid-Thigh Pull" setting (90-degree ankle/knee position, 3 x 6-second maximal contractions, 15 s rest), and the repeated-CMJ/hop protocol already run on ForceDecks (10 reps total, n=5 pairs) as the reactive-strength check. Frame every number supplied to Athletic Medicine as *supporting information*, consistent with Applied Performance's stated advisory role in RTP, not as a clearance decision.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not treat 80-85% (Nordic), 1.7-1.8x BW (calf) or "a hop test" as validated cutoffs; they are common-practice heuristics Harries himself flags as contested among practitioners. They are also AFL-context numbers; Baylor has no documented sport- or position-specific RTP force thresholds of its own yet (`method-baseline.md` names this explicitly as a gap: "no specific RTP criteria, battery, or phased-return protocol appears anywhere in this corpus"), so treat these as a starting reference to validate against Baylor's own returning-athlete data, not an imported standard.

# Closed, Then Open, Then Evasive Reactivity

**What it is** — Harries' reactivity ladder for progressing drill unpredictability: pre-planned (fully known in advance) -> closed reactivity (a single, simple cue ends the drill, e.g. a coach throwing a hand signal to cue a cut) -> open reactivity (a further task follows the first reaction, cued by a noise, another athlete, or a coach) -> evasive/competitive (genuinely live, opposed play) (~15:45-16:06, ~17:51-18:12, ~20:34-20:58).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: unpredictability should be added gradually, matched to the athlete's readiness, rather than jumping straight from fully controlled to fully live play.

**When to apply** — Use the four-step ladder shape (planned -> closed -> open -> evasive) as the ordering principle for adding reactivity to any drill, matched to the on-field rehab level.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested.** Harries' worked examples of "closed reactivity" are a coach's arbitrary hand signal or a defender mirroring a shuffle - a generic stimulus with no game meaning, not the information a player actually reads in competition (a defender's hip position, a gap opening in coverage). This is the course's clearest departure from an ecological-dynamics view of skill acquisition, which holds that the information source should be representative of the game from the start (a real defender's movement, not an arbitrary cue) and scaled in difficulty, rather than substituted with an arbitrary cue early and only made representative once complexity is judged "safe." Read ecologically, Harries' own four rungs re-map to: unopposed -> still unopposed (an arbitrary cue is not opposition) -> partly opposed -> opposed. Do not treat "closed reactivity" drills as teaching a player anything about reading a real opponent; they add unpredictability of *timing*, not unpredictability of *information*.

**Example** — The compass drill in [[framework--mdsa-drill-menu-by-level]] (Level 3) uses a coach's hand signal to cue a direction change - closed reactivity by Harries' definition, but not representative of what a defender's body actually signals in a game.

# Prescribe Early Running as Fixed Distance, Timed for Completion

**What it is** — Harries' preferred method for the first running sessions: pick a fixed distance (60, 80 or 100 m), and prescribe a target completion time rather than a "run at X% effort" instruction. This lets the practitioner plan the average speed exactly in advance: a 60 m repeat in 12 seconds equates to an 18 km/h average, with peak velocity typically 1-2 km/h higher, i.e. ~19-20 km/h (~09:14-09:58). His illustrative hamstring case-study sessions: **Session 1** - four reps each at 13 s, 12 s and 11 s over 60 m (~16.6, 18.0 and ~19.5 km/h average respectively), targeting 57-60% of that athlete's MV. **Session 2** - two reps each at 12 s, 11 s, 10.5 s, 10 s and 9.5 s over 60 m, targeting an average of ~22.7 km/h (22.2-24 km/h, ~66-69% MV) (~09:14-11:48).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: fixed-distance/timed prescription removes ambiguity about what speed the athlete actually ran, lets the practitioner plan the session's target speed ahead of time, and (with progressively increasing speed within a session) lets the athlete build confidence and learn what a given speed feels like across repetitions before being asked to hit it cold.

**When to apply** — Use for the early on-field rehab levels (submaximal running, roughly up to 70-75% MV) where steady-state pacing rather than acceleration/deceleration mechanics is the goal. It requires only a stopwatch and a measured distance, so it needs no GPS or video technology, though GPS can be layered on for confirmation.

**When NOT to apply** — Once an athlete is running above ~70-75% of MV, Harries himself moves away from full-distance timed repeats toward broken-stride timing over just the middle phase (see [[framework--broken-stride-timing-protocol]]), because a single time-for-completion over the whole distance conflates acceleration, top-speed and deceleration into one number and stops being precise enough to control intensity at higher speeds.

**Example** — See the worked session-1/session-2 numbers above; per-case variations of the same method appear in [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]] (100 m repeats at 22-26 s, ~14-16 km/h in early sessions) and [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]] (two sets of eight 100 m repeats at 14-16 then 16-18 km/h).

# Hesitation Is a Named Readiness Red Flag, With No Way to Measure It

**What it is** — Harries names hesitation as a disqualifying sign: an athlete not confidently and willingly choosing the right action under competitive pressure (e.g., not accelerating through a gap) is, in his framing, not ready to return (~10:15-10:49, and see [[principle--competitive-exposure-required-before-return-to-play]]). He never gives a way to observe, score or record it.

**Why it works** — Harries offers no mechanism, only the assertion. It is plausible on its face: hesitation under pressure plausibly reflects unresolved fear-avoidance or a lack of trust in the injured tissue. But plausibility is not the same as a defined, repeatable observation.

**When to apply** — Flag it as exactly what it is: a real, named criterion the course itself cannot defend to an objective audience. It is a legitimate prompt to look for a way to operationalize "hesitation" (a success-rate threshold on a drill, a scripted-start/live-finish task design, video-coded decision latency) rather than to rely on a coach's unaided impression, but this course supplies none of those tools itself.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not write "athlete showed no hesitation" into a Baylor RTP note as if it were a measured criterion on par with the % MV or force benchmarks in [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]]. It is currently an unvalidated, single-observer judgment call with no defined pass/fail rule, exactly the kind of subjective criterion the 75-85% gate's objective benchmarks were designed to avoid relying on alone.

**Example** — Two athletes both clear their force benchmarks and %MV targets; one accelerates confidently through a small-sided game gap, the other visibly slows and checks his own leg before committing. Harries would treat the second as not ready, but the course gives no rule for how many hesitant reps, or what kind, would actually hold up a return decision.

# Progress Max Velocity Linearly, Then Undulate Near 80-85%

**What it is** — Harries' default periodization for max-velocity exposure across sessions: increase speed session-on-session in a linear fashion through the early-to-mid part of rehab, then shift to an undulating pattern (down, up, sometimes down and back up to hold a level) once the athlete approaches roughly 80-85% of MV (~21:17-22:50; confirmed Part-3.pdf p.3). His illustrative hamstring case goes linear through session 5 (50-60% -> 65-70% -> 75-80% -> 85% -> ~90-92% of MV), pushed further into the linear zone than typical (up to 90-92%) because of time pressure toward a 3-4 week return, then brings intensity down before the next jump.

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: linear progression is appropriate early because the tissue is far from its ceiling and each step is a modest incremental stress; near 80-85% MV, sessions get close enough to true maximal effort that repeating high-intensity exposures session after session risks accumulating fatigue and reload risk faster than the tissue can adapt, so alternating higher and lower sessions manages that fatigue while still working toward more >90% exposures over time.

**When to apply** — Use linear progression as the default through on-field rehab levels 1-3 (up to ~75-85% MV), then switch to an undulating high/low pattern from roughly level 3-4 onward. How long to stay linear (and how far past 85% to push before undulating) is explicitly context-dependent on time pressure, injury severity and history, not fixed.

**When NOT to apply** — Not every case in Harries' own material follows this pattern: [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] used a flat, non-undulating linear build because the low running frequency (twice weekly) meant every session was already spaced far enough apart to serve as its own recovery; forcing an undulating pattern onto a low-frequency case would be unnecessary. Do not apply the linear-then-undulate default mechanically without checking whether session frequency already provides the recovery spacing undulation is meant to create.

**Example** — Contrast [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]] and [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]] (both undulated from around session 6) against [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] (stayed linear throughout, by design).

# A Low High-Speed-Running Threshold Can Inflate Totals

**What it is** — Harries' organization set high-speed running (HSR) at >17 km/h, very-high-speed running (VHSR) at >23 km/h, and sprint at >27 km/h, and he notes 17 km/h is only roughly 55-60% of max velocity for these AFL athletes (~10:57-11:04, repeated ~22:54-23:11). Because the HSR cutoff sits at a relatively low %MV, a rep or drill that only briefly crosses it can register as a full HSR exposure and inflate the session or weekly total, even though the athlete never approached a meaningful intensity. This happened twice in his four cases: an unexpected HSR overshoot in [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]] session 2 (100 m repeats), and an unplanned overshoot in [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]] session 4.

**Why it works** — A fixed absolute speed threshold (km/h) captures a different %MV for every athlete and, within one athlete, becomes an easier bar to clear (relatively) than a %MV-based threshold would be, so longer-distance reps or drills with any build-up phase are especially prone to briefly crossing a low absolute cutoff without the practitioner intending a high-speed exposure.

**When to apply** — When reviewing GPS load reports, check where the HSR/VHSR/sprint speed cutoffs sit relative to the individual athlete's own %MV, not just the absolute km/h number; a rep or session total should be read alongside how much of it came from brief threshold crossings versus sustained high-intensity running. This is the specific point Baylor's own gap analysis should address (see When NOT to apply).

**When NOT to apply** — Do not assume these AFL-specific thresholds (17/23/27 km/h) apply to Baylor football; Baylor's own documented data dictionary is currently generic and vendor-organized rather than sport- or position-specific (`method-baseline.md`, Load monitoring and GPS section), so equivalent thresholds need to be derived from Baylor's own Catapult/OpenField data per position, not imported from this AFL cohort. A football lineman, for instance, may rarely or never reach a comparable sprint-zone speed in a game at all, which would make an imported absolute threshold meaningless for that position without being re-checked against Baylor's own data first.

**Example** — See [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]] session 4: the athlete gained confidence running in the brace and accumulated HSR via a mix of 100 m repeats and three-minute intervals, overshooting the plan - flagged by Harries as low-risk precisely because the threshold crossed was such a low %MV for that athlete.

# Cut Running Frequency for a Recurrent Calf Injury

**What it is** — For a recurrent lateral soleus strain, Harries deliberately ran the athlete only **twice per week**, with at least 48 hours (sometimes 72-96 hours) between sessions, instead of the more frequent running used in the hamstring cases. His stated reasons: this specific athlete had responded well to reduced running frequency after past calf issues, and reduced frequency/weekly load "has also been effective in some of our recurrent calf injuries that we've come across in the past" at his organization (~27:59-28:33, ~29:53-30:01).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: lower frequency gives the calf longer recovery windows between loading bouts, which matters more for a muscle that is loaded on effectively every ground contact (unlike, say, a hamstring loaded mainly in late swing at higher speeds) and which had already re-injured once under a more standard frequency.

**When to apply** — For a recurrent (not first-time) calf/soleus strain, consider deliberately lower running frequency (e.g., twice weekly with 48+ hour gaps) as a starting strategy, especially if the athlete has a documented history of responding well to reduced frequency previously.

**When NOT to apply** — This is based on organizational pattern-matching and one athlete's own history ("he had responded well... in the past"), not a controlled comparison; it is explicitly *not* what Harries did for the hamstring cases, so do not port this frequency reduction to hamstring or other tissue types without the same recurrence-and-prior-response rationale. It also extended this athlete's total time loss to 44 days (the longest of the four cases, deliberately extended a further week for training exposure), a real cost that should be weighed against the injury-recurrence risk it aims to reduce.

**Example** — See [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] for the full case; contrast with [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]]'s six sessions across roughly the same number of weeks as this case's five sessions across a longer span.

# Sequence Interval Length by Which Tissue Is Injured

**What it is** — Across the four case studies, Harries used two different interval-length sequencing strategies depending on injury type. The hamstring cases ([[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]], [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]]) more commonly used a **long-to-short** approach (starting with longer repeats, e.g. 100 m, and moving toward shorter, faster efforts). The recurrent calf case ([[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]) deliberately used the opposite, a **short-to-long** model: beginning with 60 m repeats (10-12 s efforts) and progressing to longer intervals (100 m repeats at 20-24 s, then 40 s and 60 s intervals), explicitly to control the calf's cumulative local-fatigue exposure early (~31:41-32:04).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: the calf contributes disproportionately to running mechanics at all speeds (not just top speed), so short, well-spaced efforts early minimize repetitive local loading to the injured structure while still allowing systemic running-mechanics practice; longer intervals are then added once tolerance is established. For the hamstring, which is loaded more specifically during the late-swing phase at higher speeds, starting with longer, moderate-pace efforts and shortening toward faster, more targeted reps was the pattern used instead, though he does not spell out an equivalent explicit rationale for the hamstring ordering.

**When to apply** — When designing early on-field rehab running volume, consider the injured tissue's loading profile (does it load more with repetition frequency, as with calf, or more with peak intensity, as with hamstring at high speed) and choose interval length progression accordingly, rather than defaulting to one fixed sequencing rule for every lower-limb injury.

**When NOT to apply** — This is drawn from only two data points (one calf case, two hamstring cases) inside one practitioner's own case selection; Harries never states it as a general rule, and this entry infers the generalization from the pattern across his four cases. Treat it as a hypothesis worth testing against Baylor's own case data, not an established principle.

**Example** — Contrast [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]'s 60m-then-100m-then-longer intervals against [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]]'s and [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]]'s early use of 100 m repeats before moving to faster 60 m work.

# At Least One, Ideally Two, Exposures Above 90% MV Before Return

**What it is** — Harries' exit rule for on-field rehab: before returning an athlete to training or play, he wants at least one, ideally two, exposures above 90% of MV (~23:24-24:41). He is explicit there is no universal number: "I can't tell you whether you need to do one, two, or seven. That's entirely dependent on the injury... your organisational culture, your philosophy at your club... the history of that player and their soft tissue history... the pressure in that time of year." The one firm line he draws: he cannot imagine returning an athlete to training, and certainly not to play, without at least one, probably two, exposures above 90%.

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: exposures near true maximal velocity load the tissue in a way that submaximal running does not rehearse, so returning without ever having approached game-realistic top speed leaves an unrehearsed gap between rehab and competition, regardless of how much submaximal volume was accumulated.

**When to apply** — Use as a floor, not a target: before clearing a returning athlete, confirm at least one (preferably two) session exposures above 90% of that athlete's own MV have been logged and tolerated without a negative symptom response. Track exposures explicitly per athlete rather than assuming volume accumulated lower down the intensity scale is an adequate substitute.

**When NOT to apply** — This is expert opinion/common practice, not a validated cutoff, and Harries' own four case studies show it is routinely not met: [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]] returned with zero exposures above 90% (external season-timing pressure); [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]] returned with only one, when Harries "would have preferred a second." Do not treat missing this exit rule as an automatic hold on return; it is one input among the injury history, schedule and organizational context he lists, and both of his under-target cases returned to play regardless. Also do not assume "90% of max velocity" is the same absolute speed across sports or positions; it must be computed from the athlete's own MV, and Baylor's own GPS/max-velocity pipeline (Catapult/OpenField) is the source for that number, not a generic AFL threshold.

**Example** — [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] is the opposite case: because that athlete's low running frequency meant every late session ran near-maximal, he accumulated six separate exposures above 90% MV before return, far more than the stated floor, illustrating that the number is a byproduct of the chosen periodization, not a targeted count.

# The 75-85% Max-Velocity Gate

**What it is** — Before progressing an athlete past roughly 75-85% of MV (Harries states the gate at "75-85%" in most places and once as "75-80%," ~13:04-16:35; the broken-stride worked example itself targets 70-75%, a step below the gate, not the gate threshold), Harries checks four things (~13:31-15:45, confirmed Part-3.pdf p.3):
1. **Time for biological healing** appropriate to the injury.
2. **Symptom response**: previous running sessions completed with minimal pain or awareness of the injured area.
3. **Force production benchmarks** in the injured area, e.g. eccentric hamstring strength via Nordic at roughly 80-85% of pre-injury baseline; seated calf isometric peak force at roughly 1.7-1.8x bodyweight (spoken range) or "≥1.8x bodyweight" (Part-3.pdf p.3 states it as a single floor rather than a range - the two sources are not perfectly consistent, use 1.7-1.8x as the working range and confirm against the athlete's own baseline).
4. **Reactive strength/stretch-shortening-cycle function**, e.g. via a hopping task, to check the athlete can produce high force in a short timeframe before near-maximal speed.

He is explicit that a seated-calf-related injury term near ~15:51 is unclear in the audio (marked `[injury term unclear]` in the source transcript) and has been left unresolved rather than guessed.

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: "there are of course varied opinions in the field on this criteria, especially in regard to the assessment of force production capacities... it seems sensible to me and has almost zero downside" (~15:21-15:36). He states outright that these are expert-opinion, common-practice benchmarks, not results from trials - label them that way whenever they are used, and do not present the 80-85%, 1.7-1.8x, or hop-test criteria as validated thresholds.

**When to apply** — This is the single most transferable number in the course: a decision gate that Applied Performance can compute and hand to Athletic Medicine as a shared go/no-go check before a returning athlete is exposed to higher-velocity running. At Baylor, the direct instrument matches already exist: NordBord hamstring eccentric testing (retained specifically for small, clinically-targeted RTP groups per Applied Performance's own documented practice, not roster-wide), the Iso Seated Calf protocol on the ForceDecks "Mid-Thigh Pull" setting (90-degree ankle/knee position, 3 x 6-second maximal contractions, 15 s rest), and the repeated-CMJ/hop protocol already run on ForceDecks (10 reps total, n=5 pairs) as the reactive-strength check. Read ecologically, Harries' own four rungs re-map to: unopposed -> still unopposed (an arbitrary cue is not opposition) -> partly opposed -> opposed. Do not treat "closed reactivity" drills as teaching a player anything about reading a real opponent; they add unpredictability of *timing*, not unpredictability of *information*.

**Example** — The compass drill in [[framework--mdsa-drill-menu-by-level]] (Level 3) uses a coach's hand signal to cue a direction change - closed reactivity by Harries' definition, but not representative of what a defender's body actually signals in a game.

# Prescribe Early Running as Fixed Distance, Timed for Completion

**What it is** — Harries' preferred method for the first running sessions: pick a fixed distance (60, 80 or 100 m), and prescribe a target completion time rather than a "run at X% effort" instruction. This lets the practitioner plan the average speed exactly in advance: a 60 m repeat in 12 seconds equates to an 18 km/h average, with peak velocity typically 1-2 km/h higher, i.e. ~19-20 km/h (~09:14-09:58). His illustrative hamstring case-study sessions: **Session 1** - four reps each at 13 s, 12 s and 11 s over 60 m (~16.6, 18.0 and ~19.5 km/h average respectively), targeting 57-60% of that athlete's MV. **Session 2** - two reps each at 12 s, 11 s, 10.5 s, 10 s and 9.5 s over 60 m, targeting an average of ~22.7 km/h (22.2-24 km/h, ~66-69% MV) (~09:14-11:48).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: fixed-distance/timed prescription removes ambiguity about what speed the athlete actually ran, lets the practitioner plan the session's target speed ahead of time, and (with progressively increasing speed within a session) lets the athlete build confidence and learn what a given speed feels like across repetitions before being asked to hit it cold.

**When to apply** — Use for the early on-field rehab levels (submaximal running, roughly up to 70-75% MV) where steady-state pacing rather than acceleration/deceleration mechanics is the goal. It requires only a stopwatch and a measured distance, so it needs no GPS or video technology, though GPS can be layered on for confirmation.

**When NOT to apply** — Once an athlete is running above ~70-75% of MV, Harries himself moves away from full-distance timed repeats toward broken-stride timing over just the middle phase (see [[framework--broken-stride-timing-protocol]]), because a single time-for-completion over the whole distance conflates acceleration, top-speed and deceleration into one number and stops being precise enough to control intensity at higher speeds.

**Example** — See the worked session-1/session-2 numbers above; per-case variations of the same method appear in [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]] (100 m repeats at 22-26 s, ~14-16 km/h in early sessions) and [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]] (two sets of eight 100 m repeats at 14-16 then 16-18 km/h).

**Related** — [[framework--broken-stride-timing-protocol]]

# Hesitation Is a Named Readiness Red Flag, With No Way to Measure It

**What it is** — Harries names hesitation as a disqualifying sign: an athlete not confidently and willingly choosing the right action under competitive pressure (e.g., not accelerating through a gap) is, in his framing, not ready to return (~10:15-10:49, and see [[principle--competitive-exposure-required-before-return-to-play]]). He never gives a way to observe, score or record it.

**Why it works** — Harries offers no mechanism, only the assertion. It is plausible on its face: hesitation under pressure plausibly reflects unresolved fear-avoidance or a lack of trust in the injured tissue. But plausibility is not the same as a defined, repeatable observation.

**When to apply** — Flag it as exactly what it is: a real, named criterion the course itself cannot defend to an objective audience. It is a legitimate prompt to look for a way to operationalize "hesitation" (a success-rate threshold on a drill, a scripted-start/live-finish task design, video-coded decision latency) rather than to rely on a coach's unaided impression, but this course supplies none of those tools itself.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not write "athlete showed no hesitation" into a Baylor RTP note as if it were a measured criterion on par with the % MV or force benchmarks in [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]]. It is currently an unvalidated, single-observer judgment call with no defined pass/fail rule, exactly the kind of subjective criterion the 75-85% gate's objective benchmarks were designed to avoid relying on alone.

**Example** — Two athletes both clear their force benchmarks and %MV targets; one accelerates confidently through a small-sided game gap, the other visibly slows and checks his own leg before committing. Harries would treat the second as not ready, but the course gives no rule for how many hesitant reps, or what kind, would actually hold up a return decision.

**Related** — [[principle--competitive-exposure-required-before-return-to-play]]

# Progress Max Velocity Linearly, Then Undulate Near 80-85%

**What it is** — Harries' default periodization for max-velocity exposure across sessions: increase speed session-on-session in a linear fashion through the early-to-mid part of rehab, then shift to an undulating pattern (down, up, sometimes down and back up to hold a level) once the athlete approaches roughly 80-85% of MV (~21:17-22:50; confirmed Part-3.pdf p.3). His illustrative hamstring case goes linear through session 5 (50-60% -> 65-70% -> 75-80% -> 85% -> ~90-92% of MV), pushed further into the linear zone than typical (up to 90-92%) because of time pressure toward a 3-4 week return, then brings intensity down before the next jump.

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: linear progression is appropriate early because the tissue is far from its ceiling and each step is a modest incremental stress; near 80-85% MV, sessions get close enough to true maximal effort that repeating high-intensity exposures session after session risks accumulating fatigue and reload risk faster than the tissue can adapt, so alternating higher and lower sessions manages that fatigue while still working toward more >90% exposures over time.

**When to apply** — Use linear progression as the default through on-field rehab levels 1-3 (up to ~75-85% MV), then switch to an undulating high/low pattern from roughly level 3-4 onward. How long to stay linear (and how far past 85% to push before undulating) is explicitly context-dependent on time pressure, injury severity and history, not fixed.

**When NOT to apply** — Not every case in Harries' own material follows this pattern: [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] used a flat, non-undulating linear build because the low running frequency (twice weekly) meant every session was already spaced far enough apart to serve as its own recovery; forcing an undulating pattern onto a low-frequency case would be unnecessary. Do not apply the linear-then-undulate default mechanically without checking whether session frequency already provides the recovery spacing undulation is meant to create.

**Example** — Contrast [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]] and [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]] (both undulated from around session 6) against [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] (stayed linear throughout, by design).

**Related** — [[heuristic--two-exposures-above-90-percent-mv-exit-rule]]

# A Low High-Speed-Running Threshold Can Inflate Totals

**What it is** — Harries' organization set high-speed running (HSR) at >17 km/h, very-high-speed running (VHSR) at >23 km/h, and sprint at >27 km/h, and he notes 17 km/h is only roughly 55-60% of max velocity for these AFL athletes (~10:57-11:04, repeated ~22:54-23:11). Because the HSR cutoff sits at a relatively low %MV, a rep or drill that only briefly crosses it can register as a full HSR exposure and inflate the session or weekly total, even though the athlete never approached a meaningful intensity. This happened twice in his four cases: an unexpected HSR overshoot in [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]] session 2 (100 m repeats), and an unplanned overshoot in [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]] session 4.

**Why it works** — A fixed absolute speed threshold (km/h) captures a different %MV for every athlete and, within one athlete, becomes an easier bar to clear (relatively) than a %MV-based threshold would be, so longer-distance reps or drills with any build-up phase are especially prone to briefly crossing a low absolute cutoff without the practitioner intending a high-speed exposure.

**When to apply** — When reviewing GPS load reports, check where the HSR/VHSR/sprint speed cutoffs sit relative to the individual athlete's own %MV, not just the absolute km/h number; a rep or session total should be read alongside how much of it came from brief threshold crossings versus sustained high-intensity running. This is the specific point Baylor's own gap analysis should address (see When NOT to apply).

**When NOT to apply** — Do not assume these AFL-specific thresholds (17/23/27 km/h) apply to Baylor football; Baylor's own documented data dictionary is currently generic and vendor-organized rather than sport- or position-specific (`method-baseline.md`, Load monitoring and GPS section), so equivalent thresholds need to be derived from Baylor's own Catapult/OpenField data per position, not imported from this AFL cohort. A football lineman, for instance, may rarely or never reach a comparable sprint-zone speed in a game at all, which would make an imported absolute threshold meaningless for that position without being re-checked against Baylor's own data first.

**Example** — See [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]] session 4: the athlete gained confidence running in the brace and accumulated HSR via a mix of 100 m repeats and three-minute intervals, overshooting the plan - flagged by Harries as low-risk precisely because the threshold crossed was such a low %MV for that athlete.

**Related** — [[principle--percent-of-game-value-as-volume-metric]]

# Cut Running Frequency for a Recurrent Calf Injury

**What it is** — For a recurrent lateral soleus strain, Harries deliberately ran the athlete only **twice per week**, with at least 48 hours (sometimes 72-96 hours) between sessions, instead of the more frequent running used in the hamstring cases. His stated reasons: this specific athlete had responded well to reduced running frequency after past calf issues, and reduced frequency/weekly load "has also been effective in some of our recurrent calf injuries that we've come across in the past" at his organization (~27:59-28:33, ~29:53-30:01).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: lower frequency gives the calf longer recovery windows between loading bouts, which matters more for a muscle that is loaded on effectively every ground contact (unlike, say, a hamstring loaded mainly in late swing at higher speeds) and which had already re-injured once under a more standard frequency.

**When to apply** — For a recurrent (not first-time) calf/soleus strain, consider deliberately lower running frequency (e.g., twice weekly with 48+ hour gaps) as a starting strategy, especially if the athlete has a documented history of responding well to reduced frequency previously.

**When NOT to apply** — This is based on organizational pattern-matching and one athlete's own history ("he had responded well... in the past"), not a controlled comparison; it is explicitly *not* what Harries did for the hamstring cases, so do not port this frequency reduction to hamstring or other tissue types without the same recurrence-and-prior-response rationale. It also extended this athlete's total time loss to 44 days (the longest of the four cases, deliberately extended a further week for training exposure), a real cost that should be weighed against the injury-recurrence risk it aims to reduce.

**Example** — See [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] for the full case; contrast with [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]]'s six sessions across roughly the same number of weeks as this case's five sessions across a longer span.

**Related** — [[heuristic--short-to-long-vs-long-to-short-intervals-by-injury]]

# Sequence Interval Length by Which Tissue Is Injured

**What it is** — Across the four case studies, Harries used two different interval-length sequencing strategies depending on injury type. The hamstring cases ([[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]], [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]]) more commonly used a **long-to-short** approach (starting with longer repeats, e.g. 100 m, and moving toward shorter, faster efforts). The recurrent calf case ([[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]) deliberately used the opposite, a **short-to-long** model: beginning with 60 m repeats (10-12 s efforts) and progressing to longer intervals (100 m repeats at 20-24 s, then 40 s and 60 s intervals), explicitly to control the calf's cumulative local-fatigue exposure early (~31:41-32:04).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: the calf contributes disproportionately to running mechanics at all speeds (not just top speed), so short, well-spaced efforts early minimize repetitive local loading to the injured structure while still allowing systemic running-mechanics practice; longer intervals are then added once tolerance is established. For the hamstring, which is loaded more specifically during the late-swing phase at higher speeds, starting with longer, moderate-pace efforts and shortening toward faster, more targeted reps was the pattern used instead, though he does not spell out an equivalent explicit rationale for the hamstring ordering.

**When to apply** — When designing early on-field rehab running volume, consider the injured tissue's loading profile (does it load more with repetition frequency, as with calf, or more with peak intensity, as with hamstring at high speed) and choose interval length progression accordingly, rather than defaulting to one fixed sequencing rule for every lower-limb injury.

**When NOT to apply** — This is drawn from only two data points (one calf case, two hamstring cases) inside one practitioner's own case selection; Harries never states it as a general rule, and this entry infers the generalization from the pattern across his four cases. Treat it as a hypothesis worth testing against Baylor's own case data, not an established principle.

**Example** — Contrast [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]'s 60m-then-100m-then-longer intervals against [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]]'s and [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]]'s early use of 100 m repeats before moving to faster 60 m work.

# At Least One, Ideally Two, Exposures Above 90% MV Before Return

**What it is** — Harries' exit rule for on-field rehab: before returning an athlete to training or play, he wants at least one, ideally two, exposures above 90% of MV (~23:24-24:41). He is explicit there is no universal number: "I can't tell you whether you need to do one, two, or seven. That's entirely dependent on the injury... your organisational culture, your philosophy at your club... the history of that player and their soft tissue history... the pressure in that time of year." The one firm line he draws: he cannot imagine returning an athlete to training, and certainly not to play, without at least one, probably two, exposures above 90%.

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: exposures near true maximal velocity load the tissue in a way that submaximal running does not rehearse, so returning without ever having approached game-realistic top speed leaves an unrehearsed gap between rehab and competition, regardless of how much submaximal volume was accumulated.

**When to apply** — Use as a floor, not a target: before clearing a returning athlete, confirm at least one (preferably two) session exposures above 90% of that athlete's own MV have been logged and tolerated without a negative symptom response. Track exposures explicitly per athlete rather than assuming volume accumulated lower down the intensity scale is an adequate substitute.

**When NOT to apply** — This is expert opinion/common practice, not a validated cutoff, and Harries' own four case studies show it is routinely not met: [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]] returned with zero exposures above 90% (external season-timing pressure); [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]] returned with only one, when Harries "would have preferred a second." Do not treat missing this exit rule as an automatic hold on return; it is one input among the injury history, schedule and organizational context he lists, and both of his under-target cases returned to play regardless. Also do not assume "90% of max velocity" is the same absolute speed across sports or positions; it must be computed from the athlete's own MV, and Baylor's own GPS/max-velocity pipeline (Catapult/OpenField) is the source for that number, not a generic AFL threshold.

**Example** — [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] is the opposite case: because that athlete's low running frequency meant every late session ran near-maximal, he accumulated six separate exposures above 90% MV before return, far more than the stated floor, illustrating that the number is a byproduct of the chosen periodization, not a targeted count.

**Related** — [[framework--on-field-rehab-levels-with-mv-bands]]; [[heuristic--linear-then-undulating-mv-progression]]

# Competitive Exposure Is Not Optional Before Return

**What it is** — Harries states that the final stage of on-field rehab and the first return-to-training exposures must achieve both high intensity and high complexity together, and that exposing the athlete to genuinely competitive, high-pressure situations before return is "critical to successful return to play outcomes," not an optional nice-to-have. He frames the target behaviorally: the athlete must show restored ability, confidence and willingness to choose the right action in the right environment under competitive pressure, for example not hesitating to accelerate through a gap in the defense (~09:47-10:49).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: none of the locomotor actions rebuilt in isolation (running fast, cutting, decelerating) are performed in isolation during a game; they are always embedded in a competitive, time-pressured decision. If the last thing an athlete experiences before return is a controlled, cooperative drill, the first time they face real defensive pressure is in the game itself.

**When to apply** — Build the return-to-training block deliberately around live, competitive, small-sided or positional work at game-relevant intensity, not just a volume ramp of straight-line running. Treat "has he been exposed to live competitive pressure" as its own checklist item separate from "has he hit his MV and force benchmarks."

**When NOT to apply** — Harries gives no way to measure "confidence and willingness" other than by watching for hesitation, which is the exact gap this principle creates (see [[heuristic--hesitation-signals-unready-but-is-unmeasured]]). Do not treat a subjective "he looked confident" as equivalent to the objective force/velocity gates; it is a real criterion but currently an unmeasured one at Baylor, same as in Harries' own course.

**Example** — In Part 6, the athlete in [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] had his return delayed a full week specifically to add more training exposure rather than accept a physically-ready but under-exposed return; that decision reflects this principle even though it cost time.

**Related** — [[framework--intensity-complexity-two-independent-axes]]

# A Framework Is a Guide, Not a Protocol

**What it is** — Harries lists four reasons to build an on-field rehab framework rather than freelance each case: (1) it acts as a guardrail against progressing an athlete too fast into a negative reloading response or recurrence; (2) aligning it to the sport's actual performance requirements improves an athlete's preparedness on return; (3) it stays flexible enough to individualize the rehab, because "it can't be too rigid... a framework for me would be a guide, not a step-by-step process"; (4) it creates efficiency and consistency in programming and in-the-moment decisions, which in his experience raises trust between practitioner and athlete (~00:39-02:01).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: a framework externalizes the decision logic (what to progress, in what order, under what conditions) so decisions under time pressure are faster and more defensible, without pretending every case fits the same fixed sequence.

**When to apply** — Use this as the pitch for why Applied Performance should hand Athletic Medicine a shared decision structure (levels, gates, exit criteria) rather than case-by-case verbal negotiation each time an athlete nears return. It is also the justification for building the framework at all, before any of the specific numbers below.

**When NOT to apply** — A framework that hardens into a fixed protocol defeats its own stated purpose. If Applied Performance builds phased levels and % MV gates for Baylor, they need to stay adjustable to injury severity, athlete history, season timing and organizational culture, per Harries' own repeated point in the exit-rule discussion (see [[heuristic--two-exposures-above-90-percent-mv-exit-rule]]) that he "can't tell you whether you need one, two, or seven" exposures - that answer is context-dependent, not fixed by the framework.

**Example** — Two hamstring cases in Part 6 used the same levels and pillars but different session frequencies, interval formats and undulation patterns because of different injury histories (see [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] vs [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]]); the framework held, the prescription did not.

# The Intensity Levers Interact, They Don't Adjust Independently

**What it is** — Harries stresses that the eight (or four, coarser-grain) intensity levers for multidirectional speed and agility work "don't operate independently... changing one factor can actually have an impact on another factor." His examples: raising the magnitude of acceleration (velocity-change lever) forces a higher entry velocity into the following decel/COD; shrinking the available space constrains approach velocity, which in turn lowers the intensity of a cut even as it raises the drill's complexity (~07:45-08:29, ~09:47-10:11).

**Why it works** — The levers describe one interconnected physical system (an athlete's momentum and the space/time they have to change it), not eight separate knobs; pulling one necessarily moves at least one other, so treating them as independent will produce drills whose actual difficulty doesn't match what was intended.

**When to apply** — When designing or auditing a drill, always ask which other levers a given change will move, not just the one being adjusted. Use this explicitly to explain the counterintuitive case: shrinking a grid's size can *lower* the intensity of a cut (because it caps entry velocity) while simultaneously *raising* its complexity (because it now demands tighter spatial and decision-making precision) - intensity and complexity moving in opposite directions from the same manipulation.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not use this as an excuse to avoid the intensity/complexity plotting exercise in [[framework--intensity-complexity-drill-plotting-tool]]; the interactions are real but the plotting tool is specifically designed to let a practitioner reason about the net effect after accounting for them, rather than being defeated by the complexity of tracking every lever separately.

**Example** — A 3x3 m diamond-drill grid used at low intensity in early on-field rehab (see [[framework--mdsa-drill-menu-by-level]]) constrains approach velocity by space alone, which is why it can safely be introduced early even though lateral shuffling and direction changes are technically "COD" work.

# Track Running Volume as a Percent of the Athlete's Own Game Value

**What it is** — Rather than reporting HSR/VHSR/sprint volumes as raw meters, Harries tracks and reports them as a **percent of that athlete's own game-average value** for the metric, session by session: e.g. "VHSR peaked at 86% of game value by day 21," "sprint exposure... maybe around 50-60% of game demands," "session 8 peaked at 120% of game value" (Case 1 and 2, throughout Part 6). Game demand benchmarks are established from the athlete's own historical GPS data (Part 1's case-study demographic: ~13 km total distance, ~1000 m HSR, ~200 m VHSR, 40-50 accels/decels per game, 34.2 km/h MV) (~02:20-02:49).

**Why it works** — An absolute meters figure means nothing without a denominator; normalizing to "% of what this specific athlete actually does in a game" makes progress legible across the whole rehab (is this session under-, on-, or over-dosed relative to competition) and comparable across sessions and cases despite different absolute demands per position or per athlete.

**When to apply** — Build every RTP running report at Baylor around this same normalization: compute each returning athlete's own game-average HSR/VHSR/sprint/accel-decel numbers from their historical Catapult data, then report every rehab session as a % of that individual baseline, not as a raw distance. This directly operationalizes the review's stated first-ship recommendation (a Baylor velocity-band sheet reporting exactly this line per player).

**When NOT to apply** — This metric is only as good as the game-average baseline it's normalized against; a baseline built from too few games, an unrepresentative sample (e.g., mostly blowout or short-rotation games), or the wrong position comparison will distort every subsequent % figure. # Competitive Exposure Is Not Optional Before Return

**What it is** — Harries states that the final stage of on-field rehab and the first return-to-training exposures must achieve both high intensity and high complexity together, and that exposing the athlete to genuinely competitive, high-pressure situations before return is "critical to successful return to play outcomes," not an optional nice-to-have. He frames the target behaviorally: the athlete must show restored ability, confidence and willingness to choose the right action in the right environment under competitive pressure, for example not hesitating to accelerate through a gap in the defense (~09:47-10:49).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: none of the locomotor actions rebuilt in isolation (running fast, cutting, decelerating) are performed in isolation during a game; they are always embedded in a competitive, time-pressured decision. If the last thing an athlete experiences before return is a controlled, cooperative drill, the first time they face real defensive pressure is in the game itself.

**When to apply** — Build the return-to-training block deliberately around live, competitive, small-sided or positional work at game-relevant intensity, not just a volume ramp of straight-line running. Treat "has he been exposed to live competitive pressure" as its own checklist item separate from "has he hit his MV and force benchmarks."

**When NOT to apply** — Harries gives no way to measure "confidence and willingness" other than by watching for hesitation, which is the exact gap this principle creates (see [[heuristic--hesitation-signals-unready-but-is-unmeasured]]). Do not treat a subjective "he looked confident" as equivalent to the objective force/velocity gates; it is a real criterion but currently an unmeasured one at Baylor, same as in Harries' own course.

**Example** — In Part 6, the athlete in [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] had his return delayed a full week specifically to add more training exposure rather than accept a physically-ready but under-exposed return; that decision reflects this principle even though it cost time.

# A Framework Is a Guide, Not a Protocol

**What it is** — Harries lists four reasons to build an on-field rehab framework rather than freelance each case: (1) it acts as a guardrail against progressing an athlete too fast into a negative reloading response or recurrence; (2) aligning it to the sport's actual performance requirements improves an athlete's preparedness on return; (3) it stays flexible enough to individualize the rehab, because "it can't be too rigid... a framework for me would be a guide, not a step-by-step process"; (4) it creates efficiency and consistency in programming and in-the-moment decisions, which in his experience raises trust between practitioner and athlete (~00:39-02:01).

**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: a framework externalizes the decision logic (what to progress, in what order, under what conditions) so decisions under time pressure are faster and more defensible, without pretending every case fits the same fixed sequence.

**When to apply** — Use this as the pitch for why Applied Performance should hand Athletic Medicine a shared decision structure (levels, gates, exit criteria) rather than case-by-case verbal negotiation each time an athlete nears return. It is also the justification for building the framework at all, before any of the specific numbers below.

**When NOT to apply** — A framework that hardens into a fixed protocol defeats its own stated purpose. If Applied Performance builds phased levels and % MV gates for Baylor, they need to stay adjustable to injury severity, athlete history, season timing and organizational culture, per Harries' own repeated point in the exit-rule discussion (see [[heuristic--two-exposures-above-90-percent-mv-exit-rule]]) that he "can't tell you whether you need one, two, or seven" exposures - that answer is context-dependent, not fixed by the framework.

**Example** — Two hamstring cases in Part 6 used the same levels and pillars but different session frequencies, interval formats and undulation patterns because of different injury histories (see [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] vs [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]]); the framework held, the prescription did not.

# The Intensity Levers Interact, They Don't Adjust Independently

**What it is** — Harries stresses that the eight (or four, coarser-grain) intensity levers for multidirectional speed and agility work "don't operate independently... changing one factor can actually have an impact on another factor." His examples: raising the magnitude of acceleration (velocity-change lever) forces a higher entry velocity into the following decel/COD; shrinking the available space constrains approach velocity, which in turn lowers the intensity of a cut even as it raises the drill's complexity (~07:45-08:29, ~09:47-10:11).

**Why it works** — The levers describe one interconnected physical system (an athlete's momentum and the space/time they have to change it), not eight separate knobs; pulling one necessarily moves at least one other, so treating them as independent will produce drills whose actual difficulty doesn't match what was intended.

**When to apply** — When designing or auditing a drill, always ask which other levers a given change will move, not just the one being adjusted. Use this explicitly to explain the counterintuitive case: shrinking a grid's size can *lower* the intensity of a cut (because it caps entry velocity) while simultaneously *raising* its complexity (because it now demands tighter spatial and decision-making precision) - intensity and complexity moving in opposite directions from the same manipulation.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not use this as an excuse to avoid the intensity/complexity plotting exercise in [[framework--intensity-complexity-drill-plotting-tool]]; the interactions are real but the plotting tool is specifically designed to let a practitioner reason about the net effect after accounting for them, rather than being defeated by the complexity of tracking every lever separately.

**Example** — A 3x3 m diamond-drill grid used at low intensity in early on-field rehab (see [[framework--mdsa-drill-menu-by-level]]) constrains approach velocity by space alone, which is why it can safely be introduced early even though lateral shuffling and direction changes are technically "COD" work.
