# Part 1: What Every Field Sport Rehab Has in Common — Summary

**Source:** Downloaded Vimeo lesson, transcribed locally with faster-whisper small.en. The transcript is an automated draft and has not been checked word-for-word against the audio. Timestamps below refer to the video.

## Main point

On-field rehabilitation bridges gym-based rehabilitation and return to sport, preparing an athlete to handle the technical, tactical, and physical demands of their sport. The process should progress relevant movement demands while monitoring for adverse symptom responses or recurrence. The speaker says staff need clarity on two things: what physical and locomotor activities the sport requires, and how to progress an athlete's ability to perform those activities under sport-specific demands. (00:00–01:31)

## How the speaker builds the framework

- **Start with the sport’s demands.** The technical, tactical, and physical domains overlap. The speaker recommends mapping what athletes actually do, then working backward to build the rehabilitation process. (03:11–04:29)
- **Use common patterns in invasion sports.** Attacking examples include pressing upfield, running into space, carrying or passing the ball, and receiving it. Defending examples include covering, closing space, retreating, tackling, and intercepting. These are presented as recurring patterns across invasion-based team sports. (04:40–06:46)
- **Build around transferable locomotor actions.** Sprinting, accelerating, decelerating, and changing direction are identified as core movement demands. The speaker groups on-field work into submaximal and maximal velocity running, multidirectional speed and agility, and sport-specific skills. (06:46–08:32)
- **Contextualize drills.** Use the common attacking and defensive actions to build progressive drills in which athletes move to create or close space. (07:58–08:17)

## Case example and caveat

The course uses a professional AFL defensive back returning from a low-grade hamstring strain as a running example. The speaker cites match demands of about 13 km total distance, 1,000 m high-speed running, 200 m very-high-speed running, 40–50 accelerations/decelerations, and a 34.2 km/h maximum velocity. He explicitly describes it as one example; those values are not universal targets or a return-to-play standard. (02:15–03:11)

**Practical takeaway:** Start with the athlete’s sport-specific movement and skill demands, then build a staged progression from gym rehabilitation through on-field work toward sport participation. The video presents a framework, not an individualized clinical clearance protocol.

1. **HSR delivery-format progression.** HSR moves from structured 100/60 m repeats, to short intervals (10 s/10 s, 15 s/15 s, 20 s/20 s), to small-sided games and skill drills (Part 6 10:17-10:46, 23:14-23:30). This is a reusable progression rule, and it is buried inside the case entries.
2. **Fitting rehab into the team week.** Examples: high/moderate/high weeks, partial training midweek, a heavier modified session at the weekend, a walkthrough before the game (05:04-05:37, 17:40-18:10). Case 4 also cut frequency in week 5 to bridge into a "session comparable to match loads" before RTP week (37:24-38:11). Eric's review needs this for the team-week undulation.
3. **The mid-rehab hamstring checkpoint.** About 85% MV around day 14 is "a sound ceiling until further force production or reactive strength criteria are confirmed, as well as some adequate time for biological healing" (Part 6 20:40-21:02). This time-anchored version of the gate appears only in part, in the Case 2 entry.
4. **Speed prescription in late rehab.** He sets a target time plus a percentage bandwidth, "albeit with a ceiling on what is an acceptable progression for that session", with a walk-back conversation after each rep (Part 3 19:57-20:48). The broken-stride entry misstates the bandwidth as a replacement for the time and omits the ceiling.
5. **The five-element case-review template.** Each case is reviewed on the RTP timeline, loading structure, MV progression, MDSA progression, and sport-skill progression (Part 6 00:39-01:17). It is directly usable as the structure for a Baylor RTP case log.

**GO AFTER FIXES.** No entry's core claim is absent from the course, and both unclear-audio spots are preserved. 5. `heuristic--two-exposures-above-90-percent-mv-exit-rule`: Case 4 met the one-exposure floor; label the "not an automatic hold" inference as the writer's.
6. `heuristic--closed-vs-open-reactivity-drill-design` and `framework--mdsa-drill-menu-by-level`: the compass drill is not hand-signal cued; the closed-reactive drills include live-opponent cues; the 75-80% effort figure is from Part 6.
7. `heuristic--linear-then-undulating-mv-progression`: Case 3 was linear then flat, not "linear throughout".
8. `heuristic--low-speed-threshold-inflates-hsr-totals`: the "less worrying, 55-60%" remark belongs to Case 2, not Case 4; fix the threshold timestamp.
9. `heuristic--short-to-long-vs-long-to-short-intervals-by-injury`: the hamstring rationale "to control speed" is stated; drop Case 4 from the long-to-short example.
10. `case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl`: the source reconciles the COD delay; flag the week 7 vs week 8 RTP conflict.

14. `framework--invasion-sport-locomotor-pillars`: delete "low-collision"; tackling is named twice; label the contact pillar as Eric's.

   Part 3

 Linear submaximal &
 maximal running
 progressions

  The first major pillar of on-field rehab
  is the progression from submaximal to
  maximal running velocity. This pillar begins with preparing the athlete to return to
  running and continues through jogging, running, striding, and ultimately sprinting.
  Each step involves increasing intensity and mechanical demand, so a structured and
  careful progression is essential.

Sportsmith

=====PAGEBREAK=====
  Understanding running velocities

   Running speed categories can be broken down into clear ranges:
        Walking: <6 km/h, less than 25% of max velocity.
        Jogging: ~7�14 km/h, about 25�50% of max velocity.
        Running: ~14�20 km/h, 50�75% of max velocity.
        Striding: ~21�27 km/h, 75�85% of max velocity.
        Sprinting: >27 km/h, above 85% of max velocity.

   As speed increases, vertical ground reaction forces grow larger, contact times get
   shorter, and muscular power demands rise--especially at the hip, knee, and ankle.
   This has implications for injury-specific rehab: ankle-dominant strategies are more
   relevant at lower speeds, while hip-dominant mechanics dominate as athletes
   approach striding and sprinting.

  Preparation for running

   Before progressing into steady-state running, athletes should demonstrate
   competence in drills that reintroduce upright running mechanics and repetitive
   impact cycles. These include:

        Dribble walks and runs (over ankle, shin, and knee height) to reinforce front-
        side mechanics.
        Skipping drills (e.g., A-skips) to add stiffness and reactivity.
        Low-intensity jumping such as pogos and unilateral hops for repetitive loading.
        Scissor shuffles and bounds to target aggressive hip flexion and extension.
   These preparatory drills serve both as warm-ups and readiness assessments,
   ensuring athletes can tolerate dynamic impact and postural demands before
   progressing.

  Progressing running speed

   The transition from jogging to sprinting is managed across the on-field rehab
   levels:

        Level 1: ~50�70% of max velocity.
        Level 2: ~70�75%.
        Level 3: ~75�85%.
        Level 4: ~85�95%.
        Level 5: >95% up to 100%.

   Early sessions
   Structured progressions often use fixed distances (e.g., 60 m) with set completion
   times. For example:

        A 60 m run in 12 seconds equates to ~18 km/h (around 55�60% of max).
        Reps gradually increase in speed across the session, building confidence and
        tolerance.

Sportsmith

=====PAGEBREAK=====
   This method allows you to prescribe exact speeds, control intensity, and give
   athletes immediate feedback.

   Mid-stage sessions
   Once athletes progress beyond ~70�75%, sessions begin to resemble speed training

   structures, such as broken strides:
        20 m acceleration 20 m speed maintenance 20 m deceleration.
        Completion times are set for the middle phase to ensure target velocities are
        reached.
   This balances controlled exposure with athlete feedback, using recovery walks and
   ongoing communication to manage comfort and confidence.

  Criteria for progression

   Progressing beyond ~75�85% max velocity is a significant step, requiring more
   than simple tolerance. Objective criteria help guide decision-making:

        Biological healing time appropriate for the injury.
        Completion of previous running sessions with minimal pain or awareness.
        Force production benchmarks, such as:

             Eccentric hamstring strength (e.g., 80�85% of pre-injury levels via
             Nordics).
             Seated calf isometric benchmarks (e.g., 1.8� bodyweight peak force).
        Reactive strength assessments, such as hopping tasks, to ensure readiness for
        fast stretch-shortening cycle demands.
   Meeting these benchmarks provides confidence before exposing the athlete to high-
   velocity, high-risk tasks.

  Late-stage progression

   In the later stages, running speed is advanced using a combination of:
        Linear progressions: Increasing velocity session by session up to ~80�85%.
        Undulating approaches: Once above 85%, alternating sessions between higher
        and lower intensities to manage load and risk.

   For example, a minor hamstring injury may follow a linear path through 90�92%
   of max before tapering slightly, while more complex injuries may require holding
   speeds or cycling intensity over several sessions.

   Crucially, athletes should achieve at least one, but ideally two, exposures above
   90% of max velocity before being cleared for training or competition.

Sportsmith

=====PAGEBREAK=====
  Conclusion

   The progression from submaximal to maximal velocity running is a primary
   concern in on-field rehab. Each increase in speed brings greater intensity and
   mechanical demand, so athletes must be systematically prepared through
   preparatory drills, structured progressions, and objective readiness criteria. By
   combining linear and undulating approaches, and ensuring exposures above 90%
   are achieved, you can return athletes to competition with both confidence and
   resilience.

Sportsmith

   Part 4

 Multidirectional
 speed & agility
 progressions

  Multi-directional speed and agility is a
  broad umbrella term that describes an
  athlete's ability to accelerate, decelerate, change direction, and maintain speed in
  multiple movement patterns. Unlike agility in its narrow sense, which is often defined
  by cognitive and perceptual elements, multi-directional speed incorporates both the
  physical and decision-making aspects needed in sport. It is central to on-field rehab
  because these high-intensity locomotive actions occur constantly in invasion-based
  games.

Sportsmith

=====PAGEBREAK=====
  Breaking Down Multi-Directional Speed

   Multi-directional speed can be separated into three key components:
        Acceleration (short, explosive starts).
        Deceleration (rapid braking under load).
        Change of direction (angles ranging from shallow cuts to 180-degree turns).

   All three involve high rates of velocity change, which demand large ground reaction
   forces, rapid eccentric braking, and robust technical execution. This makes them
   both essential to performance and high risk if progressed poorly.

  What influences intensity?

   The intensity of multi-directional speed actions can be manipulated through
   several key variables:

        Magnitude of velocity change � larger accelerations or decelerations create
        higher demands.
        Entry velocity � higher approach speeds increase braking and change-of-
        direction loads.
        Angle of change � sharper cuts (e.g., 135� or 180�) are far more demanding
        than shallow ones.
        Preparation time/distance � more steps allow momentum to be dissipated; less
        time raises joint stress.
        Space available � smaller spaces constrain velocity; larger spaces increase
        intensity.
        Reactivity � drills range from pre-planned, closed tasks to open, reactive, or
        competitive scenarios.
   These factors rarely operate independently. For example, higher approach speeds
   also raise the eccentric braking demand of a cut, while reducing space naturally
   lowers approach velocity. Thinking about them in combination helps you design
   drills that match both the athlete's current capacity and the desired rehab outcome.

  Linking intensity and complexity

   Just as with straight-line running, two main objectives guide progression in multi-
   directional work:

     1.Intensity � how demanding the physical action is.
     2.Complexity � how unpredictable the environment is.
   Drills can be plotted on a matrix of intensity (vertical axis) and complexity
   (horizontal axis). Early rehab drills sit low on both, while later-stage drills push
   into high intensity and high complexity. This interplay aligns with the broader on-
   field rehab process: athletes must redevelop locomotive actions and then
   demonstrate them in chaotic environments.

Sportsmith

=====PAGEBREAK=====
  Practical drill progressions

   Using the hamstring case study as a reference, here's how drills might be
   introduced across on-field rehab levels:
   Levels 1�2: Competency at low intensity, controlled environments

        Curvilinear accelerations at submaximal speeds.
        Go-and-stop accelerations into controlled decelerations.
        30� cutting drills with pre-planned direction changes.
        Introductory lateral movement tasks (e.g., diamond drill, lateral shuffles).
   Level 3: Increasing velocity, introducing closed reactivity
        Fast�easy�fast accelerations with reactive elements.
        45� cutting drills with hand signals for direction changes.
        Defensive mirror drills in small squares, where the defender reacts to the
        attacker's movement.
   Level 4: High intensity, more open reactivity
        Partner chase-and-tag drills.
        Large-space compass drills combining cutting with reactive ball pickups.
        Stop-and-chase tasks that integrate turnovers and rapid deceleration.
   Level 5: Highly chaotic, near-maximal intensities
        Competitive, sport-specific scenarios using multiple athletes.
        Drills designed with constraints to replicate game unpredictability.
        Integration into small-sided games or positional training before full return.

  Building an exercise menu

   By plotting drills along the intensity�complexity continuum, you can create a
   library of exercises that match each stage of on-field rehab. For example,
   curvilinear sprints may begin as low-intensity, controlled drills, but when
   combined with a ball or reactive stimulus, they shift to higher complexity. This
   approach allows you to deliberately design progressions rather than relying on
   intuition alone.

  Conclusion

   Multi-directional speed and agility is about much more than isolated cutting drills.
   It is the structured redevelopment of acceleration, deceleration, and change-of-
   direction ability across both intensity and complexity continuums. By manipulating
   variables such as entry speed, angle, space, and reactivity, you can create drill
   progressions that take athletes from controlled, low-risk movements to chaotic,
   sport-specific tasks at maximum intensity. Only when athletes can execute these
   actions confidently in unpredictable environments should they be considered ready
   for full return.

Sportsmith

   Part 5

 Sport specific skill
 progression

  The final pillar of on-field rehab is
  sport-specific skill integration. It is not
  enough for an athlete to accelerate, decelerate, or change direction in isolation. They
  must also demonstrate the ability to perform these locomotive actions while executing
  the technical and tactical skills of their sport. This progression ensures that when they
  return to competition, they are ready for the dual challenge of physical performance
  and decision-making under realistic game conditions.

Sportsmith

=====PAGEBREAK=====
  Offensive and defensive skills

   When designing sport-specific drills, it helps to revisit the fundamental tactical and
   technical demands common across invasion sports:

        Offense: about creating space.
             Tactical actions: pressing forward, overlapping, running into space.
             Technical actions: moving with the ball, passing, kicking or throwing,
             catching or receiving.

        Defense: about closing space.
             Tactical actions: covering, retreating, closing down.
             Technical actions: tackling, intercepting, contesting possession.

   Sport-specific rehab drills must gradually reintroduce these actions, first in
   controlled settings, then under increasingly variable and competitive conditions.

  Objectives of sport-specific drills

   The overarching aims are twofold:
     1.Develop competency and capacity in executing technical skills and movement
        patterns.
     2.Expose athletes to progressively variable, unpredictable environments that
        mirror training and competition.

   In practice, this means designing drills that increase both intensity and complexity,
   leaning on the same continuums used in multi-directional speed work.

  Scaling intensity and complexity

   Several new continuums guide how sport-specific drills progress through rehab
   levels:

      Drill type: from stationary technical skills moving technical skills
      positional drills fatigued positional drills open competitive play.
     Practice structure: from blocked (repetitive, predictable) serial (sequenced,
     known order) random(unpredictable, game-like).

        Environmental demands: adding players, coaches, or constraints to create
        pressure, reactivity, and unpredictability.
   This structured progression ensures athletes move from tightly controlled
   environments in early rehab to chaotic, competitive environments in the later
   stages.

Sportsmith

=====PAGEBREAK=====
  Practical progressions by rehab level

   Using the hamstring case study as an example:
        Level 1:
             Stationary technical skills only.
             No use of the injured limb for kicking or striking.
             Low intensity, block practice structure.
        Level 2:
             Introduce injured limb for skills such as kicking.
             Begin moving technical skills, but still pre-planned and controlled.
             Low intensity, block practice.
        Level 3:
             Positional drills introduced, with predictable sequences.
             Moderate intensity but still limited opportunity for sprinting or chaotic
             scenarios.
             Mix of block and serial practice.
        Level 4:
             Random and unpredictable drills introduced.
             Pressure added from additional players or staff.
             Fatigue incorporated, testing the athlete's ability to maintain skill under
             stress.
             Greater crossover with multi-directional speed drills.
        Level 5:
             Fully evasive and competitive situations, ideally within modified training
             games.
             High complexity and high intensity, requiring athletes to combine
             technical, tactical, and locomotive actions at near-maximal levels.
             Examples: 2v1 or 2v2 competitive games, chase-and-evade scenarios with
             constraints.

  Examples of drills

        Early rehab (Levels 1�2): Stationary passing, controlled movements, low-
        velocity skill work.
        Mid rehab (Level 3): Positional skill sequences, pre-planned cutting or passing
        drills.

      Later rehab (Levels 4�5):
             2v1 attacking squares (progressing from small medium large spaces).
             Small-sided games with defensive pressure.
             End-to-end evasion drills where attackers attempt to score while defenders
             contest.
   These drills can be manipulated by space, defensive intensity, and involvement of
   additional players to ensure progressive exposure.

Sportsmith

=====PAGEBREAK=====
  Transition to training and competition

   The end goal is not just technical execution but confidence in executing those skills
   under realistic, chaotic conditions. By Level 5, athletes should be performing
   sport-specific actions at high intensity in competitive environments. The final
   transition to training involves further exposure to these demands in team settings
   before clearance for competition. For a low-grade hamstring injury, two additional
   sessions within team training may be sufficient. For more severe injuries, extended
   exposure is often required.

  Conclusion

   Sport-specific skills are the final bridge in on-field rehab. They ensure athletes can
   execute technical and tactical demands while performing locomotive actions under
   pressure. By systematically progressing drill type, practice structure, and
   environmental complexity, you create a pathway that takes athletes from
   controlled, stationary skill work to chaotic, competitive play. Only then can you be
   confident they are ready to return to their sport.

Sportsmith

   Part 6

 Case studies

  The best way to bring an on-field rehab
  framework to life is through case studies.
  Real-world examples highlight both the adaptability and consistency of these
  frameworks in practice. In this section, we look at four AFL case studies; two
  hamstring strains, a recurrent calf strain, and an MCL sprain with meniscal
  involvement. Each case shows how volume, intensity, and complexity were
  manipulated across the pillars of rehab: maximum velocity progression, multi-
  directional speed and agility, and sport-specific skill integration.

Sportsmith

=====PAGEBREAK=====
Case study 1: Proximal hamstring strain (grade 2)

Return to play: 28 days.

Structure: Six rehab sessions, three partial trainings, two full trainings.

Progression:

Early sessions focused on jog/walk intervals and 100 m repeats at controlled

paces.

Gradual increase in running speed through 60 m repeats, strides, and finally

flies.

Progression moved from linear to undulating to balance fatigue and exposure.

Athlete returned without exposure above 90% max velocity, highlighting how

external pressures (approaching finals) can alter the ideal plan.

Multi-directional speed and agility:

Early work: linear and lateral shuffles, non-reactive drills.

Mid-phase: controlled cutting, compass drills, defensive reaction tasks.

Later: evasive drills, attacking squares, small-sided handball games.

Sport-specific skills:                                         positional drills

    Stationary technical drills controlled movement drills
   under fatigue competitive play.

By the final sessions, athlete was exposed to small-group competitive play

under near match-like conditions.

Case study 2: Combined hamstring & adductor magnus strain

Return to play: 30 days.

Structure: Six rehab sessions, two modified trainings, three full trainings.

Progression:

Similar linear build to Case 1, but athlete accumulated two exposures above

90% max velocity before return, ideal for sprint readiness.

Repeat sprint intervals introduced late in rehab to simulate sprinting under

fatigue.

  Multi-directional speed and agility:
     From curvilinear runs and shuffles to cutting drills to high-velocity

evasive drills in realistic contexts.

Example: 505 drills and 2v1 attacking squares integrated into larger areas.

Sport-specific skills:                                         positional-specific

    Low-load stationary skills controlled movement drills
   sequences small-sided games (3v3, 5v5).

Athlete rejoined large group competitive play before clearance.

Case study 3: Recurrent calf strain (grade 2)

        Return to play: 44 days (deliberately extended).
        Structure: Five rehab sessions, one partial training, three full trainings.

Sportsmith

=====PAGEBREAK=====
     Key adaptation: Lower session frequency (two runs per week) with longer
     recovery periods.
Progression:
     Early: low volume, long recoveries to reduce calf fatigue.
     Progressed steadily to >90% max velocity from session four onward, repeated
     six times before return.
     Repeat sprint intervals used in later sessions to add fatigue at high speeds.
Multi-directional speed and agility:
     Reduced frequency meant each session had to carry suitable progressions.
     Early: ladders, shuffles.
     Mid: acceleration/deceleration and controlled cuts.
     Later: reactive drills, evasive 2v1 attacking squares.
     Athlete fully reintegrated into chaotic team drills before return.

   Sport-specific skills:
     Stationary skills added movement positional drills with fatigue
     competitive training.
     Athlete completed three high-quality full training exposures before clearance.

Case study 4: MCL sprain with meniscal involvement

Return to play: 49 days.

Structure: Eight rehab sessions, one partial training, four full trainings.

Key adaptation: First 3�4 weeks spent in a brace.

Progression:

Early: straight-line running only, with preparatory drills indoors.

Introduced change of direction gradually after brace removal (low intensity,

ladders, shuffles).

Later: braking drills, partner chase-and-tag, reactive cuts.

Only one exposure above 90% max velocity before return--conservative but

tolerated.

Multi-directional speed and agility:

Delayed COD work, then gradually introduced braking and reactive tasks.

Built toward high-velocity cutting and chase drills under reactivity.

Sport-specific skills:                                     positional drills under

    No skills in early stages stationary technical drills
   fatigue small competitive group play.

Athlete completed large group training in week eight before clearance.

Lessons across the cases

 Despite different injuries and contexts, several themes stand out:
     Linear undulating progression is common for max velocity exposure.
     Exposures above 90% are crucial before return, though contextual constraints
     may prevent this.

Sportsmith

=====PAGEBREAK=====
        Multi-directional speed and agility must progress from controlled to reactive
        and evasive environments, tailored to the injury.

     Sport-specific skill work always follows the same trajectory: stationary
       controlled positional fatigued competitive.

        Rehab frameworks are adaptable, but principles of intensity, complexity, and
        progressive exposure remain constant.

  Conclusion

   These case studies show that while every injury and athlete is unique, the

  Understanding running velocities

   Running speed categories can be broken down into clear ranges:
        Walking: <6 km/h, less than 25% of max velocity.
        Jogging: ~7�14 km/h, about 25�50% of max velocity.
        Running: ~14�20 km/h, 50�75% of max velocity.
        Striding: ~21�27 km/h, 75�85% of max velocity.
        Sprinting: >27 km/h, above 85% of max velocity.

   As speed increases, vertical ground reaction forces grow larger, contact times get
   shorter, and muscular power demands rise--especially at the hip, knee, and ankle.
   This has implications for injury-specific rehab: ankle-dominant strategies are more
   relevant at lower speeds, while hip-dominant mechanics dominate as athletes
   approach striding and sprinting.

  Preparation for running

   Before progressing into steady-state running, athletes should demonstrate
   competence in drills that reintroduce upright running mechanics and repetitive
   impact cycles. These include:

        Dribble walks and runs (over ankle, shin, and knee height) to reinforce front-
        side mechanics.
        Skipping drills (e.g., A-skips) to add stiffness and reactivity.
        Low-intensity jumping such as pogos and unilateral hops for repetitive loading.
        Scissor shuffles and bounds to target aggressive hip flexion and extension.
   These preparatory drills serve both as warm-ups and readiness assessments,
   ensuring athletes can tolerate dynamic impact and postural demands before
   progressing.

  Progressing running speed

   The transition from jogging to sprinting is managed across the on-field rehab
   levels:

        Level 1: ~50�70% of max velocity.
        Level 2: ~70�75%.
        Level 3: ~75�85%.
        Level 4: ~85�95%.
        Level 5: >95% up to 100%.

   Early sessions
   Structured progressions often use fixed distances (e.g., 60 m) with set completion
   times. For example:

        A 60 m run in 12 seconds equates to ~18 km/h (around 55�60% of max).
        Reps gradually increase in speed across the session, building confidence and
        tolerance.

Sportsmith

=====PAGEBREAK=====
   This method allows you to prescribe exact speeds, control intensity, and give
   athletes immediate feedback.

   Mid-stage sessions
   Once athletes progress beyond ~70�75%, sessions begin to resemble speed training

   structures, such as broken strides:
        20 m acceleration 20 m speed maintenance 20 m deceleration.
        Completion times are set for the middle phase to ensure target velocities are
        reached.
   This balances controlled exposure with athlete feedback, using recovery walks and
   ongoing communication to manage comfort and confidence.

   Progressing beyond ~75�85% max velocity is a significant step, requiring more

        Biological healing time appropriate for the injury.
        Completion of previous running sessions with minimal pain or awareness.
        Force production benchmarks, such as:

             Nordics).

  Multi-directional speed and agility is a
  broad umbrella term that describes an
  athlete's ability to accelerate, decelerate, change direction, and maintain speed in
  multiple movement patterns. Unlike agility in its narrow sense, which is often defined
  by cognitive and perceptual elements, multi-directional speed incorporates both the
  physical and decision-making aspects needed in sport. It is central to on-field rehab
  because these high-intensity locomotive actions occur constantly in invasion-based
  games.

Sportsmith

=====PAGEBREAK=====
  Breaking Down Multi-Directional Speed

   Multi-directional speed can be separated into three key components:
        Acceleration (short, explosive starts).
        Deceleration (rapid braking under load).
        Change of direction (angles ranging from shallow cuts to 180-degree turns).

   All three involve high rates of velocity change, which demand large ground reaction
   forces, rapid eccentric braking, and robust technical execution. This makes them
   both essential to performance and high risk if progressed poorly.

  What influences intensity?

   The intensity of multi-directional speed actions can be manipulated through
   several key variables:

        Magnitude of velocity change � larger accelerations or decelerations create
        higher demands.
        Entry velocity � higher approach speeds increase braking and change-of-
        direction loads.
        Angle of change � sharper cuts (e.g., 135� or 180�) are far more demanding
        than shallow ones.
        Preparation time/distance � more steps allow momentum to be dissipated; less
        time raises joint stress.
        Space available � smaller spaces constrain velocity; larger spaces increase
        intensity.
        Reactivity � drills range from pre-planned, closed tasks to open, reactive, or
        competitive scenarios.
   These factors rarely operate independently. For example, higher approach speeds
   also raise the eccentric braking demand of a cut, while reducing space naturally
   lowers approach velocity. Thinking about them in combination helps you design
   drills that match both the athlete's current capacity and the desired rehab outcome.

  Linking intensity and complexity

   Just as with straight-line running, two main objectives guide progression in multi-
   directional work:

     1.Intensity � how demanding the physical action is.
     2.Complexity � how unpredictable the environment is.
   Drills can be plotted on a matrix of intensity (vertical axis) and complexity
   (horizontal axis). Early rehab drills sit low on both, while later-stage drills push
   into high intensity and high complexity. This interplay aligns with the broader on-
   field rehab process: athletes must redevelop locomotive actions and then
   demonstrate them in chaotic environments.

   introduced across on-field rehab levels:

        Curvilinear accelerations at submaximal speeds.
        Go-and-stop accelerations into controlled decelerations.
        30� cutting drills with pre-planned direction changes.
        Introductory lateral movement tasks (e.g., diamond drill, lateral shuffles).
   Level 3: Increasing velocity, introducing closed reactivity
        Fast�easy�fast accelerations with reactive elements.
        45� cutting drills with hand signals for direction changes.
        Defensive mirror drills in small squares, where the defender reacts to the
        attacker's movement.
   Level 4: High intensity, more open reactivity
        Partner chase-and-tag drills.
        Large-space compass drills combining cutting with reactive ball pickups.

        Competitive, sport-specific scenarios using multiple athletes.

   library of exercises that match each stage of on-field rehab. For example,
   curvilinear sprints may begin as low-intensity, controlled drills, but when
   combined with a ball or reactive stimulus, they shift to higher complexity. This
   approach allows you to deliberately design progressions rather than relying on
   intuition alone.

   Multi-directional speed and agility is about much more than isolated cutting drills.

   progressions that take athletes from controlled, low-risk movements to chaotic,

   Part 5

 Sport specific skill
 progression

  The final pillar of on-field rehab is
  sport-specific skill integration. It is not
  enough for an athlete to accelerate, decelerate, or change direction in isolation. They
  must also demonstrate the ability to perform these locomotive actions while executing
  the technical and tactical skills of their sport. This progression ensures that when they
  return to competition, they are ready for the dual challenge of physical performance
  and decision-making under realistic game conditions.

Sportsmith

=====PAGEBREAK=====
  Offensive and defensive skills

   When designing sport-specific drills, it helps to revisit the fundamental tactical and
   technical demands common across invasion sports:

        Offense: about creating space.
             Tactical actions: pressing forward, overlapping, running into space.
             Technical actions: moving with the ball, passing, kicking or throwing,
             catching or receiving.

        Defense: about closing space.
             Tactical actions: covering, retreating, closing down.
             Technical actions: tackling, intercepting, contesting possession.

   Sport-specific rehab drills must gradually reintroduce these actions, first in
   controlled settings, then under increasingly variable and competitive conditions.

  Objectives of sport-specific drills

   The overarching aims are twofold:
     1.Develop competency and capacity in executing technical skills and movement
        patterns.
     2.Expose athletes to progressively variable, unpredictable environments that
        mirror training and competition.

   In practice, this means designing drills that increase both intensity and complexity,
   leaning on the same continuums used in multi-directional speed work.

  Scaling intensity and complexity

   Several new continuums guide how sport-specific drills progress through rehab
   levels:

      Drill type: from stationary technical skills moving technical skills
      positional drills fatigued positional drills open competitive play.
     Practice structure: from blocked (repetitive, predictable) serial (sequenced,
     known order) random(unpredictable, game-like).

        Environmental demands: adding players, coaches, or constraints to create
        pressure, reactivity, and unpredictability.
   This structured progression ensures athletes move from tightly controlled
   environments in early rehab to chaotic, competitive environments in the later
   stages.

Sportsmith

=====PAGEBREAK=====
  Practical progressions by rehab level

   Using the hamstring case study as an example:
        Level 1:
             Stationary technical skills only.
             No use of the injured limb for kicking or striking.
             Low intensity, block practice structure.
        Level 2:
             Introduce injured limb for skills such as kicking.
             Begin moving technical skills, but still pre-planned and controlled.
             Low intensity, block practice.
        Level 3:
             Positional drills introduced, with predictable sequences.
             Moderate intensity but still limited opportunity for sprinting or chaotic
             scenarios.
             Mix of block and serial practice.
        Level 4:
             Random and unpredictable drills introduced.
             Pressure added from additional players or staff.
             Fatigue incorporated, testing the athlete's ability to maintain skill under
             stress.
             Greater crossover with multi-directional speed drills.
        Level 5:
             Fully evasive and competitive situations, ideally within modified training
             games.
             High complexity and high intensity, requiring athletes to combine
             technical, tactical, and locomotive actions at near-maximal levels.
             Examples: 2v1 or 2v2 competitive games, chase-and-evade scenarios with
             constraints.

  Examples of drills

        Early rehab (Levels 1�2): Stationary passing, controlled movements, low-
        velocity skill work.
        Mid rehab (Level 3): Positional skill sequences, pre-planned cutting or passing
        drills.

      Later rehab (Levels 4�5):
             2v1 attacking squares (progressing from small medium large spaces).
             Small-sided games with defensive pressure.
             End-to-end evasion drills where attackers attempt to score while defenders
             contest.
   These drills can be manipulated by space, defensive intensity, and involvement of
   additional players to ensure progressive exposure.

Sportsmith

=====PAGEBREAK=====
  Transition to training and competition

   The end goal is not just technical execution but confidence in executing those skills
   under realistic, chaotic conditions. By Level 5, athletes should be performing
   sport-specific actions at high intensity in competitive environments. The final
   transition to training involves further exposure to these demands in team settings
   before clearance for competition. For a low-grade hamstring injury, two additional
   sessions within team training may be sufficient. For more severe injuries, extended
   exposure is often required.

  Conclusion

   Sport-specific skills are the final bridge in on-field rehab. They ensure athletes can
   execute technical and tactical demands while performing locomotive actions under
   pressure. By systematically progressing drill type, practice structure, and
   environmental complexity, you create a pathway that takes athletes from
   controlled, stationary skill work to chaotic, competitive play. Only then can you be
   confident they are ready to return to their sport.

# Case Study: Grade 3 MCL Sprain With Meniscal Involvement (Case 4)

**What it is** — Grade 3 MCL sprain with a posterior meniscal tear, direct contact mechanism, AFL - the only contact-mechanism, and only joint (rather than muscle-tendon), case of the four. # Case Study: Proximal Hamstring Strain, Grade 2 (Case 1)

**What it is** — Grade 2 strain at the musculotendinous junction of biceps femoris and semitendinosus, acute non-contact running mechanism, AFL. Return to play (RTP) day 28: six rehab-running sessions, three partial-training sessions, two full-training sessions (~01:53-02:18, ~04:18-05:04). Days 0-5 off legs (isometrics, low-intensity eccentrics, general strength, running-prep drills); first run day 6; running sessions days 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 17; modified training day 19; full training day 25; RTP day 28.

**Max velocity progression.** Sessions 1-2: basic running-mechanics drills, jog-walk intervals at 8-12 km/h, then 100 m repeats at a time-based pace. The source gives two figures for this: "16 to 20 kilometre average" (05:57) and, restating the same session later, "two sets of six 100 metre repeats... between 22 and 26 seconds... 14 to 16 km/h" (07:52); a 100 m repeat in 22-26 s works out to 13.8-16.4 km/h, so the second figure matches the arithmetic. Sessions 3-4: 60 m repeats progressing 13 s down to 10.5 s (18-22.5 km/h target). Session 5: strides with an acceleration/maintenance/deceleration structure targeting 70-85% MV. Session 8: continued strides plus higher-intensity flies at 85-92% MV. From session 6 onward, periodization shifted from linear to undulating. **The athlete did not reach above 90% MV before returning to play** - Harries attributes this to external pressure (approaching finals), calling it "an example of... a tension here between the ideal programming and some of the contextual demands" (~06:48-07:09).

**HSR/VHSR/sprint volumes.** Speed thresholds for this dataset: high-speed running (HSR) >17 km/h, very-high-speed running (VHSR) >23 km/h, sprint >27 km/h (~85% max for these athletes) (~09:57-10:17). VHSR peaked at 86% of game value by day 21 ("slightly lower than desired, but still okay"). Sprint-zone exposure was under-dosed: Harries states he wanted closer to 50-60% of game demands and did not get the drill design and execution right to hit it (~10:53-11:04; this passage is somewhat garbled in the transcript and should not be conflated with Case 2's separate 40%-of-game-volume under-dose at its own session 7).

**Multidirectional speed/agility (MDSA).** Session 3: introductory curvilinear/S-bend runs, forward/backward ladders, non-reactive diamond drills (low intensity, fully planned). Session 5: fast-easy-fast accelerations, go-and-stop drills, a closed-reactive compass drill (45-135 degrees at ~75-80% effort), a defensive reaction (mirror) drill. Session 8: higher-velocity crossover cuts and Z-runs at 85-90% effort, extended compass drills (added evasive movement after the cut), 2v1 attacking squares (small to large), modified handball games with obstacles (3v2, three x two-minute efforts with two-minute recovery). From session 10, MDSA was delivered mainly through sport-specific/competitive drills.

**Sport-specific skill.** Sessions 3-5: low-intensity technical actions (stationary kicking/handball), then controlled movement. From session 6: positional-specific drills under fatigue (volume/technical output under load). Sessions 8-10: competitive play in modified small-sided formats (3v2 handball), increasing decision-making demand. Full training at session 10 included large-group competitive play under near-match conditions.

Inference: this case shows the 90%-MV exit rule and the sprint-volume target can both be missed and still result in a tolerated return. This cuts against Harries' own stated floor elsewhere in the course: "I can't imagine a situation where I'd want to put an athlete back into training... if they haven't achieved at least one but probably two exposures above that 90% plus" (Part 3, 24:27-24:41). Do not read this case as evidence the floor doesn't matter, only that it can be missed under pressure.

**When NOT to apply** — This is n=1, retrospective and self-reported by the practitioner who ran it; there is no outcome data here beyond "returned to play," no re-injury follow-up window reported, and no independent verification of the %MV or %game-value figures. =================== case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl.md
---
# Case Study: Recurrent Lateral Soleus Strain, Grade 2 (Case 3)
**What it is** — Grade 2 recurrent lateral soleus strain, acute non-contact running incident, AFL. RTP day 44: five rehab-running sessions, one partial-training session, three full-training sessions. **Return to play was deliberately delayed a further week** by the medical/performance team specifically to add training exposure (~26:59-27:28). Twelve days off legs (longer than Cases 1-2); running resumed day 13 after two low-intensity running-prep sessions (days 9, 11). From that point, **running occurred only twice per week** with at least 48 hours (sometimes 72-96 hours) between sessions - a deliberate low-frequency strategy because this athlete had responded well to reduced running frequency in the past, and reduced frequency/weekly load has worked for the club's other recurrent calf injuries (~27:59-28:33).
**Max velocity progression.** Familiar stages (mechanics, 60 m repeats, strides, flies), but periodization was distinct: the first four sessions built linearly, then **from session 4 onward the athlete consistently exceeded 90% MV in every remaining session** - a flat, non-undulating pattern, which Harries attributes simply to "the low frequency" of running (29:26). Inference: the reduced frequency meant each session's spacing already provided adequate inherent recovery, so an undulating pattern was unnecessary. The athlete accumulated **six separate exposures above 90% MV before return - the most of any of the four cases** (~29:03-29:37). Session 1 deliberately used low volume and long recoveries to minimize localized calf fatigue: 60 m repeats limited to four reps per set every 45 seconds, then a couple of 100 m repeats at four reps per set every 60 seconds. Session 4 transitioned to higher intensity: progressive 60 m repeats, 60 m strides, and a single 60 m fly at 88-93% MV. The return-to-sport-phase session (~session 7) used two 60 m strides in the warm-up, three 60 m fly runs building to peak effort, and **one set** (not two, unlike Case 2) of three to four 40 m repeat sprints above 85% MV on a 30-second turnaround.
**HSR/VHSR/sprint volumes.** Sessions 1-3 deliberately held HSR very low (30-40% of match load) and did not progress it, specifically to protect the calf from cumulative loading. Interval durations followed a **short-to-long model** (60 m repeats first, progressing to longer 100 m repeats and 40-60 s intervals) - the opposite sequencing from the hamstring cases' long-to-short approach (see [[heuristic--short-to-long-vs-long-to-short-intervals-by-injury]]). Between sessions 7-9, HSR exposure was deliberately *reduced* to prioritize mechanical (accel/decel/COD) and sport-specific loads instead, once the extended timeline had already banked enough HSR volume. VHSR/sprint built linearly sessions 3-8, reaching 75% of game values on days 30 and 38 (Harries would have preferred 85-100% for more robust preparation).
**MDSA and sport-skill.** Because of the reduced running frequency, "each session entailed a suitable progression" on its own (session = progression step), rather than being spread across many sessions: sessions 2-3 change-of-direction introduction, session 4 low-velocity cutting/accel/decel, session 5 moderate velocity change with closed reactivity (the athlete placed only in the offensive role, matching his real game role), session 6 higher entry velocities and evasion in smaller spaces, sessions 7-9 high-velocity evasive MDSA fully integrated into live team training (no isolated MDSA work needed by session 7). Sport skill followed the standard stationary -> movement -> positional/fatigue -> competitive-play progression, with three high-quality full-training sessions carrying complex tactical demands before return.
**Why it works** — This case demonstrates the framework's structure (levels, intensity/complexity progression) holding while the actual periodization (frequency, undulation, interval length sequencing) was substantially rebuilt around one specific, recurring-injury constraint: minimizing cumulative local fatigue to the calf.
**When to apply** — Use as the template for adapting session frequency and interval sequencing for a *recurrent* soft-tissue injury, not just a first-time strain - see [[heuristic--reduce-frequency-for-recurrent-calf-injury]].
**When NOT to apply** — n=1, retrospective, self-reported. This is also the case with the most conservative constraint (recurrence) and the most extended timeline; its specific frequency/interval choices should not be generalized to a first-time strain of the same tissue.
**Related** — [[heuristic--reduce-frequency-for-recurrent-calf-injury]]; [[heuristic--short-to-long-vs-long-to-short-intervals-by-injury]]; [[heuristic--linear-then-undulating-mv-progression]] (this case is the exception to that default)
=================== case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl.md
---
# Case Study: Semimembranosus Strain With Adductor Magnus Involvement (Case 2)
**What it is** — Grade 2 strain, classified as "`[classification name unclear]` 2B, proximal hamstring strain with a longitudinal tendon split" (the classification system name is unclear in the audio near ~02:24 and is left unresolved here), acute non-contact running mechanism, AFL. RTP day 30: six rehab-running sessions, two modified-training sessions, three full-training sessions. **The athlete returned to play one week earlier than the medical/performance team's own recommendation** - Harries flags this explicitly as "the real world nature of decision making" (~02:36-02:46).
**Max velocity progression.** Days 0-4 off legs; two non-consecutive running exposures week 1 (days 5, 7); three non-consecutive sessions week 2, increasing intensity/volume. Sessions 1-5: linear increase (mechanics drills, time-based 100 m repeats, then faster 60 m repeats, then strides, then flies). Sessions 6-8: undulating pattern. **Two exposures above 90% MV were achieved before return**: day 22 at 96.7% and day 27 at 92.1% - Harries calls this "a strong application of progressive loading." Session 5 is stated to be functionally identical to Case 1's session 5 (60 m reps building 18-22.5 km/h, then six strides: two at 70-75%, two at 75-80%, two at ~82.5% MV, effort-based and GPS-confirmed), which he says typifies a mid-rehab max-velocity checkpoint around day 10-14 post-injury, with ~85% MV treated as a sound ceiling until force-production and reactive-strength criteria are confirmed. Session 8 (coinciding with return to full training): progressive 60 m strides, three 20 m flies at 85-95% MV, and **repeat sprint intervals**: two sets of three to four reps over 40 m, all above 85% MV, on a 30-second rolling start (rep 1 at 0 s, rep 2 at 30 s, rep 3 at 60 s) - see [[framework--repeat-sprint-interval-format-under-fatigue]].
**HSR/VHSR/sprint volumes.** Same thresholds as Case 1 (17/23/27 km/h). Session 2 produced an unexpected HSR overshoot via 100 m repeats; Harries notes this matters less here because 17 km/h is only ~55-60% of max for these athletes (see [[heuristic--low-speed-threshold-inflates-hsr-totals]]). From session 3, HSR delivered via short-interval formats (10 s on/10 s off, 20 s on/20 s off); from session 8, small-sided games contributed HSR organically. VHSR/sprint built linearly sessions 4-8, but **session 7/day 19 under-dosed at only 40% of game volume** (Harries wanted 70-80%); session 8 then peaked at 120% of game value.
**MDSA.** Sessions 2-3: basic curvilinear runs, linear/lateral shuffling. Session 4: low-velocity cutting, basic accel/decel drills. Sessions 5-6: velocity change graded up, closed reactivity (visual/verbal cues) added. Session 7: higher entry/change velocities, larger spaces, still closed-reactive. Session 8: evasive drills at lower velocities in smaller spaces (deliberately lower isolated-MDSA volume that session, offset by a fortunate scheduling window - the reserves team's bye gave more athletes for higher-quality skill-drill exposure instead). Session 9 onward: high-velocity evasive MDSA in realistic/competitive contexts.
**Sport-specific skill.** Sessions 2-3: low-load stationary handball/short kicking. Sessions 3-4: controlled movement added to technical execution. Sessions 5-6: positional-specific drills with movement fatigue. Sessions 7-8: small-group competitive play (3v3, 5v5 handball). Week 4: large-group competitive play in the main training session before return.
**Why it works** — This case shows the framework producing a well-dosed sprint exposure (two exposures >90% MV, repeat-sprint intervals for fatigue-state sprinting) even while the actual return date was moved up by organizational decision-making outside the physical-readiness plan.
**When to apply** — Use as the reference case for "physical readiness criteria met or exceeded, but the actual return decision still overridden by other factors" - a reminder that meeting the framework's numbers does not by itself control the return-to-play date.
**When NOT to apply** — n=1, retrospective, self-reported; the one-week-early return is presented as a fact of what happened, not validated as safe by any outcome data beyond it being reported without a stated recurrence.
**Example** — See [[framework--repeat-sprint-interval-format-under-fatigue]] for the reusable session-design pattern this case's session 8 exemplifies.
**Related** — [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]]; [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]
=================== claim--ankle-then-hip-dominant-speed-mechanism.md
---
# Speed Gains Shift From Ankle-Dominant to Hip-Dominant
**What it is** — Harries claims that the mechanism by which an athlete increases running speed changes as speed rises. From slow jogging to moderate running speeds (~6-7 m/s), speed is gained mainly by increasing stride length, which he calls "typically an ankle-dominant strategy... which has implications for how we might tailor the rehab to particular injuries, such as an injury to the calf or the Achilles or the ankle" (~02:44-02:53). Once an athlete reaches moderate speeds where a striding pattern emerges, further speed increases come mainly from increasing stride frequency, which he calls "typically a more hip-dominant strategy, and thus has some implications for how we might rehab injuries that are impacting or involved in movement about the hip" (~03:09-03:19). He does not spell out a specific drill-selection rule beyond these two sentences.
**Why it works** — No mechanism or citation is given beyond the assertion itself; it reads as an established coaching heuristic in sprint biomechanics circles (stride length increases dominate early acceleration, stride frequency and ground-contact mechanics dominate near top speed) but Harries presents it as fact without evidence.
**When to apply** — Inference (entry writer's application, not stated by Harries): sequence drill emphasis by injury site: for an ankle/Achilles/calf injury, prioritize competency in the lower-speed, longer-ground-contact, ankle-loaded phases (jogging, running) before pushing toward striding; for a hip-region injury (adductor, proximal hamstring), be more cautious as speed approaches the striding-to-sprinting transition where hip-dominant, higher-frequency mechanics take over.
**When NOT to apply** — This is stated as fact, not tested against Baylor's own case data or cited to a specific biomechanics source in the course. Do not use this as a precise cutoff for clearing an athlete to a given speed based on which joint "took over"; use it only as a soft prioritization heuristic, and verify any specific injury-tailoring decision against the athlete's own force-plate and Nordic/Iso Seated Calf data rather than this claim alone.
**Example** — A returning athlete with an Achilles repair would spend more deliberate time in ankle-loaded dribble/A-skip preparatory drills (see [[framework--running-prep-drill-menu]]) before advancing toward the striding-pattern band (~75-85% MV) where hip-dominant mechanics become more prominent, per this claim.
**Related** — [[framework--running-gait-speed-categories]]; [[framework--running-prep-drill-menu]]
=================== claim--speed-threshold-percent-of-max-velocity-conversion.md
---
# 17 km/h ≈ 55-60% MV, 27 km/h ≈ 85% MV, For This AFL Cohort
**What it is** — Harries states the organization's fixed GPS speed-zone cutoffs converted, for these athletes, to roughly: high-speed running threshold (17 km/h) ≈ 55-60% of max velocity; sprint threshold (27 km/h) ≈ 85% of max velocity "for most of our athletes in that club" (~09:57-10:17, ~22:54-23:11). Very-high-speed running (23 km/h) sits between the two; the entry writer's calculation from his own two figures puts it at roughly 72-80% MV, though Harries does not state that conversion explicitly.
**Why it works** — This is a cohort-average conversion, presented as an observed fact about this specific group of AFL athletes' typical max velocities relative to the club's fixed absolute speed zones, not a derived or universal formula.
**When to apply** — Use as a worked example of *how* to convert an absolute GPS speed threshold into a %MV figure for a given population, and as the reason a fixed km/h threshold behaves differently across athletes with different MVs (see [[heuristic--low-speed-threshold-inflates-hsr-totals]]).
**When NOT to apply** — This conversion is specific to Harries' AFL cohort's own average max velocities; it should not be applied to Baylor football athletes, whose MV distribution (and therefore the %MV a given km/h threshold represents) will differ by sport and very likely by position. Baylor's own speed-zone thresholds are not yet position-specific (`method-baseline.md`), so the correct move is to compute the equivalent conversion from Baylor's own Catapult MV data per player or position group, not to reuse these percentages.
**Example** — A Baylor GPS threshold set generically at, say, 16 km/h for "high-speed running" would represent a very different %MV for a 30 km/h-MV wide receiver than for a 24 km/h-MV offensive lineman; this claim is the reminder to check that conversion per player/position rather than assume it.
**Related** — [[heuristic--low-speed-threshold-inflates-hsr-totals]]; [[principle--percent-of-game-value-as-volume-metric]]
=================== framework--broken-stride-timing-protocol.md
---
# Broken-Stride Timing: Time Only the Middle Phase
**What it is** — Once an athlete progresses beyond ~70-75% of MV, Harries moves from full-distance timed repeats to a "broken stride": a run divided into an acceleration phase, a speed-maintenance phase and a deceleration phase, e.g. 60 m split into 20 m / 20 m / 20 m (adjustable, e.g. 15/10/15 to demand a more aggressive acceleration into the same target speed) (~17:01-18:20). Critically, he times only the middle (speed-maintenance) phase, not the whole distance, because that isolates the actual target speed from the acceleration and deceleration mechanics around it. Worked example: hitting 2.88-3.0 seconds across the middle phase equates to ~24-25 km/h, which is ~70-75% of that athlete's MV (~18:29-18:51); the next progression steps require 2.77-2.88 seconds through the same phase, pushing speed up roughly 1 km/h more. He prefers a stopwatch for immediate feedback, using GPS/video as a secondary confirmation of peak velocity, not the primary control method (~18:51-19:17).
**Why it works** — Inference (entry writer's rationale, not stated by Harries this way): timing the whole distance conflates three different physical demands (accelerating, holding speed, decelerating) into one number, so it can't precisely control what speed was actually reached in the middle. Harries' own stated reason is narrower: the middle-phase time is set "to equate to a given speed through that middle distance... that's going to correspond to the athlete's max velocity" (~18:18-18:29) - i.e. it gives a direct, controllable readout of the target velocity.
**When to apply** — Use from ~70-75% MV (Level 3) onward, once an athlete moves "beyond around about this 70 to 75% of max velocity" (~17:01-17:07), as the standard method for prescribing and verifying max-velocity exposures. At later levels, continue shortening the acceleration-phase distance (while keeping the target maintenance speed) to increase acceleration magnitude, and build in fatiguing conditions before high-%MV maintenance-phase reps.
**When NOT to apply** — Harries explicitly becomes "far less rigid" with these time targets in later rehab stages. He does not replace the target time with a bandwidth; he adds a percentage bandwidth in addition to the target completion time, "albeit with a ceiling on what is an acceptable progression for that session" (~20:30-20:48), because forcing a fixed time can push an athlete faster than they are comfortable with or unnecessarily hold them back; he pairs each rep with a conversation (how did that feel, are you comfortable) rather than treating the stopwatch number as absolute (~20:17-20:48). Do not apply this as a rigid pass/fail number in late-stage rehab without that check-in, and do not drop the target time itself once the bandwidth is added.
**Example** — See [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]] for the objective criteria Harries applies before letting an athlete progress past the 70-75% zone this protocol is designed to hit precisely.
**Related** — [[heuristic--fixed-distance-timed-repeats-for-pacing]]; [[framework--repeat-sprint-interval-format-under-fatigue]]
=================== framework--eight-intensity-levers-mdsa.md
---
# Eight Intensity Levers for Multidirectional Speed and Agility
**What it is** — Harries names the dials that manipulate the intensity of acceleration, deceleration and change-of-direction (COD) work. Part 4 gives six mechanical/environmental levers explicitly (~04:54-06:52; confirmed cleanly in Part-4.pdf p.2): **velocity change magnitude** (bigger accel/decel = higher force), **entry velocity** (higher approach speed raises eccentric braking demand into a decel or COD), **COD angle** (sharper cuts, e.g. 135-180 degrees, load the plant/penultimate step harder than shallow ones and raise knee joint loading), **preparation distance/time** (more distance/time to prepare allows multiple foot contacts to dissipate braking force across steps; less time raises knee valgus moment on side-step cuts), **space available** (smaller spaces constrain approach velocity), and **reactivity** (a four-rung ladder: pre-planned -> closed reactivity -> open reactivity -> evasive, ~05:53-05:57). Two further, more perceptual continuums are layered on top: **% effort** (a self-regulated prescribed effort cap, e.g. "70-75% effort today") and **% of max velocity**, giving eight total levers. In Part 6's case-study review, he re-frames this as "four main levers" (rate of velocity change, entry velocity, COD angle, and decision time/anticipation), primarily adjusted via three channels: perceived effort/intensity, space, and reactivity (~11:39-12:26) - the same set of factors, described at a coarser grain for retrospective case analysis.
**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: these are the mechanical and perceptual variables that actually determine how physically and cognitively demanding a cutting/accel/decel task is, so naming them turns "make this drill harder" from a feel-based judgment into an explicit, adjustable checklist.
**When to apply** — Use this as the input schema for designing or auditing any acceleration/deceleration/COD drill in on-field rehab: state which levers are set high or low, rather than describing a drill only by its name. Eric's review judges this "the most useful single table in the course" for building a drill-design tool or checklist.
**When NOT to apply** — The levers do not operate independently (see [[principle--intensity-levers-interact-not-independent]]); do not treat them as separately tunable dials without checking cross-effects. Eric's review judges the "reactivity" lever the course's weakest link theoretically - see [[heuristic--closed-vs-open-reactivity-drill-design]] for why "closed reactivity" as Harries defines it is not the same as game-representative information.
**Example** — See [[framework--mdsa-drill-menu-by-level]] for how these levers map onto concrete drills across on-field rehab levels 1-5.
**Related** — [[research-papers/young-2022-agility-in-invasion-sports-position-stand-of-the-iusca]] (the peer-reviewed position stand on the multidirectional-speed/agility split Harries uses informally; suggested reciprocal link: "a practitioner course's intensity-lever operationalization of this position stand's speed/agility distinction, see on-field-rtp--harries"); [[framework--intensity-complexity-drill-plotting-tool]]
=================== framework--four-step-recipe-for-building-a-rehab-framework.md
---
# A Four-Step Recipe for Building Your Own On-Field Rehab Framework
**What it is** — Harries closes the course with an explicit recipe for building a local on-field rehab framework, independent of his own specific numbers (~01:28-03:10):
1. **Split rehab into levels** - however many suits the environment (he used five; "if you want two, if you want three, if you want seven, that's up to you").
2. **Identify your pillars** - his three were submaximal/maximal velocity running, multidirectional speed and agility, and sport-specific skills; he explicitly invites extending or subdividing this list.
3. **Decide your intensity factors** - the levers used to raise or lower intensity and complexity of drills within each level/pillar (see [[framework--eight-intensity-levers-mdsa]]).
4. **Decide which exercises/drills** fit into each level, pillar and intensity-factor combination.
He closes with an explicit disclaimer: "there is very rarely a right way or a wrong way to do things in rehab... it is just one perspective... find what works for you and your environment," restating that the two equally important objectives throughout are progressing intensity and progressing complexity of sport-relevant locomotor activity.
**Why it works** — This is a template-of-a-template: rather than prescribing Harries' own five levels and three pillars as fixed, it gives the four design decisions that produced them, so a practitioner in a different sport can rebuild an equivalent framework suited to that sport's own demands.
**When to apply** — Use this exact four-step sequence as the design process for a Baylor-football-specific on-field rehab framework: keep Harries' levels/intensity-lever logic, and build a football-specific drill menu at step 4 rather than reusing his AFL drill catalogue directly. Eric's review proposes adding a contact/collision pillar at step 2 (per [[framework--invasion-sport-locomotor-pillars]]); that is a proposed addition, not something Harries' course itself specifies.
**When NOT to apply** — This recipe describes how to *build* a framework's structure; it says nothing about the specific thresholds, force benchmarks or exit criteria a framework needs to be safe (that layer is [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]] and [[heuristic--two-exposures-above-90-percent-mv-exit-rule]]). Building the four steps is necessary but not sufficient for a clinically defensible RTP process.
**Example** — Applied Performance's own review of this course already used exactly this four-step logic to plan next work: keep Harries' five levels and eight-lever table, add a football-specific contact pillar with its own dials (opponent size/intent, stance/start, hand-fighting, live vs. thud), and build a drill menu on the resulting intensity x complexity matrix by position group.
**Related** — [[framework--invasion-sport-locomotor-pillars]]; [[framework--eight-intensity-levers-mdsa]]
