Session 2 produced an unexpected HSR overshoot via 100 m repeats; Harries notes this matters less here because 17 km/h is only ~55-60% of max for these athletes (see [[heuristic--low-speed-threshold-inflates-hsr-totals]]). From session 3, HSR delivered via short-interval formats (10 s on/10 s off, 20 s on/20 s off); from session 8, small-sided games contributed HSR organically. VHSR/sprint built linearly sessions 4-8, but **session 7/day 19 under-dosed at only 40% of game volume** (Harries wanted 70-80%); session 8 then peaked at 120% of game value.
**MDSA.** Sessions 2-3: basic curvilinear runs, linear/lateral shuffling. Session 4: low-velocity cutting, basic accel/decel drills. Sessions 5-6: velocity change graded up, closed reactivity (visual/verbal cues) added. Session 7: higher entry/change velocities, larger spaces, still closed-reactive. Session 8: evasive drills at lower velocities in smaller spaces (deliberately lower isolated-MDSA volume that session, offset by a fortunate scheduling window - the reserves team's bye gave more athletes for higher-quality skill-drill exposure instead). Session 9 onward: high-velocity evasive MDSA in realistic/competitive contexts.
**Sport-specific skill.** Sessions 2-3: low-load stationary handball/short kicking. Sessions 3-4: controlled movement added to technical execution. Sessions 5-6: positional-specific drills with movement fatigue. Sessions 7-8: small-group competitive play (3v3, 5v5 handball). Week 4: large-group competitive play in the main training session before return.
**Why it works** — This case shows the framework producing a well-dosed sprint exposure (two exposures >90% MV, repeat-sprint intervals for fatigue-state sprinting) even while the actual return date was moved up by organizational decision-making outside the physical-readiness plan.
**When to apply** — Use as the reference case for "physical readiness criteria met or exceeded, but the actual return decision still overridden by other factors" - a reminder that meeting the framework's numbers does not by itself control the return-to-play date.
**When NOT to apply** — n=1, retrospective, self-reported; the one-week-early return is presented as a fact of what happened, not validated as safe by any outcome data beyond it being reported without a stated recurrence.
**Example** — See [[framework--repeat-sprint-interval-format-under-fatigue]] for the reusable session-design pattern this case's session 8 exemplifies.
**Related** — [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]]; [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]
=================== claim--ankle-then-hip-dominant-speed-mechanism.md
---
# Speed Gains Shift From Ankle-Dominant to Hip-Dominant
**What it is** — Harries claims that the mechanism by which an athlete increases running speed changes as speed rises. From slow jogging to moderate running speeds (~6-7 m/s), speed is gained mainly by increasing stride length, which he calls "typically an ankle-dominant strategy... which has implications for how we might tailor the rehab to particular injuries, such as an injury to the calf or the Achilles or the ankle" (~02:44-02:53). Once an athlete reaches moderate speeds where a striding pattern emerges, further speed increases come mainly from increasing stride frequency, which he calls "typically a more hip-dominant strategy, and thus has some implications for how we might rehab injuries that are impacting or involved in movement about the hip" (~03:09-03:19). He does not spell out a specific drill-selection rule beyond these two sentences.
**Why it works** — No mechanism or citation is given beyond the assertion itself; it reads as an established coaching heuristic in sprint biomechanics circles (stride length increases dominate early acceleration, stride frequency and ground-contact mechanics dominate near top speed) but Harries presents it as fact without evidence.
**When to apply** — Inference (entry writer's application, not stated by Harries): sequence drill emphasis by injury site: for an ankle/Achilles/calf injury, prioritize competency in the lower-speed, longer-ground-contact, ankle-loaded phases (jogging, running) before pushing toward striding; for a hip-region injury (adductor, proximal hamstring), be more cautious as speed approaches the striding-to-sprinting transition where hip-dominant, higher-frequency mechanics take over.
**When NOT to apply** — This is stated as fact, not tested against Baylor's own case data or cited to a specific biomechanics source in the course. Do not use this as a precise cutoff for clearing an athlete to a given speed based on which joint "took over"; use it only as a soft prioritization heuristic, and verify any specific injury-tailoring decision against the athlete's own force-plate and Nordic/Iso Seated Calf data rather than this claim alone.
**Example** — A returning athlete with an Achilles repair would spend more deliberate time in ankle-loaded dribble/A-skip preparatory drills (see [[framework--running-prep-drill-menu]]) before advancing toward the striding-pattern band (~75-85% MV) where hip-dominant mechanics become more prominent, per this claim.
**Related** — [[framework--running-gait-speed-categories]]; [[framework--running-prep-drill-menu]]
=================== claim--speed-threshold-percent-of-max-velocity-conversion.md
---
# 17 km/h ≈ 55-60% MV, 27 km/h ≈ 85% MV, For This AFL Cohort
**What it is** — Harries states the organization's fixed GPS speed-zone cutoffs converted, for these athletes, to roughly: high-speed running threshold (17 km/h) ≈ 55-60% of max velocity; sprint threshold (27 km/h) ≈ 85% of max velocity "for most of our athletes in that club" (~09:57-10:17, ~22:54-23:11). Very-high-speed running (23 km/h) sits between the two; the entry writer's calculation from his own two figures puts it at roughly 72-80% MV, though Harries does not state that conversion explicitly.
**Why it works** — This is a cohort-average conversion, presented as an observed fact about this specific group of AFL athletes' typical max velocities relative to the club's fixed absolute speed zones, not a derived or universal formula.
**When to apply** — Use as a worked example of *how* to convert an absolute GPS speed threshold into a %MV figure for a given population, and as the reason a fixed km/h threshold behaves differently across athletes with different MVs (see [[heuristic--low-speed-threshold-inflates-hsr-totals]]).
**When NOT to apply** — This conversion is specific to Harries' AFL cohort's own average max velocities; it should not be applied to Baylor football athletes, whose MV distribution (and therefore the %MV a given km/h threshold represents) will differ by sport and very likely by position. Baylor's own speed-zone thresholds are not yet position-specific (`method-baseline.md`), so the correct move is to compute the equivalent conversion from Baylor's own Catapult MV data per player or position group, not to reuse these percentages.
**Example** — A Baylor GPS threshold set generically at, say, 16 km/h for "high-speed running" would represent a very different %MV for a 30 km/h-MV wide receiver than for a 24 km/h-MV offensive lineman; this claim is the reminder to check that conversion per player/position rather than assume it.
**Related** — [[heuristic--low-speed-threshold-inflates-hsr-totals]]; [[principle--percent-of-game-value-as-volume-metric]]
=================== framework--broken-stride-timing-protocol.md
---
# Broken-Stride Timing: Time Only the Middle Phase
**What it is** — Once an athlete progresses beyond ~70-75% of MV, Harries moves from full-distance timed repeats to a "broken stride": a run divided into an acceleration phase, a speed-maintenance phase and a deceleration phase, e.g. 60 m split into 20 m / 20 m / 20 m (adjustable, e.g. 15/10/15 to demand a more aggressive acceleration into the same target speed) (~17:01-18:20). Critically, he times only the middle (speed-maintenance) phase, not the whole distance, because that isolates the actual target speed from the acceleration and deceleration mechanics around it. Worked example: hitting 2.88-3.0 seconds across the middle phase equates to ~24-25 km/h, which is ~70-75% of that athlete's MV (~18:29-18:51); the next progression steps require 2.77-2.88 seconds through the same phase, pushing speed up roughly 1 km/h more. He prefers a stopwatch for immediate feedback, using GPS/video as a secondary confirmation of peak velocity, not the primary control method (~18:51-19:17).
**Why it works** — Inference (entry writer's rationale, not stated by Harries this way): timing the whole distance conflates three different physical demands (accelerating, holding speed, decelerating) into one number, so it can't precisely control what speed was actually reached in the middle. Harries' own stated reason is narrower: the middle-phase time is set "to equate to a given speed through that middle distance... that's going to correspond to the athlete's max velocity" (~18:18-18:29) - i.e. it gives a direct, controllable readout of the target velocity.
**When to apply** — Use from ~70-75% MV (Level 3) onward, once an athlete moves "beyond around about this 70 to 75% of max velocity" (~17:01-17:07), as the standard method for prescribing and verifying max-velocity exposures. At later levels, continue shortening the acceleration-phase distance (while keeping the target maintenance speed) to increase acceleration magnitude, and build in fatiguing conditions before high-%MV maintenance-phase reps.
**When NOT to apply** — Harries explicitly becomes "far less rigid" with these time targets in later rehab stages. He does not replace the target time with a bandwidth; he adds a percentage bandwidth in addition to the target completion time, "albeit with a ceiling on what is an acceptable progression for that session" (~20:30-20:48), because forcing a fixed time can push an athlete faster than they are comfortable with or unnecessarily hold them back; he pairs each rep with a conversation (how did that feel, are you comfortable) rather than treating the stopwatch number as absolute (~20:17-20:48). Do not apply this as a rigid pass/fail number in late-stage rehab without that check-in, and do not drop the target time itself once the bandwidth is added.
**Example** — See [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]] for the objective criteria Harries applies before letting an athlete progress past the 70-75% zone this protocol is designed to hit precisely.
**Related** — [[heuristic--fixed-distance-timed-repeats-for-pacing]]; [[framework--repeat-sprint-interval-format-under-fatigue]]
=================== framework--eight-intensity-levers-mdsa.md
---
# Eight Intensity Levers for Multidirectional Speed and Agility
**What it is** — Harries names the dials that manipulate the intensity of acceleration, deceleration and change-of-direction (COD) work. Part 4 gives six mechanical/environmental levers explicitly (~04:54-06:52; confirmed cleanly in Part-4.pdf p.2): **velocity change magnitude** (bigger accel/decel = higher force), **entry velocity** (higher approach speed raises eccentric braking demand into a decel or COD), **COD angle** (sharper cuts, e.g. 135-180 degrees, load the plant/penultimate step harder than shallow ones and raise knee joint loading), **preparation distance/time** (more distance/time to prepare allows multiple foot contacts to dissipate braking force across steps; less time raises knee valgus moment on side-step cuts), **space available** (smaller spaces constrain approach velocity), and **reactivity** (a four-rung ladder: pre-planned -> closed reactivity -> open reactivity -> evasive, ~05:53-05:57). Two further, more perceptual continuums are layered on top: **% effort** (a self-regulated prescribed effort cap, e.g. "70-75% effort today") and **% of max velocity**, giving eight total levers. In Part 6's case-study review, he re-frames this as "four main levers" (rate of velocity change, entry velocity, COD angle, and decision time/anticipation), primarily adjusted via three channels: perceived effort/intensity, space, and reactivity (~11:39-12:26) - the same set of factors, described at a coarser grain for retrospective case analysis.
**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: these are the mechanical and perceptual variables that actually determine how physically and cognitively demanding a cutting/accel/decel task is, so naming them turns "make this drill harder" from a feel-based judgment into an explicit, adjustable checklist.
**When to apply** — Use this as the input schema for designing or auditing any acceleration/deceleration/COD drill in on-field rehab: state which levers are set high or low, rather than describing a drill only by its name. Eric's review judges this "the most useful single table in the course" for building a drill-design tool or checklist.
**When NOT to apply** — The levers do not operate independently (see [[principle--intensity-levers-interact-not-independent]]); do not treat them as separately tunable dials without checking cross-effects. Eric's review judges the "reactivity" lever the course's weakest link theoretically - see [[heuristic--closed-vs-open-reactivity-drill-design]] for why "closed reactivity" as Harries defines it is not the same as game-representative information.
**Example** — See [[framework--mdsa-drill-menu-by-level]] for how these levers map onto concrete drills across on-field rehab levels 1-5.
**Related** — [[research-papers/young-2022-agility-in-invasion-sports-position-stand-of-the-iusca]] (the peer-reviewed position stand on the multidirectional-speed/agility split Harries uses informally; suggested reciprocal link: "a practitioner course's intensity-lever operationalization of this position stand's speed/agility distinction, see on-field-rtp--harries"); [[framework--intensity-complexity-drill-plotting-tool]]
=================== framework--four-step-recipe-for-building-a-rehab-framework.md
---
# A Four-Step Recipe for Building Your Own On-Field Rehab Framework
**What it is** — Harries closes the course with an explicit recipe for building a local on-field rehab framework, independent of his own specific numbers (~01:28-03:10):
1. **Split rehab into levels** - however many suits the environment (he used five; "if you want two, if you want three, if you want seven, that's up to you").
2. **Identify your pillars** - his three were submaximal/maximal velocity running, multidirectional speed and agility, and sport-specific skills; he explicitly invites extending or subdividing this list.
3. **Decide your intensity factors** - the levers used to raise or lower intensity and complexity of drills within each level/pillar (see [[framework--eight-intensity-levers-mdsa]]).
4. **Decide which exercises/drills** fit into each level, pillar and intensity-factor combination.
He closes with an explicit disclaimer: "there is very rarely a right way or a wrong way to do things in rehab... it is just one perspective... find what works for you and your environment," restating that the two equally important objectives throughout are progressing intensity and progressing complexity of sport-relevant locomotor activity.
**Why it works** — This is a template-of-a-template: rather than prescribing Harries' own five levels and three pillars as fixed, it gives the four design decisions that produced them, so a practitioner in a different sport can rebuild an equivalent framework suited to that sport's own demands.
**When to apply** — Use this exact four-step sequence as the design process for a Baylor-football-specific on-field rehab framework: keep Harries' levels/intensity-lever logic, and build a football-specific drill menu at step 4 rather than reusing his AFL drill catalogue directly. Eric's review proposes adding a contact/collision pillar at step 2 (per [[framework--invasion-sport-locomotor-pillars]]); that is a proposed addition, not something Harries' course itself specifies.
**When NOT to apply** — This recipe describes how to *build* a framework's structure; it says nothing about the specific thresholds, force benchmarks or exit criteria a framework needs to be safe (that layer is [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]] and [[heuristic--two-exposures-above-90-percent-mv-exit-rule]]). Building the four steps is necessary but not sufficient for a clinically defensible RTP process.
**Example** — Applied Performance's own review of this course already used exactly this four-step logic to plan next work: keep Harries' five levels and eight-lever table, add a football-specific contact pillar with its own dials (opponent size/intent, stance/start, hand-fighting, live vs. thud), and build a drill menu on the resulting intensity x complexity matrix by position group.
**Related** — [[framework--invasion-sport-locomotor-pillars]]; [[framework--eight-intensity-levers-mdsa]]

=================== framework--intensity-complexity-two-independent-axes.md
---
chapter: "2"
confidence: supported
---
# Intensity and Complexity as Two Independent Axes
**What it is** — Harries frames on-field rehab progression along two separate continuums that must both be advanced but do not have to move together. **Intensity** runs from a competency focus (reintroducing movements, building toward submaximal) to a capacity focus (submaximal through maximal, under added metabolic/mechanical demand). **Complexity** runs along what he explicitly credits as Matt Taberner's control-to-chaos continuum: control means high structure, predictable behavior/actions/movement (low risk); chaos means unpredictable, random or reactive behavior (high risk) (~04:48-08:00). Early on-field rehab levels are low-complexity and highly controlled; later levels deliberately build unpredictability. The **explicit misconception he corrects**: moving to a later on-field rehab level does not mean every drill in that level becomes more chaotic. Some locomotor actions are still climbing the intensity continuum (submaximal to maximal) and need a controlled environment even at a late stage, while other, already-developed actions can be pushed into more complex environments sooner (~08:44-09:47). By the end of on-field rehab, the target is both high intensity and high complexity simultaneously.
**Why it works** — Treating intensity and complexity as one variable causes two failure modes: pushing speed and unpredictability up together (risking a reload injury before the athlete can handle either alone), or holding both down together (leaving the athlete underprepared for the chaos of competition even though physically capable). Separating them lets a practitioner grade each independently and combine them deliberately only when both are ready.
**When to apply** — Use this distinction explicitly with Athletic Medicine and coaching staff: "he's ready for near-max speed but not yet ready for it in an unpredictable drill" is a defensible, gradeable statement under this framework, whereas "he's at level 4" alone is not. Baylor's own control-chaos foundation is Taberner's own published work already in the library (see Related). Eric's review argues Harries adds nothing new to the theory here; his contribution is packaging it with the specific %MV numbers (see [[framework--on-field-rehab-levels-with-mv-bands]]).
**When NOT to apply** — Eric's review argues the complexity axis as Harries operationalizes it rests on an older, information-processing model of motor learning (blocked-to-serial-to-random practice, described in Part 5; see [[framework--practice-structure-block-serial-random-by-level]]), not on ecological dynamics/representative learning design. Eric's review's example: Harries' "closed reactivity" is a coach throwing a hand signal - a generic, arbitrary stimulus, not the game-relevant information a player actually reads (a defender's hips, a gap opening). Harries himself names "constraints-based learning design" once, in this same module, and never operationalizes it. Eric's review argues that in this model, complexity is switched on once intensity is judged safe, while in an ecological model representative information should be present and scaled from the start, not withheld until Level 4. This is disputed by the library's ecological-dynamics sources, not a reason to discard the intensity/complexity distinction itself, which still holds and stays `supported`.
**Example** — A hamstring athlete at 82% max velocity with force benchmarks not yet cleared should still run in a controlled, closed environment even if his skill work has already moved to a positional, semi-random drill; conversely, an athlete cleared on force benchmarks but still hesitant in decision-making needs complexity pushed even at a plateaued running intensity.
**Related** — [[research-papers/taberner-2022-contextual-considerations-using-the-control-chaos-continuum-for-return-to-sport-in-elite-f]] (Taberner's own control-chaos continuum, the framework Harries is built on: suggested reciprocal link, "applied and re-dosed by a Sportsmith practitioner course, see on-field-rtp--harries"); [[research-papers/taberner-2019-physical-preparation-and-return-to-sport-of-the-football-player-with-a-tibia-fibula-fractu]]; [[skill-acquisition/enhancing-skill--myszka/framework--nonlinear-pedagogy-and-constraint-classes]] and [[skill-acquisition/enhancing-skill--myszka/principle--representative-design]] (the ecological-dynamics alternative to Harries' complexity operationalization); [[framework--practice-structure-block-serial-random-by-level]]
=================== framework--invasion-sport-locomotor-pillars.md
---
chapter: "1"
confidence: supported
---
# Invasion-Sport Locomotor Pillars
**What it is** — Harries' starting point for building any on-field rehab process: map a sport's technical, tactical and physical domains, then simplify by using what invasion-based team sports (e.g. soccer, AFL) have in common. He uses "football" to mean soccer (Part 1 ~03:37); he never names American football or rugby specifically. Every invasion sport reduces to two tactical patterns, offense (creating space: pressing forward, overlapping, running into space; technically: moving/passing/catching the ball) and defense (closing space: covering, retreating, closing down; technically: tackling, intercepting, contesting possession) (~03:33-06:46). Underneath both are the same physical actions: sprinting, accelerating, decelerating and changing direction. He names these four as the **primary locomotor pillars of on-field rehab**, usable as a starting template "to any rehab running framework you create" regardless of sport (~07:41-08:22).
**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: the exact loading numbers differ by sport, but the actual locomotor actions "don't change too much" across invasion sports, so building a rehab framework around them is a transferable shortcut instead of having to model every sport's full technical/tactical catalogue from scratch (~07:19-07:41).
**When to apply** — Use as the skeleton for any Baylor RTP conversation with Athletic Medicine: whatever the sport or position, the questions are the same four - can this athlete sprint, accelerate, decelerate and change direction at the required intensity, in an environment as complex as competition. It gives Applied Performance and Athletic Medicine a shared, sport-agnostic starting vocabulary before adding position-specific detail (GPS zones, skill demands).
**When NOT to apply** — Harries' own case-study sport is AFL, a continuous invasion game. Two gaps matter for Baylor football specifically: (1) Eric's review: **contact is missing as a pillar.** Tackling is named (Part 1 ~06:34, "tackling of various kinds"; Part 5 ~02:03) but never given its own progression. For football, collision and contact (block, shed, tackle, hand-fight, stance start) functions as a fourth pillar with its own dosage question, and this course gives it none. (2) The four pillars are a taxonomy of locomotor actions, not a testing or clearance protocol; they tell you what to progress, not how much force production or healing time is required before progressing it (see [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]] for that layer). Do not treat "the four pillars are covered" as equivalent to "the athlete is ready."
**Example** — A returning offensive lineman needs sprint/accel/decel/COD rebuilt like any other position, but the highest-risk gap in his return is a pillar this course never names: reintroducing collision tolerance. That has to be built separately, in coordination with position coaching, not inferred from his running progression.
**Related** — [[framework--on-field-rehab-levels-with-mv-bands]] (how the levels operationalize these pillars); Baylor's own documented gap that GPS/load thresholds are not yet sport- or position-specific (`method-baseline.md`, Load monitoring and GPS).

# Multidirectional Speed & Agility Drill Menu by On-Field Rehab Level
**What it is** — Harries' worked drill menu for the hamstring case study, by level (~11:56-21:11; confirmed Part-4.pdf p.3):
- **Levels 1-2** (low intensity, low complexity): fast-easy-fast accelerations (accelerate ~5 m, ease off, re-accelerate); go-and-stop accelerations (accelerate a set distance, brake to a stop in a deceleration zone); curvy-linear ("half bend") accelerations; 30-degree cutting gates with a pre-planned side step, crossover step, or split step; a 3x3 m diamond/square drill with athlete-chosen lateral/forward/backward shuffling.
- **Level 3** (rising velocity/space, controlled/closed reactivity introduced): fast-easy-fast acceleration with a closed-reactive defender (defender moves laterally to open space); a defensive reaction (mirror) drill in a small square; a "compass drill" where the athlete pre-determines a 45/90/135-degree direction change (17:00-17:21). A separate example - a 45-degree cutting drill cued by a coach's hand signal - is what Harries uses to introduce the concept of closed reactivity (15:50-16:06); it is not the compass drill. The ~75-80% effort figure for the compass drill comes from the Case 1 worked example in Part 6, not Part 4 (Part 6, 13:52-14:01).
- **Level 4** (near-maximal velocity, bigger spaces, more open reactivity): partner chase-and-tag; a large-space gate drill with a turnover cue requiring a hard deceleration and chase; a reactive compass drill in a bigger space followed by a second reactive task (react to a rolled ball). Part 4 puts Level 4 velocity at ~80-85% (18:21-18:23); this is below the ~85-95% Level 4 band in [[framework--on-field-rehab-levels-with-mv-bands]], which is a linear-running band, not necessarily the same figure as MDSA velocity - the course does not reconcile the two numbers.
- **Level 5** (highly chaotic, near-maximal/maximal): sport-specific, competitive, multi-athlete scenarios; where extra players/coaches aren't available, use constrained drills designed to replicate unpredictability as closely as possible.
**Why it works** — Each level's drills are the concrete output of running the levers in [[framework--eight-intensity-levers-mdsa]] through the plotting exercise in [[framework--intensity-complexity-drill-plotting-tool]]: space shrinks or grows, reactivity moves from none to closed to open, and entry velocity/COD angle both rise, in a sequence matched to the level's target physical readiness.
**When to apply** — Use this menu as a starting drill bank for building a Baylor-specific version; the drill *shapes* (accelerate-then-react, gated cutting, chase-and-tag, compass drill) transfer across sports even where the specific angles or spaces would be adjusted for football positions.
**When NOT to apply** — This is one practitioner's AFL menu, built for an athlete with no contact restriction; none of these drills involve or prepare for a blocking, tackling or hand-fighting demand, so a football-specific menu needs an added contact-drill category this course does not supply (see [[framework--invasion-sport-locomotor-pillars]]). Eric's review argues the Level 3 closed-reactive cues (hand signal, mirrored defender) are generic, while later levels already add opponent- and ball-based cues (partner chase-and-tag, turnover cue, rolled ball) - see [[heuristic--closed-vs-open-reactivity-drill-design]] for the fuller critique.
**Example** — In [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]], sessions 3, 5 and 8 map closely onto this Level 1-3 / Level 3-4 / Level 4-5 menu progression.
**Related** — [[framework--eight-intensity-levers-mdsa]]; [[heuristic--closed-vs-open-reactivity-drill-design]]
=================== framework--on-field-rehab-levels-with-mv-bands.md
---
chapter: "3"
confidence: supported
---
# The Five On-Field Rehab Levels, With Max-Velocity Bands
**What it is** — Harries splits on-field rehab into five levels, aligned to early/mid/late rehab, followed by return-to-training and return-to-play (Part 2, ~02:54-04:16). Each level targets a max-velocity (MV) band for linear running (Part 3, ~08:39-09:14; confirmed Part-3.pdf p.2):
| Level | Target % of max velocity |
|---|---|
| 1 | ~50-70% |
| 2 | ~70-75% |
| 3 | ~75-85% |
| 4 | ~85-95% |
| 5 | >95% up to 100% |
For his illustrative low-grade hamstring case, this maps to one session per level (sessions 1-5), then two return-to-training sessions (sessions 6-7) with the team, then return to play as session 8 (~03:30-04:16). He is explicit this is a minor-injury example: "with a more severe injury or different type of injury... you may do a number of sessions in each level before moving on."
**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: splitting rehab into named levels gives structure to the gradual stressing of sport-specific locomotor actions, aligned to where the athlete sits in the overall rehab (gym-based early, on-field mid, transition-to-training late).
**When to apply** — Use the five-level structure as the shared vocabulary between Applied Performance and Athletic Medicine: "Level 3" means a defined, measurable thing (75-85% of *that athlete's own* MV, from the Catapult pipeline), not a vague stage description. The number of sessions per level is explicitly not fixed by the framework and should scale with injury severity and history (see [[principle--framework-is-a-guide-not-a-protocol]]).

# Block, Then Serial, Then Random Practice Across the Levels
**What it is** — Harries maps sport-specific skill drills onto a practice-structure continuum borrowed from motor-learning theory: **block practice** (the same drill repeated, low variability), **serial practice** (a known sequence of actions, predictable order), and **random practice** (unpredictable, variable order/decisions). He assigns these across levels (~04:03-07:26, confirmed Part-5.pdf p.2-3: p.2 states the general block-to-serial-to-random progression, p.3 gives the per-level breakdown): Level 1 - solely block, tightly controlled; Level 2 - still block, intensity of the drills rises; Level 3 - roughly 50/50 block and serial, chaining action sequences; Level 4 - block dropped entirely, mostly serial with some random; Level 5 - substantial random practice, with some serial retained deliberately for actions not yet ready for full unpredictability. On return to training, levels 1-2 of training itself are "pretty much all" random.
**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: block-to-serial-to-random is a graded route from fully predictable to fully unpredictable practice, which lets an athlete build a skill under low cognitive/decision load first and only add decision-making demand once the movement itself is competent.
**When to apply** — Use the general shape (predictable early, unpredictable late) as the practice-structure axis alongside drill type and movement level (see [[framework--sport-skill-drill-type-continuum-by-level]]) when designing sport-specific skill sessions.
**When NOT to apply** — **Contested.** Eric's review argues that block/serial/random and its associated "contextual interference effect" come from the Schmidt information-processing tradition of motor learning, not from ecological dynamics/representative learning design, which the library's skill-acquisition sources treat as the better-supported model for sport skill transfer. The practical difference: under an information-processing view, predictability itself is the variable being controlled, and the task's informational content is secondary; under an ecological view, the key variable is whether the *information* driving the action is representative of the game (a real defender, a real developing gap) regardless of how "predictable" the drill's structure is. A block-practice drill against a live, representative defender can be more transferable than a "random" drill built on arbitrary, non-representative cues. Do not assume moving along this block-serial-random axis is equivalent to moving toward game transfer; check whether the *information* in the drill, not just its unpredictability, is representative.
**Example** — Harries' own hamstring case study at Level 1 uses stationary, block-practiced kicking with the uninjured limb only (see [[principle--tailor-skill-restrictions-to-injured-structure]]); by Level 5 it moves to a 2v1 attacking-squares game, which is "random" in his sense but still uses arbitrary defender constraints rather than a fully representative game defense.
**Related** — [[skill-acquisition/enhancing-skill--myszka/framework--newell-interacting-constraints]] and [[skill-acquisition/enhancing-skill--myszka/framework--nonlinear-pedagogy-and-constraint-classes]] (suggested reciprocal link: "a practitioner RTP course whose practice-structure continuum this framework's representative-design view supersedes, see on-field-rtp--harries"); [[heuristic--closed-vs-open-reactivity-drill-design]]; [[framework--intensity-complexity-two-independent-axes]]

# Repeat-Sprint Interval Format for Late-Stage Fatigue Exposure
**What it is** — In the back half of late-rehab sessions, Harries introduces repeat-sprint intervals to expose the athlete to high velocity under fatigue and simulate conditioning demand alongside sprint load. The format, used across three of the four case studies: **1-2 sets of three to four repetitions over 40 m, all above 85% MV, on a 30-second rolling start** (rep 1 at 0 s, rep 2 at 30 s, rep 3 at 60 s, etc.). Case 2 used **two sets**; Cases 3 and 4 used **one set** (~21:23-21:59, ~30:49-30:58, ~40:14-40:23).
**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: placing these in the back half of the session, after other running/skill work has already introduced some fatigue, "blends" high-speed exposure with a controlled recovery interval, giving both a sprint-load-accumulation stimulus and a conditioning stimulus at once. Inference (entry writer's, not stated by Harries): this rehearses producing near-maximal velocity in a fatigued state closer to what a game actually demands late in a match.
**When to apply** — Use in the return-to-sport-phase session(s), once an athlete has already cleared the 75-85% MV gate and is accumulating >90% MV exposures elsewhere in the session (see [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]] and [[heuristic--two-exposures-above-90-percent-mv-exit-rule]]). Inference: scale the number of sets (one vs two) to the athlete's overall session load and injury type - the lower-frequency recurrent-calf case ([[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]) used only one set, though Harries does not state this as a rule.
**When NOT to apply** — This is placed deliberately late in rehab, after force-production benchmarks are already cleared; it should not be used as an early-rehab or pre-gate exposure, since it combines near-maximal velocity with accumulated fatigue, precisely the combination the earlier gate criteria are designed to screen for readiness against.
**Example** — See [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]] session 8 for the two-set version and [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]] session 10 for the one-set version used alongside a knee-joint injury.

# Running Gait Speed Categories
**What it is** — Harries defines a shared vocabulary for running speed categories, each with a km/h range and a %MV range (~00:31-01:57, confirmed Part-3.pdf p.2). The spoken audio gives most of these ranges but does not state an explicit upper bound for "running" (it says running continues "through to about 75%" and striding starts around "21, 22... through to about 27" km/h); the 20 km/h figure below comes from Part-3.pdf p.2, which states the full table explicitly:
| Category | Speed | % of max velocity |
|---|---|---|
| Walking | <6 km/h | <25% |
| Jogging | ~7-14 km/h | ~25-50% |
| Running | ~14-20 km/h | ~50-75% |
| Striding | ~21-27 km/h | ~75-85% |
| Sprinting | >27 km/h | >85% |
As speed increases, vertical ground reaction force, the rate of force application, muscle activity, and hip/knee/ankle power all increase (~02:15-02:35).
**Why it works** — This is a descriptive taxonomy of gait mechanics at increasing speed, not a claim requiring justification beyond the mechanical logic: faster locomotion demands larger forces applied in shorter ground-contact times.
**When to apply** — Use this vocabulary to translate a GPS speed-zone reading into a plain-language gait category when talking with Athletic Medicine or coaching staff, and to sanity-check whether a prescribed drill speed is actually eliciting the gait pattern intended (e.g., confirming a "striding" prescription isn't accidentally just a fast jog for a given athlete's own MV).
**When NOT to apply** — These are population-typical bin edges from Harries' AFL context, not a fixed physiological law; an individual athlete's actual transition points between jogging/running/striding/sprinting will vary with limb length, MV, and technique, so the km/h numbers should be treated as illustrative, with %MV as the more transferable anchor.
**Example** — A player with a 34.2 km/h max velocity (Harries' hamstring case-study demographic, Part 1 ~02:20-02:33) would be striding at roughly 25.5-29 km/h and sprinting above 29 km/h, meaningfully different absolute speeds than a player with a lower MV even though both are in the same %MV band.

# Running Preparation Drill Menu (Pre-Running to Level 1)
**What it is** — Before an athlete returns to actual running, Harries prescribes a menu of low-intensity drills to re-familiarize the athlete with upright-running postures and prepare tissue for repetitive loading (~03:41-08:03; confirmed Part-3.pdf p.2):
- **Dribble walks/runs** over ankle, shin and knee height - front-side mechanics focus, flat foot contact, "nothing goes out the back."
- **Dribble transitions** between ankle/shin/knee heights over 5 m segments, transitioning into a typical running gait.
- **Skipping variations**, e.g. A-skips, to add stiffness and reactivity on ground contact.
- **Low-intensity jumping**: pogos and unilateral pogos, for repetitive loading-cycle and system-stiffness preparation.
- **Scissor shuffles and scissor bounds**: aggressive hip flexion/extension, striking under center of mass, building horizontal displacement.
Basic clinical criteria (appropriate range of motion, minimal pain/swelling, sufficient local endurance/strength) plus a demonstrated ability to produce force quickly in a dynamic task and tolerate repetitive impact are the prerequisites before commencing actual running; often this is judged functionally (can they do these drills without issue) rather than via a formal test (~07:43-08:28).
**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: these drills rebuild the specific postures, coordination and ground-contact stiffness of upright running at low tissue stress before loading the same patterns at running speed, and build the athlete's confidence in the injured area.
**When to apply** — Use as the standard Level-1/pre-running menu for any lower-limb soft-tissue RTP at Baylor. Because these are low intensity, they can also stay in the warm-up throughout later on-field rehab levels, not just at the start (~07:32-07:43).
**When NOT to apply** — This is a generic menu, not tailored by injury site beyond the general logic in [[claim--ankle-then-hip-dominant-speed-mechanism]]. Do not treat "completed the drill menu" as a substitute for the actual clinical criteria (ROM, pain, strength) it is meant to sit alongside; the drills demonstrate functional tolerance, they do not replace a clinical assessment.
**Example** — Harries' hamstring case study begins on-field rehab with this drill menu before any timed running, confirming the athlete can tolerate repetitive ground contact and produce force dynamically before session 1's 60 m repeats begin (see [[heuristic--fixed-distance-timed-repeats-for-pacing]]).

# Sport-Specific Skill Drill Type, by Level
**What it is** — Harries' drill-type continuum for sport-specific technical/tactical skill work, layered on top of the intensity/complexity model (~03:14-03:52, confirmed Part-5.pdf p.2-3): Level 1 - technical skill actions performed stationary; Level 2 - technical skill actions with some low-velocity movement, still pre-planned; Level 3 - positional-specific drills, still predictable/sequenced, with limited sprinting or high-intensity multidirectional opportunity; Level 4 - positional-specific drills with an added fatigue layer, testing capacity to hold technical output under load; Level 5 - random/unpredictable, evasive and competitive drills, ideally in a modified training or small-sided-game environment, using additional players/coaches to add pressure. His hamstring case study's specific progression: Level 1, stationary technical skills only, uninjured limb only; Level 2, kicking introduced on the injured limb but still stationary/pre-planned; Level 3, positional sequences with some unpredictability, still limited sprinting; Level 4, random/unpredictable drills with added player/coach pressure; Level 5, evasive 2v1 attacking-squares (small -> medium -> large grids) and small-sided handball games with variable defensive pressure and interval length.
**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: technical/tactical execution and locomotor intensity have to be rebuilt together because neither is performed in isolation in a game; sequencing drill type, movement level and practice structure together lets both climb in a controlled, matched way rather than one racing ahead of the other.
**When to apply** — Use this level-by-level drill-type shape as the sport-skill-specific analogue to the MDSA drill menu (see [[framework--mdsa-drill-menu-by-level]]), adapted to the sport's actual technical/tactical catalogue (for football: throwing/catching/blocking/route-running rather than kicking/handballing).
**When NOT to apply** — This continuum assumes the practitioner can freely withhold or reintroduce specific skill actions by injured limb or structure (see [[principle--tailor-skill-restrictions-to-injured-structure]]); for injuries where the relevant skill action cannot be cleanly isolated by limb (e.g., a core or trunk injury affecting throwing generally), the level-by-level withholding logic needs to be rebuilt around whatever structure is actually load-bearing for that skill.
**Example** — A low-grade hamstring case completes only two additional sport-training sessions after Level 5 before return to competition; Harries states explicitly this amount of exposure is specific to a low-grade injury and "will vary significantly with other and more serious injuries" (~12:18-12:32; confirmed Part-5.pdf p.4).

# Intensity and Complexity as Two Independent Axes
**What it is** — Harries frames on-field rehab progression along two separate continuums that must both be advanced but do not have to move together. **Intensity** runs from a competency focus (reintroducing movements, building toward submaximal) to a capacity focus (submaximal through maximal, under added metabolic/mechanical demand). **Complexity** runs along what he explicitly credits as Matt Taberner's control-to-chaos continuum: control means high structure, predictable behavior/actions/movement (low risk); chaos means unpredictable, random or reactive behavior (high risk) (~04:48-08:00). Early on-field rehab levels are low-complexity and highly controlled; later levels deliberately build unpredictability. The **explicit misconception he corrects**: moving to a later on-field rehab level does not mean every drill in that level becomes more chaotic. Some locomotor actions are still climbing the intensity continuum (submaximal to maximal) and need a controlled environment even at a late stage, while other, already-developed actions can be pushed into more complex environments sooner (~08:44-09:47). By the end of on-field rehab, the target is both high intensity and high complexity simultaneously.
**Why it works** — Treating intensity and complexity as one variable causes two failure modes: pushing speed and unpredictability up together (risking a reload injury before the athlete can handle either alone), or holding both down together (leaving the athlete underprepared for the chaos of competition even though physically capable). Separating them lets a practitioner grade each independently and combine them deliberately only when both are ready.
**When to apply** — Use this distinction explicitly with Athletic Medicine and coaching staff: "he's ready for near-max speed but not yet ready for it in an unpredictable drill" is a defensible, gradeable statement under this framework, whereas "he's at level 4" alone is not. Baylor's own control-chaos foundation is Taberner's own published work already in the library (see Related). Eric's review argues Harries adds nothing new to the theory here; his contribution is packaging it with the specific %MV numbers (see [[framework--on-field-rehab-levels-with-mv-bands]]).
**When NOT to apply** — Eric's review argues the complexity axis as Harries operationalizes it rests on an older, information-processing model of motor learning (blocked-to-serial-to-random practice, described in Part 5; see [[framework--practice-structure-block-serial-random-by-level]]), not on ecological dynamics/representative learning design. Eric's review's example: Harries' "closed reactivity" is a coach throwing a hand signal - a generic, arbitrary stimulus, not the game-relevant information a player actually reads (a defender's hips, a gap opening). Harries himself names "constraints-based learning design" once, in this same module, and never operationalizes it. Eric's review argues that in this model, complexity is switched on once intensity is judged safe, while in an ecological model representative information should be present and scaled from the start, not withheld until Level 4. This is disputed by the library's ecological-dynamics sources, not a reason to discard the intensity/complexity distinction itself, which still holds and stays `supported`.
**Example** — A hamstring athlete at 82% max velocity with force benchmarks not yet cleared should still run in a controlled, closed environment even if his skill work has already moved to a positional, semi-random drill; conversely, an athlete cleared on force benchmarks but still hesitant in decision-making needs complexity pushed even at a plateaued running intensity.
**Related** — [[research-papers/taberner-2022-contextual-considerations-using-the-control-chaos-continuum-for-return-to-sport-in-elite-f]] (Taberner's own control-chaos continuum, the framework Harries is built on: suggested reciprocal link, "applied and re-dosed by a Sportsmith practitioner course, see on-field-rtp--harries"); [[research-papers/taberner-2019-physical-preparation-and-return-to-sport-of-the-football-player-with-a-tibia-fibula-fractu]]; [[skill-acquisition/enhancing-skill--myszka/framework--nonlinear-pedagogy-and-constraint-classes]] and [[skill-acquisition/enhancing-skill--myszka/principle--representative-design]] (the ecological-dynamics alternative to Harries' complexity operationalization); [[framework--practice-structure-block-serial-random-by-level]]

# Invasion-Sport Locomotor Pillars
**What it is** — Harries' starting point for building any on-field rehab process: map a sport's technical, tactical and physical domains, then simplify by using what invasion-based team sports (e.g. soccer, AFL) have in common. He uses "football" to mean soccer (Part 1 ~03:37); he never names American football or rugby specifically. Every invasion sport reduces to two tactical patterns, offense (creating space: pressing forward, overlapping, running into space; technically: moving/passing/catching the ball) and defense (closing space: covering, retreating, closing down; technically: tackling, intercepting, contesting possession) (~03:33-06:46). Underneath both are the same physical actions: sprinting, accelerating, decelerating and changing direction. He names these four as the **primary locomotor pillars of on-field rehab**, usable as a starting template "to any rehab running framework you create" regardless of sport (~07:41-08:22).
**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: the exact loading numbers differ by sport, but the actual locomotor actions "don't change too much" across invasion sports, so building a rehab framework around them is a transferable shortcut instead of having to model every sport's full technical/tactical catalogue from scratch (~07:19-07:41).
**When to apply** — Use as the skeleton for any Baylor RTP conversation with Athletic Medicine: whatever the sport or position, the questions are the same four - can this athlete sprint, accelerate, decelerate and change direction at the required intensity, in an environment as complex as competition. It gives Applied Performance and Athletic Medicine a shared, sport-agnostic starting vocabulary before adding position-specific detail (GPS zones, skill demands).
**When NOT to apply** — Harries' own case-study sport is AFL, a continuous invasion game. Two gaps matter for Baylor football specifically: (1) Eric's review: **contact is missing as a pillar.** Tackling is named (Part 1 ~06:34, "tackling of various kinds"; Part 5 ~02:03) but never given its own progression. For football, collision and contact (block, shed, tackle, hand-fight, stance start) functions as a fourth pillar with its own dosage question, and this course gives it none. (2) The four pillars are a taxonomy of locomotor actions, not a testing or clearance protocol; they tell you what to progress, not how much force production or healing time is required before progressing it (see [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]] for that layer). Do not treat "the four pillars are covered" as equivalent to "the athlete is ready."
**Example** — A returning offensive lineman needs sprint/accel/decel/COD rebuilt like any other position, but the highest-risk gap in his return is a pillar this course never names: reintroducing collision tolerance. That has to be built separately, in coordination with position coaching, not inferred from his running progression.
**Related** — [[framework--on-field-rehab-levels-with-mv-bands]] (how the levels operationalize these pillars); Baylor's own documented gap that GPS/load thresholds are not yet sport- or position-specific (`method-baseline.md`, Load monitoring and GPS).

# Multidirectional Speed & Agility Drill Menu by On-Field Rehab Level
**What it is** — Harries' worked drill menu for the hamstring case study, by level (~11:56-21:11; confirmed Part-4.pdf p.3):
- **Levels 1-2** (low intensity, low complexity): fast-easy-fast accelerations (accelerate ~5 m, ease off, re-accelerate); go-and-stop accelerations (accelerate a set distance, brake to a stop in a deceleration zone); curvy-linear ("half bend") accelerations; 30-degree cutting gates with a pre-planned side step, crossover step, or split step; a 3x3 m diamond/square drill with athlete-chosen lateral/forward/backward shuffling.
- **Level 3** (rising velocity/space, controlled/closed reactivity introduced): fast-easy-fast acceleration with a closed-reactive defender (defender moves laterally to open space); a defensive reaction (mirror) drill in a small square; a "compass drill" where the athlete pre-determines a 45/90/135-degree direction change (17:00-17:21). A separate example - a 45-degree cutting drill cued by a coach's hand signal - is what Harries uses to introduce the concept of closed reactivity (15:50-16:06); it is not the compass drill. The ~75-80% effort figure for the compass drill comes from the Case 1 worked example in Part 6, not Part 4 (Part 6, 13:52-14:01).
- **Level 4** (near-maximal velocity, bigger spaces, more open reactivity): partner chase-and-tag; a large-space gate drill with a turnover cue requiring a hard deceleration and chase; a reactive compass drill in a bigger space followed by a second reactive task (react to a rolled ball). Part 4 puts Level 4 velocity at ~80-85% (18:21-18:23); this is below the ~85-95% Level 4 band in [[framework--on-field-rehab-levels-with-mv-bands]], which is a linear-running band, not necessarily the same figure as MDSA velocity - the course does not reconcile the two numbers.
- **Level 5** (highly chaotic, near-maximal/maximal): sport-specific, competitive, multi-athlete scenarios; where extra players/coaches aren't available, use constrained drills designed to replicate unpredictability as closely as possible.
**Why it works** — Each level's drills are the concrete output of running the levers in [[framework--eight-intensity-levers-mdsa]] through the plotting exercise in [[framework--intensity-complexity-drill-plotting-tool]]: space shrinks or grows, reactivity moves from none to closed to open, and entry velocity/COD angle both rise, in a sequence matched to the level's target physical readiness.
**When to apply** — Use this menu as a starting drill bank for building a Baylor-specific version; the drill *shapes* (accelerate-then-react, gated cutting, chase-and-tag, compass drill) transfer across sports even where the specific angles or spaces would be adjusted for football positions.
**When NOT to apply** — This is one practitioner's AFL menu, built for an athlete with no contact restriction; none of these drills involve or prepare for a blocking, tackling or hand-fighting demand, so a football-specific menu needs an added contact-drill category this course does not supply (see [[framework--invasion-sport-locomotor-pillars]]). Eric's review argues the Level 3 closed-reactive cues (hand signal, mirrored defender) are generic, while later levels already add opponent- and ball-based cues (partner chase-and-tag, turnover cue, rolled ball) - see [[heuristic--closed-vs-open-reactivity-drill-design]] for the fuller critique.
**Example** — In [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]], sessions 3, 5 and 8 map closely onto this Level 1-3 / Level 3-4 / Level 4-5 menu progression.

|---|---|

| 2 | ~70-75% |
| 3 | ~75-85% |
| 4 | ~85-95% |
| 5 | >95% up to 100% |

# Block, Then Serial, Then Random Practice Across the Levels
**What it is** — Harries maps sport-specific skill drills onto a practice-structure continuum borrowed from motor-learning theory: **block practice** (the same drill repeated, low variability), **serial practice** (a known sequence of actions, predictable order), and **random practice** (unpredictable, variable order/decisions). He assigns these across levels (~04:03-07:26, confirmed Part-5.pdf p.2-3: p.2 states the general block-to-serial-to-random progression, p.3 gives the per-level breakdown): Level 1 - solely block, tightly controlled; Level 2 - still block, intensity of the drills rises; Level 3 - roughly 50/50 block and serial, chaining action sequences; Level 4 - block dropped entirely, mostly serial with some random; Level 5 - substantial random practice, with some serial retained deliberately for actions not yet ready for full unpredictability. On return to training, levels 1-2 of training itself are "pretty much all" random.
**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: block-to-serial-to-random is a graded route from fully predictable to fully unpredictable practice, which lets an athlete build a skill under low cognitive/decision load first and only add decision-making demand once the movement itself is competent.
**When to apply** — Use the general shape (predictable early, unpredictable late) as the practice-structure axis alongside drill type and movement level (see [[framework--sport-skill-drill-type-continuum-by-level]]) when designing sport-specific skill sessions.
**When NOT to apply** — **Contested.** Eric's review argues that block/serial/random and its associated "contextual interference effect" come from the Schmidt information-processing tradition of motor learning, not from ecological dynamics/representative learning design, which the library's skill-acquisition sources treat as the better-supported model for sport skill transfer. The practical difference: under an information-processing view, predictability itself is the variable being controlled, and the task's informational content is secondary; under an ecological view, the key variable is whether the *information* driving the action is representative of the game (a real defender, a real developing gap) regardless of how "predictable" the drill's structure is. A block-practice drill against a live, representative defender can be more transferable than a "random" drill built on arbitrary, non-representative cues. Do not assume moving along this block-serial-random axis is equivalent to moving toward game transfer; check whether the *information* in the drill, not just its unpredictability, is representative.
**Example** — Harries' own hamstring case study at Level 1 uses stationary, block-practiced kicking with the uninjured limb only (see [[principle--tailor-skill-restrictions-to-injured-structure]]); by Level 5 it moves to a 2v1 attacking-squares game, which is "random" in his sense but still uses arbitrary defender constraints rather than a fully representative game defense.
**Related** — [[skill-acquisition/enhancing-skill--myszka/framework--newell-interacting-constraints]] and [[skill-acquisition/enhancing-skill--myszka/framework--nonlinear-pedagogy-and-constraint-classes]] (suggested reciprocal link: "a practitioner RTP course whose practice-structure continuum this framework's representative-design view supersedes, see on-field-rtp--harries"); [[heuristic--closed-vs-open-reactivity-drill-design]]; [[framework--intensity-complexity-two-independent-axes]]

# Repeat-Sprint Interval Format for Late-Stage Fatigue Exposure
**What it is** — In the back half of late-rehab sessions, Harries introduces repeat-sprint intervals to expose the athlete to high velocity under fatigue and simulate conditioning demand alongside sprint load. The format, used across three of the four case studies: **1-2 sets of three to four repetitions over 40 m, all above 85% MV, on a 30-second rolling start** (rep 1 at 0 s, rep 2 at 30 s, rep 3 at 60 s, etc.). Case 2 used **two sets**; Cases 3 and 4 used **one set** (~21:23-21:59, ~30:49-30:58, ~40:14-40:23).
**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: placing these in the back half of the session, after other running/skill work has already introduced some fatigue, "blends" high-speed exposure with a controlled recovery interval, giving both a sprint-load-accumulation stimulus and a conditioning stimulus at once. Inference (entry writer's, not stated by Harries): this rehearses producing near-maximal velocity in a fatigued state closer to what a game actually demands late in a match.
**When to apply** — Use in the return-to-sport-phase session(s), once an athlete has already cleared the 75-85% MV gate and is accumulating >90% MV exposures elsewhere in the session (see [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]] and [[heuristic--two-exposures-above-90-percent-mv-exit-rule]]). Inference: scale the number of sets (one vs two) to the athlete's overall session load and injury type - the lower-frequency recurrent-calf case ([[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]) used only one set, though Harries does not state this as a rule.
**When NOT to apply** — This is placed deliberately late in rehab, after force-production benchmarks are already cleared; it should not be used as an early-rehab or pre-gate exposure, since it combines near-maximal velocity with accumulated fatigue, precisely the combination the earlier gate criteria are designed to screen for readiness against.
**Example** — See [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]] session 8 for the two-set version and [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]] session 10 for the one-set version used alongside a knee-joint injury.

# Running Gait Speed Categories
**What it is** — Harries defines a shared vocabulary for running speed categories, each with a km/h range and a %MV range (~00:31-01:57, confirmed Part-3.pdf p.2). The spoken audio gives most of these ranges but does not state an explicit upper bound for "running" (it says running continues "through to about 75%" and striding starts around "21, 22... through to about 27" km/h); the 20 km/h figure below comes from Part-3.pdf p.2, which states the full table explicitly:
| Category | Speed | % of max velocity |
|---|---|---|
| Walking | <6 km/h | <25% |
| Jogging | ~7-14 km/h | ~25-50% |
| Running | ~14-20 km/h | ~50-75% |
| Striding | ~21-27 km/h | ~75-85% |
| Sprinting | >27 km/h | >85% |
As speed increases, vertical ground reaction force, the rate of force application, muscle activity, and hip/knee/ankle power all increase (~02:15-02:35).
**Why it works** — This is a descriptive taxonomy of gait mechanics at increasing speed, not a claim requiring justification beyond the mechanical logic: faster locomotion demands larger forces applied in shorter ground-contact times.
**When to apply** — Use this vocabulary to translate a GPS speed-zone reading into a plain-language gait category when talking with Athletic Medicine or coaching staff, and to sanity-check whether a prescribed drill speed is actually eliciting the gait pattern intended (e.g., confirming a "striding" prescription isn't accidentally just a fast jog for a given athlete's own MV).
**When NOT to apply** — These are population-typical bin edges from Harries' AFL context, not a fixed physiological law; an individual athlete's actual transition points between jogging/running/striding/sprinting will vary with limb length, MV, and technique, so the km/h numbers should be treated as illustrative, with %MV as the more transferable anchor.
**Example** — A player with a 34.2 km/h max velocity (Harries' hamstring case-study demographic, Part 1 ~02:20-02:33) would be striding at roughly 25.5-29 km/h and sprinting above 29 km/h, meaningfully different absolute speeds than a player with a lower MV even though both are in the same %MV band.
**Related** — [[claim--ankle-then-hip-dominant-speed-mechanism]] (the mechanism behind these transitions); [[framework--on-field-rehab-levels-with-mv-bands]]

# Running Preparation Drill Menu (Pre-Running to Level 1)
**What it is** — Before an athlete returns to actual running, Harries prescribes a menu of low-intensity drills to re-familiarize the athlete with upright-running postures and prepare tissue for repetitive loading (~03:41-08:03; confirmed Part-3.pdf p.2):
- **Dribble walks/runs** over ankle, shin and knee height - front-side mechanics focus, flat foot contact, "nothing goes out the back."
- **Dribble transitions** between ankle/shin/knee heights over 5 m segments, transitioning into a typical running gait.
- **Skipping variations**, e.g. A-skips, to add stiffness and reactivity on ground contact.
- **Low-intensity jumping**: pogos and unilateral pogos, for repetitive loading-cycle and system-stiffness preparation.
- **Scissor shuffles and scissor bounds**: aggressive hip flexion/extension, striking under center of mass, building horizontal displacement.
Basic clinical criteria (appropriate range of motion, minimal pain/swelling, sufficient local endurance/strength) plus a demonstrated ability to produce force quickly in a dynamic task and tolerate repetitive impact are the prerequisites before commencing actual running; often this is judged functionally (can they do these drills without issue) rather than via a formal test (~07:43-08:28).
**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: these drills rebuild the specific postures, coordination and ground-contact stiffness of upright running at low tissue stress before loading the same patterns at running speed, and build the athlete's confidence in the injured area.
**When to apply** — Use as the standard Level-1/pre-running menu for any lower-limb soft-tissue RTP at Baylor. Because these are low intensity, they can also stay in the warm-up throughout later on-field rehab levels, not just at the start (~07:32-07:43).
**When NOT to apply** — This is a generic menu, not tailored by injury site beyond the general logic in [[claim--ankle-then-hip-dominant-speed-mechanism]]. Do not treat "completed the drill menu" as a substitute for the actual clinical criteria (ROM, pain, strength) it is meant to sit alongside; the drills demonstrate functional tolerance, they do not replace a clinical assessment.
**Example** — Harries' hamstring case study begins on-field rehab with this drill menu before any timed running, confirming the athlete can tolerate repetitive ground contact and produce force dynamically before session 1's 60 m repeats begin (see [[heuristic--fixed-distance-timed-repeats-for-pacing]]).
**Related** — [[claim--ankle-then-hip-dominant-speed-mechanism]]; [[framework--on-field-rehab-levels-with-mv-bands]]

# Sport-Specific Skill Drill Type, by Level
**What it is** — Harries' drill-type continuum for sport-specific technical/tactical skill work, layered on top of the intensity/complexity model (~03:14-03:52, confirmed Part-5.pdf p.2-3): Level 1 - technical skill actions performed stationary; Level 2 - technical skill actions with some low-velocity movement, still pre-planned; Level 3 - positional-specific drills, still predictable/sequenced, with limited sprinting or high-intensity multidirectional opportunity; Level 4 - positional-specific drills with an added fatigue layer, testing capacity to hold technical output under load; Level 5 - random/unpredictable, evasive and competitive drills, ideally in a modified training or small-sided-game environment, using additional players/coaches to add pressure. His hamstring case study's specific progression: Level 1, stationary technical skills only, uninjured limb only; Level 2, kicking introduced on the injured limb but still stationary/pre-planned; Level 3, positional sequences with some unpredictability, still limited sprinting; Level 4, random/unpredictable drills with added player/coach pressure; Level 5, evasive 2v1 attacking-squares (small -> medium -> large grids) and small-sided handball games with variable defensive pressure and interval length.
**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: technical/tactical execution and locomotor intensity have to be rebuilt together because neither is performed in isolation in a game; sequencing drill type, movement level and practice structure together lets both climb in a controlled, matched way rather than one racing ahead of the other.
**When to apply** — Use this level-by-level drill-type shape as the sport-skill-specific analogue to the MDSA drill menu (see [[framework--mdsa-drill-menu-by-level]]), adapted to the sport's actual technical/tactical catalogue (for football: throwing/catching/blocking/route-running rather than kicking/handballing).
**When NOT to apply** — This continuum assumes the practitioner can freely withhold or reintroduce specific skill actions by injured limb or structure (see [[principle--tailor-skill-restrictions-to-injured-structure]]); for injuries where the relevant skill action cannot be cleanly isolated by limb (e.g., a core or trunk injury affecting throwing generally), the level-by-level withholding logic needs to be rebuilt around whatever structure is actually load-bearing for that skill.
**Example** — A low-grade hamstring case completes only two additional sport-training sessions after Level 5 before return to competition; Harries states explicitly this amount of exposure is specific to a low-grade injury and "will vary significantly with other and more serious injuries" (~12:18-12:32; confirmed Part-5.pdf p.4).
**Related** — [[framework--practice-structure-block-serial-random-by-level]]; [[principle--tailor-skill-restrictions-to-injured-structure]]

=================== heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate.md
---
