# The 75-85% Max-Velocity Gate
**What it is** — Before progressing an athlete past roughly 75-85% of MV (Harries states the gate at "75-85%" in most places and once as "75-80%," ~13:04-16:35; the broken-stride worked example itself targets 70-75%, a step below the gate, not the gate threshold), Harries checks four things (~13:31-15:45, confirmed Part-3.pdf p.3):
1. **Time for biological healing** appropriate to the injury.
2. **Symptom response**: previous running sessions completed with minimal pain or awareness of the injured area.
3. **Force production benchmarks** in the injured area, e.g. eccentric hamstring strength via Nordic at roughly 80-85% of pre-injury baseline; seated calf isometric peak force. Harries states this two ways in the same module: as a range, "1.7 to 1.8 times body weight" (14:25-14:49), and, restated about a minute later, as a single floor, "a minimum benchmark relative to body weight such as 1.8x body weight" alongside "a minimum of 80% of pre-injury baseline outputs" for the hamstring figure (15:56-16:06). Part-3.pdf p.3 matches the floor framing for the calf number (">=1.8x bodyweight") and the range framing for the hamstring number (80-85%). Use 1.7-1.8x as the working range for the calf figure and confirm against the athlete's own baseline.
4. **Reactive strength/stretch-shortening-cycle function**, e.g. via a hopping task, to check the athlete can produce high force in a short timeframe before near-maximal speed.
The transcript checker, not Harries, marks an injury term near ~15:51 as unclear (`[injury term unclear] strain` in the source transcript); it has been left unresolved rather than guessed.
**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: "there are of course varied opinions in the field on this criteria, especially in regard to the assessment of force production capacities... it seems sensible to me and has almost zero downside" (~15:21-15:36). Eric's review classifies these as expert opinion, not trial results; Harries himself only says "varied opinions in the field," not that framing. Label them that way whenever they are used, and do not present the 80-85%, 1.7-1.8x, or hop-test criteria as validated thresholds.
**When to apply** — Eric's review judges this the single most transferable number in the course: a decision gate that Applied Performance can compute and hand to Athletic Medicine as a shared go/no-go check before a returning athlete is exposed to higher-velocity running. At Baylor, the direct instrument matches already exist, per `method-baseline.md`: NordBord hamstring eccentric testing (retained specifically for small, clinically-targeted RTP groups per Applied Performance's own documented practice, not roster-wide), the Iso Seated Calf protocol on the ForceDecks "Mid-Thigh Pull" setting (90-degree ankle/knee position, 3 x 6-second maximal contractions, 15 s rest), and the repeated-CMJ/hop protocol already run on ForceDecks (10 reps total, n=5 pairs) as the reactive-strength check. Frame every number supplied to Athletic Medicine as *supporting information*, consistent with Applied Performance's stated advisory role in RTP, not as a clearance decision.
**When NOT to apply** — Do not treat 80-85% (Nordic), 1.7-1.8x BW (calf) or "a hop test" as validated cutoffs; Harries himself flags "varied opinions in the field" on this criteria (~15:21-15:26), and Eric's review classifies them as expert-opinion/common-practice benchmarks rather than trial results. They are also AFL-context numbers; Baylor has no documented sport- or position-specific RTP force thresholds of its own yet (`method-baseline.md` names this explicitly as a gap: "no specific RTP criteria, battery, or phased-return protocol appears anywhere in this corpus"), so treat these as a starting reference to validate against Baylor's own returning-athlete data, not an imported standard.
**Example** — In [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]], the calf-specific rehab used a deliberately low running frequency (twice weekly) precisely because of concern about cumulative local fatigue to the same tissue this gate is trying to protect.
**Related** — [[strength-and-conditioning/fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--isometric-set-positions-ankle-knee-hip]] and [[strength-and-conditioning/fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/heuristic--derive-isometric-loads-from-the-push-test]] (isometric-testing methodology, suggested reciprocal link: "an RTP-specific force-benchmark application of isometric testing, see on-field-rtp--harries"); [[research-papers/wollin-2020-a-novel-hamstring-strain-injury-prevention-system-post-match-strength-testing-for-secondar]] (post-match hamstring strength testing, a closer evidence base than Harries' own citation-free benchmark); [[framework--on-field-rehab-levels-with-mv-bands]]
=================== heuristic--closed-vs-open-reactivity-drill-design.md
---
confidence: contested
---
# Closed, Then Open, Then Evasive Reactivity
**What it is** — Harries' reactivity ladder for progressing drill unpredictability: pre-planned (fully known in advance) -> closed reactivity (a single, simple cue ends the drill, e.g. a coach throwing a hand signal to cue a cut) -> open reactivity (a further task follows the first reaction, cued by a noise, another athlete, or a coach) -> evasive/competitive (genuinely live, opposed play) (~15:45-16:06, ~17:51-18:12, ~20:34-20:58).
**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: unpredictability should be added gradually, matched to the athlete's readiness, rather than jumping straight from fully controlled to fully live play.
**When to apply** — Use the four-step ladder shape (planned -> closed -> open -> evasive) as the ordering principle for adding reactivity to any drill, matched to the on-field rehab level.
**When NOT to apply** — **Contested.** Some of Harries' closed-reactive cues are arbitrary: a 45-degree cutting drill cued by a coach's hand signal (Part 4, 15:50-16:06) is his own example of closed reactivity. But his Level 3 closed-reactive drills are not limited to that: a "beat the defender" fast-easy-fast acceleration where the defender moves laterally to open space (16:16-16:34), and a defensive-reaction drill where the defender mirrors the attacking player's lateral shuffle (16:37-16:57, 17:25-17:47), already use a live opponent's movement as the cue. Eric's review argues that even these still fall short of an ecological-dynamics view of skill acquisition, which holds that the information source should be representative of the game from the start (a real defender's own decision-making, not a scripted mirror or a coach's cue) and scaled in difficulty, rather than substituted with an arbitrary cue early and only made representative once complexity is judged "safe." Read this way, Eric's review re-maps Harries' four rungs to: unopposed -> still unopposed (an arbitrary cue is not opposition) -> partly opposed -> opposed. Do not treat the hand-signal or mirror-defender drills as teaching a player anything about reading a genuinely live opponent; they add unpredictability of *timing*, not unpredictability of *information*.
**Example** — The 45-degree cutting drill in Part 4 (15:50-16:06) uses a coach's hand signal to cue the direction change - closed reactivity by Harries' own definition, but not representative of what a defender's body actually signals in a game. Contrast the compass drill in [[framework--mdsa-drill-menu-by-level]] (Level 3), where the athlete pre-determines the direction change rather than reacting to a cue at all.
**Related** — [[skill-acquisition/enhancing-skill--myszka/principle--representative-design]] and [[skill-acquisition/enhancing-skill--myszka/framework--ecological-dynamics-athlete-environment]] (suggested reciprocal link: "a practitioner course whose 'closed reactivity' concept this framework's representative-design principle directly critiques, see on-field-rtp--harries"); [[framework--intensity-complexity-two-independent-axes]]
=================== heuristic--fixed-distance-timed-repeats-for-pacing.md
---
confidence: supported
---
# Prescribe Early Running as Fixed Distance, Timed for Completion
**What it is** — Harries' preferred method for the first running sessions: pick a fixed distance (60, 80 or 100 m), and prescribe a target completion time rather than a "run at X% effort" instruction. This lets the practitioner plan the average speed exactly in advance: a 60 m repeat in 12 seconds equates to an 18 km/h average, with peak velocity typically 1-2 km/h higher, i.e. ~19-20 km/h (~09:14-09:58). His illustrative hamstring case-study sessions: **Session 1** - four reps each at 13 s, 12 s and 11 s over 60 m (~16.6, 18.0 and ~19.5 km/h average respectively), targeting 57-60% of that athlete's MV. **Session 2** - two reps each at 12 s, 11 s, 10.5 s, 10 s and 9.5 s over 60 m, targeting an average of ~22.7 km/h (22.2-24 km/h, ~66-69% MV) (~09:14-11:48).
**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: fixed-distance/timed prescription removes ambiguity about what speed the athlete actually ran, lets the practitioner plan the session's target speed ahead of time, and (with progressively increasing speed within a session) lets the athlete build confidence and learn what a given speed feels like across repetitions before being asked to hit it cold.
**When to apply** — Use for the early on-field rehab levels (submaximal running, roughly up to 70-75% MV) where steady-state pacing rather than acceleration/deceleration mechanics is the goal. It requires only a stopwatch and a measured distance, so it needs no GPS or video technology, though GPS can be layered on for confirmation.
**When NOT to apply** — Once an athlete is running above ~70-75% of MV, Harries himself moves away from full-distance timed repeats toward broken-stride timing over just the middle phase (see [[framework--broken-stride-timing-protocol]]); his own stated reason is that he would "move away from steady state running efforts" at that point (~16:38-16:46). Inference (entry writer's, not stated by Harries): a single time-for-completion over the whole distance conflates acceleration, top-speed and deceleration into one number and stops being precise enough to control intensity at higher speeds.
**Example** — See the worked session-1/session-2 numbers above; per-case variations of the same method appear in [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]] (100 m repeats at 22-26 s, ~14-16 km/h in early sessions) and [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]] (two sets of eight 100 m repeats at 14-16 then 16-18 km/h).
**Related** — [[framework--broken-stride-timing-protocol]]
=================== heuristic--hesitation-signals-unready-but-is-unmeasured.md
---
confidence: untested
---
# Confidence and Willingness Under Competitive Pressure Is Required, But Unmeasured
**What it is** — Harries requires the athlete to show restored ability, confidence and willingness to choose the right action under competitive pressure, for example "not hesitating to accelerate through a gap in the defence" (Part 2, 10:08-10:20, and see [[principle--competitive-exposure-required-before-return-to-play]]). This is stated as a positive requirement to demonstrate, not as a named disqualifying red flag; hesitation is his example of what failing to meet it would look like. He never gives a way to observe, score or record it.
**Why it works** — Harries offers no mechanism, only the assertion. It is plausible on its face: hesitation under pressure plausibly reflects unresolved fear-avoidance or a lack of trust in the injured tissue. But plausibility is not the same as a defined, repeatable observation.
**When to apply** — Eric's review flags this as a real, named criterion the course itself cannot defend to an objective audience, and treats it as a legitimate prompt to look for a way to operationalize "hesitation" (a success-rate threshold on a drill, a scripted-start/live-finish task design, video-coded decision latency) rather than to rely on a coach's unaided impression. This course supplies none of those tools itself.
**When NOT to apply** — Do not write "athlete showed no hesitation" into a Baylor RTP note as if it were a measured criterion on par with the % MV or force benchmarks in [[heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]]. It is currently an unvalidated, single-observer judgment call with no defined pass/fail rule, exactly the kind of subjective criterion the 75-85% gate's objective benchmarks were designed to avoid relying on alone.
**Example** — Two athletes both clear their force benchmarks and %MV targets; one accelerates confidently through a small-sided game gap, the other visibly slows and checks his own leg before committing. Under this criterion the second athlete would not yet meet the requirement, but the course gives no rule for how many hesitant reps, or what kind, would actually hold up a return decision.
**Related** — [[principle--competitive-exposure-required-before-return-to-play]]
=================== heuristic--linear-then-undulating-mv-progression.md
---
confidence: supported
---
# Progress Max Velocity Linearly, Then Undulate Near 80-85%
**What it is** — Harries' default periodization for max-velocity exposure across sessions: increase speed session-on-session in a linear fashion through the early-to-mid part of rehab, then shift to an undulating pattern (down, up, sometimes down and back up to hold a level) once the athlete approaches roughly 80-85% of MV (~21:17-22:50; confirmed Part-3.pdf p.3). His illustrative hamstring case goes linear through session 5 (50-60% -> 65-70% -> 75-80% -> 85% -> ~90-92% of MV), pushed further into the linear zone than typical (up to 90-92%) because of time pressure toward a 3-4 week return, then brings intensity down before the next jump.
**Why it works** — Harries gives the reasoning in two places. In Part 3, he says linear progression through early rehab is "quite normal and quite appropriate," and how long to stay linear before undulating "really depends on the context of the injury, how severe it was and the length of time that someone's spending in each of these on-field rehab levels" (~22:37-22:50) - a context-dependency statement, not a mechanistic one. In Part 6 (Case 1, session 6 undulation), he gives the more concrete reason: shifting to undulating "manages fatigue and the frequency of those exposures" to higher velocities (~06:43-06:46). Inference (entry writer's elaboration, not stated this way by Harries): near 80-85% MV, sessions get close enough to true maximal effort that repeating high-intensity exposures session after session could accumulate fatigue and reload risk faster than the tissue can adapt.
**When to apply** — Use linear progression as the default through on-field rehab levels 1-3 (up to ~75-85% MV), then switch to an undulating high/low pattern from roughly level 3-4 onward. How long to stay linear (and how far past 85% to push before undulating) is explicitly context-dependent on time pressure, injury severity and history, not fixed.
**When NOT to apply** — Not every case in Harries' own material follows this pattern: [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] built linearly for its first four sessions, then ran flat above 90% MV in every session from session 4 onward, with no undulating pattern, because the low running frequency (twice weekly) meant every session was already spaced far enough apart to serve as its own recovery. Do not apply the linear-then-undulate default mechanically without checking whether session frequency already provides the recovery spacing undulation is meant to create.
**Example** — Contrast [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]] and [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]] (both undulated from around session 6) against [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] (linear for four sessions, then flat above 90% MV, by design of its reduced frequency, not by undulation).
**Related** — [[heuristic--two-exposures-above-90-percent-mv-exit-rule]]
=================== heuristic--low-speed-threshold-inflates-hsr-totals.md
---
confidence: supported
---
# A Low High-Speed-Running Threshold Can Inflate Totals
**What it is** — Harries' organization set high-speed running (HSR) at >17 km/h, very-high-speed running (VHSR) at >23 km/h, and sprint at >27 km/h (~09:57-10:17), and he notes 17 km/h is only roughly 55-60% of max velocity for these AFL athletes (~22:54-23:11). Because the HSR cutoff sits at a relatively low %MV, a rep or drill that only briefly crosses it can register as a full HSR exposure and inflate the session or weekly total, even though the athlete never approached a meaningful intensity. This happened twice in his four cases: an unexpected HSR overshoot in [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]] session 2 (100 m repeats), and an unplanned overshoot in [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]] session 4.
**Why it works** — A fixed absolute speed threshold (km/h) captures a different %MV for every athlete and, within one athlete, becomes an easier bar to clear (relatively) than a %MV-based threshold would be, so longer-distance reps or drills with any build-up phase are especially prone to briefly crossing a low absolute cutoff without the practitioner intending a high-speed exposure.

# Prescribe Early Running as Fixed Distance, Timed for Completion
**What it is** — Harries' preferred method for the first running sessions: pick a fixed distance (60, 80 or 100 m), and prescribe a target completion time rather than a "run at X% effort" instruction. This lets the practitioner plan the average speed exactly in advance: a 60 m repeat in 12 seconds equates to an 18 km/h average, with peak velocity typically 1-2 km/h higher, i.e. ~19-20 km/h (~09:14-09:58). His illustrative hamstring case-study sessions: **Session 1** - four reps each at 13 s, 12 s and 11 s over 60 m (~16.6, 18.0 and ~19.5 km/h average respectively), targeting 57-60% of that athlete's MV. **Session 2** - two reps each at 12 s, 11 s, 10.5 s, 10 s and 9.5 s over 60 m, targeting an average of ~22.7 km/h (22.2-24 km/h, ~66-69% MV) (~09:14-11:48).
**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: fixed-distance/timed prescription removes ambiguity about what speed the athlete actually ran, lets the practitioner plan the session's target speed ahead of time, and (with progressively increasing speed within a session) lets the athlete build confidence and learn what a given speed feels like across repetitions before being asked to hit it cold.
**When to apply** — Use for the early on-field rehab levels (submaximal running, roughly up to 70-75% MV) where steady-state pacing rather than acceleration/deceleration mechanics is the goal. It requires only a stopwatch and a measured distance, so it needs no GPS or video technology, though GPS can be layered on for confirmation.
**When NOT to apply** — Once an athlete is running above ~70-75% of MV, Harries himself moves away from full-distance timed repeats toward broken-stride timing over just the middle phase (see [[framework--broken-stride-timing-protocol]]); his own stated reason is that he would "move away from steady state running efforts" at that point (~16:38-16:46). Inference (entry writer's, not stated by Harries): a single time-for-completion over the whole distance conflates acceleration, top-speed and deceleration into one number and stops being precise enough to control intensity at higher speeds.

# Progress Max Velocity Linearly, Then Undulate Near 80-85%
**What it is** — Harries' default periodization for max-velocity exposure across sessions: increase speed session-on-session in a linear fashion through the early-to-mid part of rehab, then shift to an undulating pattern (down, up, sometimes down and back up to hold a level) once the athlete approaches roughly 80-85% of MV (~21:17-22:50; confirmed Part-3.pdf p.3). His illustrative hamstring case goes linear through session 5 (50-60% -> 65-70% -> 75-80% -> 85% -> ~90-92% of MV), pushed further into the linear zone than typical (up to 90-92%) because of time pressure toward a 3-4 week return, then brings intensity down before the next jump.

**When NOT to apply** — Not every case in Harries' own material follows this pattern: [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] built linearly for its first four sessions, then ran flat above 90% MV in every session from session 4 onward, with no undulating pattern, because the low running frequency (twice weekly) meant every session was already spaced far enough apart to serve as its own recovery. RTP for this case was day 44 - the second-longest of the four cases, after Case 4's 49 days - and one week of that was a deliberate delay by the medical/performance team specifically to add training exposure, not a consequence of the reduced running frequency itself (see [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]).
**Example** — See [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] for the full case; contrast with [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]]'s six sessions across roughly the same number of weeks as this case's five sessions across a longer span.

# Sequence Interval Length by Which Tissue Is Injured
**What it is** — Across the four case studies, Harries used two different interval-length sequencing strategies depending on injury type. Harries says hamstring rehab "might more commonly" use a **long-to-short** approach (starting with longer repeats, e.g. 100 m, and moving toward shorter, faster efforts) "to control speed" (~31:59-32:04); Cases 1 and 2 (proximal hamstring, semimembranosus/adductor) both started with 100 m repeats before moving to 60 m work, consistent with this. The recurrent calf case ([[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]) deliberately used the opposite, a **short-to-long** model: beginning with 60 m repeats (10-12 s efforts) and progressing to longer intervals (100 m repeats at 20-24 s, then 40 s and 60 s intervals), explicitly to control the calf's cumulative local-fatigue exposure early (~31:41-32:04).
**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: the calf contributes disproportionately to running mechanics at all speeds (not just top speed), so short, well-spaced efforts early minimize repetitive local loading to the injured structure while still allowing systemic running-mechanics practice; longer intervals are then added once tolerance is established. For the hamstring, his stated rationale is narrower: a long-to-short approach is used "to control speed" (~32:04).
**When to apply** — When designing early on-field rehab running volume, consider the injured tissue's loading profile (does it load more with repetition frequency, as with calf, or more with peak intensity, as with hamstring at high speed) and choose interval length progression accordingly, rather than defaulting to one fixed sequencing rule for every lower-limb injury.
**When NOT to apply** — This is drawn from only two data points (one calf case, two hamstring cases) inside one practitioner's own case selection; Harries never states it as a general rule, and this entry infers the generalization from the pattern across his four cases. Treat it as a hypothesis worth testing against Baylor's own case data, not an established principle.
**Example** — Contrast [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]]'s 60m-then-100m-then-longer intervals against [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]]'s early use of 100 m repeats before moving to faster 60 m work. [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]] does not fit this contrast cleanly: its session 3 used 100 m repeats and its session 5 used longer 400 m repeats before returning to 60 m strides, a short-to-long sequence within a knee (not hamstring or calf) case.
**Related** — [[heuristic--reduce-frequency-for-recurrent-calf-injury]]

---
confidence: contested

# At Least One, Ideally Two, Exposures Above 90% MV Before Return
**What it is** — Harries' exit rule for on-field rehab: before returning an athlete to training or play, he wants at least one, ideally two, exposures above 90% of MV (~23:24-24:41). He is explicit there is no universal number: "I can't tell you whether you need to do one, two, or seven. That's entirely dependent on the injury... your organisational culture, your philosophy at your club... the history of that player and their soft tissue history... the pressure in that time of year." The one firm line he draws: he cannot imagine returning an athlete to training, and certainly not to play, without at least one, probably two, exposures above 90%.
**Why it works** — Inference (entry writer's rationale, not stated this way by Harries in Part 3): exposures near true maximal velocity load the tissue in a way that submaximal running does not rehearse, so returning without ever having approached game-realistic top speed leaves an unrehearsed gap between rehab and competition, regardless of how much submaximal volume was accumulated.
**When to apply** — Use as a floor, not a target: before clearing a returning athlete, confirm at least one (preferably two) session exposures above 90% of that athlete's own MV have been logged and tolerated without a negative symptom response. Track exposures explicitly per athlete rather than assuming volume accumulated lower down the intensity scale is an adequate substitute.
**When NOT to apply** — This is expert opinion/common practice, not a validated cutoff. Of Harries' four case studies, only [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]] returned with zero exposures above 90% (external season-timing pressure); [[case-study--mcl-sprain-meniscal-case-4-afl]] returned with one, meeting Harries' stated floor of "at least one but probably two," though he "would have preferred a second." Inference (entry writer's, drawn from the case pattern; Harries himself does not say this): do not treat missing this exit rule as an automatic hold on return, since Case 1 returned to play regardless of missing the floor entirely. But Harries' own firm line is narrower than that: "I can't imagine a situation where I'd want to put an athlete back into training... if they haven't achieved at least one but probably two exposures above that 90% plus" (~24:27-24:41) - Case 1 is the exception to his own stated position, not an endorsement of skipping it. Also do not assume "90% of max velocity" is the same absolute speed across sports or positions; it must be computed from the athlete's own MV, and Baylor's own GPS/max-velocity pipeline (Catapult/OpenField) is the source for that number, not a generic AFL threshold.
**Example** — [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]] is the opposite case: because that athlete's low running frequency meant every late session ran near-maximal, he accumulated six separate exposures above 90% MV before return, far more than the stated floor, illustrating that the number is a byproduct of the chosen periodization, not a targeted count.
**Related** — [[framework--on-field-rehab-levels-with-mv-bands]]; [[heuristic--linear-then-undulating-mv-progression]]

=================== principle--framework-is-a-guide-not-a-protocol.md
---

---
# A Framework Is a Guide, Not a Protocol
**What it is** — Harries lists four reasons to build an on-field rehab framework rather than freelance each case: (1) it acts as a guardrail against progressing an athlete too fast into a negative reloading response or recurrence; (2) aligning it to the sport's actual performance requirements improves an athlete's preparedness on return; (3) it stays flexible enough to individualize the rehab, because "it can't be too rigid... a framework for me would be a guide, not a step-by-step process"; (4) it creates efficiency and consistency in programming and in-the-moment decisions, which in his experience raises trust between practitioner and athlete (~00:39-02:01).
**Why it works** — Harries' rationale: a framework externalizes the decision logic (what to progress, in what order, under what conditions) so decisions under time pressure are faster and more defensible, without pretending every case fits the same fixed sequence.
**When to apply** — Use this as the pitch for why Applied Performance should hand Athletic Medicine a shared decision structure (levels, gates, exit criteria) rather than case-by-case verbal negotiation each time an athlete nears return. It is also the justification for building the framework at all, before any of the specific numbers below.
**When NOT to apply** — A framework that hardens into a fixed protocol defeats its own stated purpose. If Applied Performance builds phased levels and % MV gates for Baylor, they need to stay adjustable to injury severity, athlete history, season timing and organizational culture, per Harries' own repeated point in the exit-rule discussion (see [[heuristic--two-exposures-above-90-percent-mv-exit-rule]]) that he can't say "whether you need to do one, two, or seven" exposures (~23:55-23:59) - that answer is context-dependent, not fixed by the framework.
**Example** — A hamstring case and a recurrent calf case in Part 6 used the same levels and pillars but different session frequencies, interval formats and undulation patterns because of different injury histories (see [[case-study--recurrent-lateral-soleus-strain-case-3-afl]], calf, vs [[case-study--proximal-hamstring-strain-case-1-afl]], hamstring); the framework held, the prescription did not.
**Related** — [[framework--intensity-complexity-two-independent-axes]]
=================== principle--intensity-levers-interact-not-independent.md
---
confidence: supported
---
# The Intensity Levers Interact, They Don't Adjust Independently
**What it is** — Harries stresses that the eight (or four, coarser-grain) intensity levers for multidirectional speed and agility work "don't operate independently... changing one factor can actually have an impact on another factor." His examples: raising the magnitude of acceleration (velocity-change lever) forces a higher entry velocity into the following decel/COD; shrinking the available space "constrain[s] the approach velocity into a deceleration or change direction" (~07:45-08:29). He does not himself draw out the further complexity-side implication of the space example in this passage.
**Why it works** — The levers describe one interconnected physical system (an athlete's momentum and the space/time they have to change it), not eight separate knobs; pulling one necessarily moves at least one other, so treating them as independent will produce drills whose actual difficulty doesn't match what was intended.
**When to apply** — When designing or auditing a drill, always ask which other levers a given change will move, not just the one being adjusted. Eric's review's reading of the counterintuitive case: shrinking a grid's size can *lower* the intensity of a cut (because it caps entry velocity) while simultaneously *raising* its complexity (because it now demands tighter spatial and decision-making precision) - intensity and complexity moving in opposite directions from the same manipulation.
**When NOT to apply** — Do not use this as an excuse to avoid the intensity/complexity plotting exercise in [[framework--intensity-complexity-drill-plotting-tool]]; the interactions are real but the plotting tool is specifically designed to let a practitioner reason about the net effect after accounting for them, rather than being defeated by the complexity of tracking every lever separately.
**Example** — A 3x3 m diamond-drill grid used at low intensity in early on-field rehab (see [[framework--mdsa-drill-menu-by-level]]) constrains approach velocity by space alone, which is why it can safely be introduced early even though lateral shuffling and direction changes are technically "COD" work.
**Related** — [[framework--eight-intensity-levers-mdsa]]
=================== principle--percent-of-game-value-as-volume-metric.md
---
confidence: supported
---
# Track Running Volume as a Percent of Game Value
**What it is** — Rather than reporting HSR/VHSR/sprint volumes as raw meters, Harries tracks and reports them as a **percent of game value** for the metric, session by session: e.g. "VHSR peaked at 86% of game value by day 21," "sprint exposure... maybe around 50-60% of game demands," "session 8 peaked at 120% of game value" (Case 1 and 2, throughout Part 6). Harries uses "game value," "game demands," "game volume" and "match load" without ever defining the denominator; the course does not say whether it is the athlete's own historical GPS average, a club/position norm, or something else. Part 1's case-study demographic gives one athlete's per-game numbers as an example of the kind of figure a game-demand benchmark would draw on (~13 km total distance, ~1000 m HSR, ~200 m VHSR, 40-50 accels/decels per game, 34.2 km/h MV, ~02:20-02:49), but the course never states that this is how the "% of game value" denominator in the case studies was actually built.
**Why it works** — An absolute meters figure means nothing without a denominator; normalizing to "% of what this specific athlete actually does in a game" makes progress legible across the whole rehab (is this session under-, on-, or over-dosed relative to competition) and comparable across sessions and cases despite different absolute demands per position or per athlete.
**When to apply** — Build every RTP running report at Baylor around a %-of-game-value normalization so a session reads as under-, on-, or over-dosed relative to competition, rather than as a raw distance. The existing Baylor velocity-band sheet lists each position group's game averages; a per-player %-of-game-value line for a specific returning athlete is a later piece still to be built (Review and Plan, sections 3-4), not something the current sheet already reports.
**When NOT to apply** — This metric is only as good as the game-average baseline it's normalized against; a baseline built from too few games, an unrepresentative sample (e.g., mostly blowout or short-rotation games), or the wrong position comparison will distort every subsequent % figure. It is also an AFL-cohort practice built on a continuous, high-running sport; Baylor football is intermittent and position-specific, so the same %-of-game-value logic transfers, but the underlying km/h zone definitions and accel/decel counts have to be re-derived per position from Baylor's own GPS, not copied from AFL norms. Eric's review: many linemen, for instance, may rarely or never reach a comparable sprint-zone speed in a game at all, which would make a raw %-of-game-value sprint figure close to meaningless for that position without checking the baseline first.
**Example** — See [[case-study--semimembranosus-adductor-strain-case-2-afl]], where the same session (session 8) simultaneously showed a 120%-of-game-value peak in VHSR/sprint alongside a lower isolated-MDSA volume - both numbers only interpretable relative to that athlete's own game baseline.
**Related** — [[heuristic--low-speed-threshold-inflates-hsr-totals]]; [[claim--speed-threshold-percent-of-max-velocity-conversion]]
=================== principle--tailor-skill-restrictions-to-injured-structure.md
---
confidence: supported
---
# Withhold Sport Skills by Which Structure They Load, Not by Level Alone
**What it is** — Harries tailors sport-specific skill drills to the specific injured structure, not just to the generic level number. In his hamstring case: at Level 1, kicking is withheld entirely on the injured limb (only the uninjured limb performs stationary technical actions); at Level 2, kicking is reintroduced on the injured limb but kept stationary and pre-planned (~08:16-08:50). The general logic: identify which specific technical action loads the injured tissue, and progress that action's introduction on its own timeline distinct from the general level progression.
**Why it works** — A generic level-based progression ("Level 2 = some movement") would not by itself capture that kicking loads the hamstring specifically; withholding by structure adds a second, injury-specific axis to the generic drill-type continuum in [[framework--sport-skill-drill-type-continuum-by-level]].
**When to apply** — For any RTP case, identify up front which specific sport skills load the injured structure (kicking for a hamstring/hip flexor; throwing for a shoulder/elbow; blocking or a three-point stance for a knee or ankle) and build a separate withhold-then-reintroduce timeline for that specific action, layered on top of the general level progression.
**When NOT to apply** — This only works cleanly when a skill action can be isolated to one limb or structure. Bilateral or trunk-driven skills (a quarterback's throwing motion after a core or oblique strain, a lineman's stance after a hip injury) don't decompose this cleanly into "injured-limb version withheld, uninjured-limb version allowed," so the isolation logic needs to be rebuilt case-by-case rather than assumed.
**Example** — A returning kicker/punter with a hamstring strain would follow this exact logic: stationary technical work with the uninjured limb only at Level 1 (not full participation in every drill), with kicking itself withheld until Level 2 and only reintroduced stationary at first.
**Related** — [[framework--sport-skill-drill-type-continuum-by-level]]

- **`framework--sport-skill-drill-type-continuum-by-level`: correct.** The Example timestamp 12:18-12:32 matches "they would return to training and complete a further two sessions … will vary significantly with other and more serious injuries". - Non-blocking: in linear-then-undulating When NOT, label the recovery-spacing cause as inference, as the Case 3 entry already does.

**Not yet PROMOTE. Promote after 6 one-line edits.** These are the remaining blockers:
